docs.text:
Each bullet records a later check of a first-round entry. It overrides the mark in the first-round row.

Verification of first-round sources

  • [40] Hilton & Gao, "Measuring Goodhart's law" (OpenAI) [text] -> [seen]. The live page returns 403. The Wayback snapshot of 2022-04-13 (/blog/ URL) has the full text and only one chart (div#webgpt-chart), drawn at load time by Observable notebook d/801bb307960c00df from a GitHub gist of data. I rendered the original notebook code and data in headless Chrome (oai_chart.png). It shows: title "Best-of-n performance for WebGPT 175B"; x = "KL from original (nats)", square-root scale, 0 to about 3.2, with a second axis n = 1, 4, 16, 64; y = "Preference to original", 50 % to 70 %. There are three rising lines with ±1 SE bands: training RM, validation RM, human preference. All reach about 68 % at n = 64. Human preference stays flat from n = 4 to n = 16 (about 62 %). There is no hump and no fall. The caption says "There isn't much over-optimization... we would expect there to be at higher KLs." Note: this is a re-render from OpenAI's own notebook and data, not the static image they served. Closeness: medium -> low–medium. Proxy and true are both on y against KL, and no divergence is shown. URLs: https://web.archive.org/web/20220413184222/https://openai.com/blog/measuring-goodharts-law/ ; https://api.observablehq.com/d/801bb307960c00df.js?v=3 . The 2023 /research/ snapshots exist in the CDX index. I did not open them, because the 2022 snapshot already gave the chart source.
  • [4] Baker 1992 (JPE) [not opened] -> [not opened]. I found no open-access version. OpenAlex has no OA location; Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429; IDEAS has no download; I found no NBER working paper with this title. The citing working papers I opened do not reproduce a Baker figure. Rating unchanged (medium, dual space, from Gibbons Fig. 3).
  • [5] Baker 2002 (JHR) [not opened] -> [not opened]. The only OA link is the JSTOR pdfplus/3069615, which needs a login. I found no author PDF or course-note copy of the figure. Rating unchanged.
  • Feltham & Xie 1994 (Accounting Review) [not opened] -> [not opened]. No OA copy. Thiele 2007 [N2] and the papers that build on Feltham & Xie use the same congruity-angle picture in effort space (see the new row).
  • Datar, Kulp & Lambert 2001 (JAR) [not opened] -> [not opened]. No OA location in OpenAlex; a web search found no PDF.
  • [65] Bevan & Hood 2006 [snippet] -> [snippet]. LSE Research Online (eprint 16211) says "Full text not available from this repository." Wiley returns 403. Rating unchanged (low; no axes known).
  • [68] Hood 2006 (PAR) [snippet] -> [snippet]. Wiley PDF returns 403. No OA location.
  • [66] Smith 1995 [snippet] -> [snippet]. No OA location (Taylor & Francis).
  • Courty & Marschke 2004 (JOLE) [not opened] -> [not opened]. OpenAlex points to CORE 41100428, but the page has no download link. IDEAS (Albany WP 02-06) says "not available for download". The CEPR DP3164 page was not tried for a PDF.
  • [33] Fleming & DeMets 1996 original [seen†] via slides -> [seen] via slides; the original is still [not opened] (Annals returns 403). DeMets slide 6 (demets-06.png), "Reasons for failure of surrogate end points", has four time-flow diagrams (Disease → Surrogate → True clinical outcome, with an Intervention node): A, the surrogate is not in the causal pathway; B, the intervention acts only through the surrogate pathway of several; C, the intervention bypasses the surrogate; D, the intervention acts by mechanisms independent of the disease (dotted). There are no axes. Rating unchanged (low).
  • [93] VanderWeele 2013 [not opened] -> [seen] (PMC4221255, author manuscript). Fig. 1 (a, b): DAGs A → S → Y with a dashed direct A → Y arrow, and with an unmeasured U → S, U → Y. Fig. 2: an A → Y path that does not pass through S. Fig. 3: S has no effect on Y, and U confounds S and Y. These are DAGs only, with no axes. Rating: none (no plane). It is a causal-Goodhart typology for surrogates, the same family as Manheim & Garrabrant [15]. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4221255/
  • [28] Buyse et al. 2000 original [seen] slide; paper [not opened] -> unchanged. OUP returns 403 and there is no OA location.
  • Zöllner & Pritchard 2007 (AJHG) [not opened] -> [seen] (PMC1852705). Fig. 1: x = three power classes (low 0.03, moderate 0.54, high 0.97); y = "Additive effect". For each class there are 100 significant studies: uncorrected estimates (diamonds), ascertainment-corrected estimates (circles), replication (squares), a horizontal line for the true parameter, and bars for the averages. At low power, the uncorrected estimates (about 0.074) sit far above the true value (about 0.042). The correction brings them back to the true value but with a wide spread. This is the winner's curse drawn as estimate against truth, with a mitigation (correction) in the same panel. Closeness: medium (estimate and true value on the same y axis, stratified by power; not an x–y plane). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1852705/
  • Capen, Clapp & Campbell 1971 (JPT) [not opened] -> [not opened]. OnePetro returns 403. I found no OA copy or reproduction of the figure.
  • Harrison & March 1984 (ASQ) [not opened] -> [not opened]. No OA copy found.
  • Brown 1974 [not opened] -> [not opened]. I could not resolve the exact DOI (my guess resolved to a different 1974 paper). No copy found.
  • [73] "Optimizing the score, losing sight of the task: Reward hacking across weights, selection, and prompts" [text] -> [seen]. Author (arXiv metadata, citation_author): Vansh Wahi, a single author. Submitted 2026-09-22. Fig. 1 (a73_fig1.png): x = "Optimization pressure"; y = "Reward (schematic)". A dashed proxy-reward line rises linearly. A solid "True task quality" curve rises, peaks at a dotted vertical line labelled "Task quality peaks", then falls below its starting value. The caption calls it an illustrative pattern, not data. Closeness unchanged (medium; it is the Gao-style hump against pressure). https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25848
  • [74] "Inference-time reward hacking in large language models" (authors not verified) -> authors verified: Hadi Khalaf, Claudio Mayrink Verdun, Alex Oesterling, Himabindu Lakkaraju, Flavio du Pin Calmon (arXiv v1 2025-06-24; revised 2025-11-04). Fig. 1 [seen]; see new Q1 row N1. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19248
  • [96] Armstrong, "When Goodharting is optimal" [text] -> [seen]. The post has five Dropbox images: a 3-cell robot grid (L, centre, R); a 2×3 grid with cells L, R, L_R, R_L ("gains from trade"); a "losses from trade" grid; and two Pareto-frontier plots on unlabelled unit axes (one concave "rounded" frontier; one "spiky" piecewise-linear frontier below a dashed straight chord). The axes are the values of two candidate reward functions, not proxy against true. Closeness: medium -> low.
  • [22] Kaarbøe & Olsen 2006, Fig. 1 [text] -> [seen] (PDF p. 31). Two-dimensional effort space with axes labelled "f1, k1, g1" and "f2, k2, g2". The value vector is f = (1, 1); the measure vectors are g = (0, g2) (vertical) and k = (k1, 0) (horizontal). Each measure captures one task, and neither is aligned with f. Rating unchanged (medium, dual space).
  • [41] Coste et al. 2023 [text] -> [seen] (BoN figure, bon_scores_44m_46k.png). x = KL divergence (0 to about 8.3); left y = gold score (solid lines); right y = proxy score (dashed lines). There are four RM types: single RM, mean, WCO, UWO λ = 0.5. Proxy rises for all of them. Gold for the single RM flattens at about 0.66, while gold for the ensembles keeps rising to about 0.83–0.87. Fig. 1 is a pipeline diagram. Rating unchanged (medium).
  • [42] Eisenstein et al. 2023, Fig. 1 [text] -> [seen]. This is not a plot. It shows two real response cards with five RM scores each: on the left, the ensemble works (mean −0.40 ≈ true r −1.13); on the right, it fails (all five RMs are positive, +1.89 to +2.83, printed mean +2.31, against r −1.04). It shows the mitigation and its failure for one mitigation (ensembles), as cards, not on a plane. This is relevant to our pessimistic-ensemble "fails when" card. Rating unchanged.
  • [29] Daniels & Hughes 1997, Fig. 1 [seen†] -> [seen] (PDF p. 9). x = "difference in mean change in CD4 count (cells/mm^3)", −50 to 100; y = "log hazard ratio for AIDS/Death", −3 to 2. One confidence ellipse per trial, labelled "a" (active-controlled) or "p" (placebo-controlled), with crosshairs at 0. There is no fitted line and no diagonal. Rating unchanged (high).
  • [39] Stiennon et al. 2020, Fig. 5 [seen†] -> [seen] (PDF p. 8). x = KL from the supervised baseline (0 to 250, nonlinear ticks); y = fraction preferred to reference. "RM prediction" (dashed) rises to about 1.0. "Actual preference" (solid) peaks at about 0.47 near KL 10–25 and falls to about 0.1 at KL 250. Rating unchanged (medium).
  • [21] Zhuang & Hadfield-Menell 2020, Fig. 2 [seen†] -> [seen] (PDF p. 5). Left: x = iterations; y = utility change; proxy utility rises to about 12; true utility rises to about 1.5, then falls below 0 near iteration 140. Right: true utility for six proxy-attribute pairs (A,B … C,D); every one peaks, then goes negative. Rating unchanged (medium).
  • [47] Everitt et al. 2021 [seen†] -> [seen] (PDF pp. 10, 12). Fig. 5a: a causal influence diagram with nodes Θ*R, Θ1R–Θ3R, S1–S3, A1–A2, R1–R3; the red path A1 → Θ2R → R2 marks the tampering incentive. Fig. 5b: the rocks-and-diamonds grid. Fig. 6: a two-agent CID for TI-considering current-RF optimization, with red paths showing the instrumental goal to influence Θ2R. This confirms that the report row is correct.

docs.title: (e) What is still distinctive about our figure
docs.text:
Stated carefully. Each claim is bounded by what the search covered (English-language web; arXiv; LW/AF; the fields listed in (c)).

  1. Expanded synthesis. Fifteen panels use a consistent visual vocabulary, drawing on prior panels and mitigation figures. The shared canvas itself is not a novelty claim.
  2. Reference-relative quadrants. The chosen labels are teaching devices. Harmful transitions can lie outside the lower-right quadrant, and quadrant membership changes with the reference.
  3. Optimization pressure. Rightward pressure describes the objective, not monotonic motion of training runs. Arrow directions do not identify mechanisms.
  4. Four mitigations and their assumptions. Learning graders, KL regularization, quantilization and ensembles are presented with limitations. Obfuscation is a failure mode. Prior art already depicts mitigation failures, notably Armstrong [10], the quantilizer limits in Demski & Garrabrant [2] and, outside AI, Deming's funnel [G1].
  5. Explanations and investigations. Cards describe mechanisms and the tables suggest investigations, without treating observed shapes as sufficient diagnoses.
  6. The Baker mapping. In a linear effort model, a feasible change d maps to (g·d, f·d). This describes differences, and its interpretation depends on feasible directions. The search did not establish novelty of this elementary map.

Do not claim: - "First proxy-versus-true plane": false ([12] 1939; [1] 2018). - "First to draw the four variants on proxy-versus-value axes": false ([1]). - "First to draw a mitigation on the plane": false ([3] [10]; [1] quantilizer). - "First Goodhart taxonomy with per-entry figures": false ([47] has one CID per entry; [45] has three sketches).

Second-round additions to "Do not claim": - "First to use a calibrated diagonal": false ([F1] 2019 and the ML-evaluation literature; [S6] 2011). - "First to name the lower-right region" or "first named quadrants": false ([A1] 2026; [S1]). - "First to plot changes from a reference policy": false ([A1]; [S3]). - "First to state the push-right rule": false in words ([F4] 2019); the arrow form for all variants was not found. - "First catalogue with a failure condition per mitigation": false outside AI (bow-tie degradation factors [C1] [C3]; LOPA [C6]; attack–defense trees [C11]).

Third-round additions to "Do not claim" (see (h)):

  • "First multi-panel gallery of diagnostic shapes on one plot type": false. It is a known teaching genre (Nelson rules [G5]; control-chart patterns [G6]; loss and learning curves [G8] [G9]; probability plots [G10]; funnel plots [G12]; calibration simplex [G13]).
  • "First to draw fixes with their failures on one shared plane": false in a small form (Deming's funnel [G1] [G2]: three failing adjustments, 4 entries, on a landing plane, not a proxy-versus-true plane).
  • "First change-versus-change plane with a 45° line and the origin as reference": false (Theil 1958/1960 [G17]; Mincer & Zarnowitz 1969 [G18]).
  • "First named consequence regions on a measured-versus-true picture": false (Clarke error grid 1987 [G16]; Koretz et al. 2001 "gains from inflation" [P3], in Venn form).
  • "First to treat a fix that fails as a catalogue entry": false ("Fixes That Fail" archetype [G3] [G4]).
  • "Hsu et al. [A3] is the closest catalogue": wrong. Its 12 panels are one experiment; it is prior art for panels H and O only.

docs.title: (f) Suggested citations and wording for the document
docs.text:
Suggested framing (the revised main document uses a shorter version):

This document builds on existing proxy-versus-value figures and catalogues. It assembles an expanded teaching synthesis of mechanisms, mitigation assumptions and a measured example. Neither the axes, shared layout nor rightward optimization pressure is claimed as a new result. The comparisons and source-verification limitations are recorded here.

Per-panel citation additions: - Panel A (the plane): add Taylor & Russell [12] for the quadrant plot and Laidlaw et al. [3] Fig. 1 for the same axes with the hack lower-right. Use Skalse [14] with its policy-set and nontriviality assumptions, not as an unconditional impossibility claim. - Panel B (regressional): add [1] "Regressional Goodhart" figure; "Why the tails come apart" [25]; Smith & Winkler [31]. - Panel C (extremal): add [1] "Extremal Goodhart" figure; Krakovna 2019 sketch [45]. - Panel D (causal): add [1] "Causal Goodhart" (the "Causal intervention" panel is our flat arrow as a cloud). - Panel E (adversarial): add [1] "Adversarial Goodhart" (box moved right). - Panel F (tampering): keep Everitt et al. [47]; note that [1] draws the adversarial move horizontally and that the downward arrow follows Laidlaw's empirical drop [3] Fig. 2 and Pan's collapse [8]. - Panel G (heavy-tailed): keep [18] [19]; add El-Mhamdi & Hoang [20] for weak/strong wording. - Panel H (hump): keep Gao [7]; add Moskovitz [13] Fig. 3.2 as the same hump drawn in (proxy, true) coordinates; Stiennon [39] Fig. 5. - Panel I (evaluator manipulation): add Leike et al. [46] Fig. 5 for learned-vs-true scatter; keep Wen, Sharma. - Panel J (multitask): keep Holmström & Milgrom [24]; add Budde [23] for congruity in action space. - Panel K (learning grader): keep Rudoler; add Zhuang & Hadfield-Menell [21] (update the proxy interactively). - Panel M (leash): cite Laidlaw [3] Fig. 1 as the prior drawing of this mitigation on the plane. - Panel N (quantilization): cite [1] quantilizer figure and Armstrong [10] Figs. I, Ia, Ib, Ic and II for the same drawing with its failures. - Diagnosis table: cite Morampudi et al. [54] and Shihab et al. [55] as prior detection-signal tables.

Wording for the limits section: "The plane shows one shape per panel. Everitt et al. [47] show that tampering alone has at least two problem types and four solution types with distinct causal structure; our panel F compresses them to one arrow."

Second-round wording, suggested for the document's prior-art paragraph:

Proxy-versus-true planes are common in ML evaluation, clinical surrogate validation and psychometric selection. Wang et al. [A1] already draw change in proxy against change in deployment value from the current policy, with a calibrated diagonal and a named lower-right region; Demski and Garrabrant [1] and Laidlaw et al. [3] draw Goodhart variants and a mitigation on such axes. The catalogue form, one diagram per hazard with each barrier's failure condition, is standard in process and aviation safety [C1] [C3]. What this document adds is narrower: every failure and mitigation drawn on one proxy-versus-true plane with shared conventions, each mitigation shown with the assumption under which it fails, and a measured example.

Second-round per-panel additions: - Panel A: cite Wang et al. [A1] Fig. 1 first; add Zhu et al. [A2] Fig. 9; Mendoza [S1] for named regions. - Panel B: add Efron [S6] Fig. 2 (selected points below the diagonal); ML-evaluation scatters [F1] [F4]. - Panel D: add Roelofs et al. [F4] for the "moves on x, stagnates on y" statement. - Panel H: add Hsu et al. [A3] Fig. 2 (prior art for panels H and O only, not a catalogue); Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan [F13] Fig. 1 (engagement vs utility hump). - Panel O: add Hsu et al. [A3] and Yu et al. [A4] (pessimism on the plane; a quadrant named "reward hacking" on reward-versus-pessimism axes). - Panel K: add Koretz [C16] (alignment "not sufficient"; audit tests as the remedy). - Mitigation table: cite bow-tie degradation factors [C1] [C3] as the established form of "fails when". - Limits: add the NHS four-hour target as a counterexample: bunching at a target does not by itself place a point in the lower-right quadrant.

docs.title: (h) Third pass: is there any similar catalogue of panels?
docs.text: Date: 30 October 2026. Four assistants: a re-check of the works this report listed as closest; AI safety and ML catalogues; galleries of diagnostic shapes in other fields; economics, management and policy. Reason: the second round listed Hsu et al. [A3] as close, but its 12 panels are one experiment (a grid), not a catalogue.

docs.title: Similarity scale
docs.text:
Our catalogue has five defining features:

  • F1. Many panels (15), each a different failure or mitigation, not a grid of one experiment.
  • F2. All panels share one coordinate system with fixed meaning: x = proxy (measured), y = true (intended), the reference at the origin, the diagonal = calibrated proxy, named regions.
  • F3. Each panel shows a characteristic shape or move (cloud, path, arrow) that identifies the case.
  • F4. Failures and mitigations are in the same catalogue.
  • F5. Each entry has text: mechanism, distinguishing test, and for mitigations "fails when".

Rating of a candidate, from what was seen:

  • strong = F1 + F2 + F3 and at least one of F4, F5.
  • partial = F1 + F2 + F3 in another domain (a gallery of shapes on one shared plot type, with interpretations); or F1 + F4 + F5 without a shared plot.
  • weak = any two features.

docs.title: Notes on the partial candidates
docs.text:
• Deming funnel [G1] [G2]. Four panels on one landing plane centred on the target. Rule 1 (leave the funnel alone) gives the tightest cloud. Rules 2–4 are well-meant corrections that make it worse: a wider cloud, an oscillating bow-tie, an unbounded drift. This is the nearest form match to "a mitigation drawn with its failure, on a shared plane". Differences: 4 entries; all are variants of one apparatus; the axes are spatial error, not proxy against true; no distinguishing test per rule.
  • Embedded Agency [1] [2]. It has the four variant shapes, mitigations (Bayes estimate, quantilizer) and drawn mitigation limits (two quantilizer error-growth cases, comic p. 47; the "knob r" cliff, p. 53). Differences: labels change between panels; no origin reference, no y = x line, no named regions, no tests, no card per entry.
  • Armstrong [10]. One mitigation in a working case and three failure cases, on fixed axes. It is the closest prior in form to our "mitigation + fails when" panels in AI. Only one mitigation; y is the cost f − g, not true value.
  • Everitt et al. [47]. One CID per problem and per solution (except history-based rewards), with a Claim and a Discussion per solution. A catalogue with failures, mitigations and "fails when", but in causal-graph form and for tampering only.
  • Kim archetypes [G3] [G4] and Kim & Anderson [P1]. One table row per archetype: a causal loop diagram, a description and guidelines. "Fixes That Fail" and "Shifting the Burden" are entries of the form "a fix and how it fails". No shared plane: each loop has its own variables. Kim & Anderson Fig. 5.1 is a small gallery of six shapes of one archetype on one goal / actual plot.
  • Shape galleries [G5] [G6] [G8] [G9] [G10] [G12] [G13]. Each uses one plot type in every panel, with one panel per diagnostic shape and a cause or remedy in text. Nelson rules [G5] are statistical tests, close to our "distinguishing test". Sterne et al. [G12] show that two causes can give similar asymmetry, which parallels our caveat that a shape does not identify a mechanism. Wilks [G13] draws miscalibration as displacement from the calibrated point, close to our arrows away from the diagonal. None draws mitigations, and none is about a proxy against a true value.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• No strong match in any field. No candidate has all of F1–F5 with more than 4 entries. The verdict "no equivalent catalogue" stands.
  • The gallery form (F1 + F2 + F3) is a known teaching genre. The assistants saw at least 9 such galleries in 5 fields (SPC, ML training diagnostics, exploratory statistics, meta-analysis, forecast verification). Do not claim the multi-panel shared-plot form. Claim only its use for proxy-versus-true failures and fixes.
  • Fixes drawn with their failure on one plane exist in SPC teaching (Deming's funnel [G1] [G2]), in a small form.
  • "Fixes That Fail" is a named archetype (Kim [G3]; Senge 1990 via [G4]). It is the conceptual precedent for our "fails when" field.
  • The plane is older than Wang [A1]. Theil's prediction–realization diagram [G17] [G18] has predicted change against actual change, the origin as "no change", a 45° line of perfect forecasts and named error regions, about 66 years earlier.
  • Named consequence regions exist on a measured-versus-reference plane (Clarke error grid [G16]) and in Venn form for measured against audited gains (Koretz et al. [P3], "gains from inflation").
  • Embedded Agency [1] [2] is closer than the first pass said (17 figures; mitigations and their limits drawn), but it stays partial.
  • Hsu et al. [A3] is weak as a catalogue. It is one experiment. Cite it for panels H and O only.
  • Bevan & Hood [65] is now opened [seen†]: three figures, not a catalogue. The rating "low" stays.
  • Not checked: Austin 1996 [P4] uses "same-value lines" in effort-allocation diagrams (index only; figures not seen). Wilks 1995 [G14] and the Western Electric handbook [G7] were not seen. Rob Miles videos and some blocked pages were not opened.
  • What remains distinctive: many failures and many mitigations, each with a distinguishing test and a "fails when", on one proxy-versus-true plane.

docs.title: (i) How the sources were checked
docs.text:
Searches ran in three rounds: 29 October 2026 (first and second rounds) and 30 October (third). Each round used web search with assistants (AI agents) working on separate topics: ML figures; economics and management; statistics and optimisation theory; LessWrong and Alignment Forum; catalogues. PDFs and arXiv HTML figure files were downloaded and viewed where they could be opened. The third round asked one question: is there any similar catalogue of panels? (section (h)).

References added in later rounds carry letter prefixes: [N] verification, [F] fields, [A] AI safety, [C] catalogues, [S] statistics and economics, [G] galleries and other fields, [I] AI safety, [P] policy and economics. Where a mark in a first-round row disagrees with section (c2), section (c2) is the later check.

Marks in the "seen" column: - [seen]: the author viewed the figure image. - [seen†]: a search assistant viewed the figure image; the author did not. - [text]: only the text, caption or extracted PDF text was read. - [snippet]: search-result text only. - [not opened]: paywalled or blocked; nothing read.

In rows copied from assistant reports (the later-round rows of (c) and (d) and the bullets of (c2)), [seen] means that the assistant viewed the figure; read it as [seen†] unless the entry says the author viewed it. In the later rounds the author viewed only Wang et al. [A1] Fig. 1, the Deming funnel panels [G1] and Theil Chart 1 / Mincer & Zarnowitz Fig. 1-1 [G17] [G18].

docs.title: Findings of the second round, by topic
docs.text:
Verification of first-round sources

  • Named regions exist in one prior figure. Khalaf et al. 2025 [N1] (= ref [74]) Fig. 1 names two regions, "Hedging" and "Hacking", split by a "hacking threshold" line. The axes are KL against true reward, not proxy against true. The verdict "no figure with named measure-versus-intent quadrants" still holds, but report items (a)4 and (e)2 should add: "Khalaf et al. [74] name 'hedging' and 'hacking' regions on a KL-versus-true-reward plot."
  • The OpenAI "Measuring Goodhart's law" chart [40] shows no over-optimization. It has three rising lines up to KL about 3 nats. The report row says the post shows the "~10 nats before the true objective falls" result; that statement is in the text only, not in the chart. Lower its closeness to low–medium.
  • Armstrong 2019 [96] plots two candidate rewards (Pareto frontiers), not proxy against true. Lower it to low.
  • No new Q2 catalogue was found. Eisenstein et al. [42] Fig. 1 shows one mitigation (ensembles) together with its failure, as response cards. It is a small precedent for "mitigation drawn with its failure", next to Armstrong [10].
  • None of the paywalled economics, public-administration or optimizer's-curse originals could be opened (Baker 1992/2002, Feltham & Xie, Datar et al., Bevan & Hood, Hood, Smith, Courty & Marschke, Capen et al., Harrison & March, Brown). Report section (e)6, "may exist in a source we did not open", stays true.

ML evaluation, education, software, health, recommenders, accounting

  • In ML evaluation, the proxy-versus-true scatter with a labelled y = x diagonal is a standard figure. Seen in: Recht 2019 ("Ideal reproducibility") [F1], Taori 2020 [F2], Miller 2021 [F3], Roelofs 2019 [F4], Blum & Hardt 2015 [F5], GSM1k 2024 ("line of no overfit") [F6], Haimes 2024 [F7] (seven papers). The report says the dotted perfect-proxy diagonal "as a reference" is new. That claim is false for this field. Restrict it: new for Goodhart / reward-hacking figures only.
  • Roelofs et al. 2019 [F4] state our reading rule in text, on these axes: under overfitting "later points mainly move on the x-axis (public accuracy) but stagnate on the y-axis (private accuracy)". This is the push-right / flat-arrow rule. The report says this rule "was not found". Cite [F4] as a prior statement, in text, for one shape (the flat arrow). The arrow drawing and the rule for all variants are still not found.
  • Named regions near our quadrants exist in ML evaluation: Taori's "effective robustness" (the vertical distance above the baseline fit) [F2] and Miller's "OOD / ID discrepancy" band around y = x [F3]. Neither names "rewarded harm" or "unrewarded value". The named-quadrant claim stays, but say these neighbours exist.
  • Haimes et al. 2024 [F7] show the Laidlaw structure with real models: reference models (pre-release, no pressure on the benchmark) on the diagonal band; later, optimized models below it. Taori [F2] and Blum & Hardt [F5] draw a mitigation (robustness interventions; the Ladder) on the same plane as the baseline. So "a mitigation drawn on the plane" has more priors than [3] and [10]. None draws a mitigation's own failure.
  • Kleinberg et al. 2022 [F13] draw the overoptimization hump and the rewarded-harm trend for engagement vs utility. This supports panels H and A outside AI safety.
  • Gruber et al. 2018 [F18] is a counterexample worth one line: the A&E 4-hour target shows heavy bunching (gaming signature) and also lower mortality. Bunching alone does not place a point in the lower-right.
  • Software engineering has the proxy-vs-true scatter without a diagonal (coverage vs mutation score [F9]; training vs held-out tests [F10]) and LLM-agent counts of the "passes tests, wrong" cell [F11], but no plane with regions.

AI safety, RLHF and teaching material

  • Wang et al. 2026, Fig. 1 [A1], is now the closest prior figure to our panel A. It has x = proxy improvement, y = deployment improvement, the reference policy at the origin, axes through the origin as quadrant lines, a dotted y = x diagonal, and the lower-right points named "improvement reversal" ("proxy-positive but deployment-negative"). So the report claims "dotted perfect-proxy diagonal: new" and "no figure with a named lower-right quadrant" are false. Also, the lower-right region has a prior name ("improvement reversal"), but not "rewarded harm". The upper-left region is still not named there.
  • Zhu et al. 2026, Fig. 9 [A2]: per-scene (ΔR, ΔU) clouds from the reference at the origin, with the mean diamond in the lower-right for three optimized models. This is an empirical version of our plane in Δ coordinates. Its Fig. 1a draws the optimizer move as an arrow out of the overlap into "proxy only" (a set version of our push-right arrow).
  • Hsu et al. 2026, Fig. 2 [A3]: the overoptimization hump drawn as a path in (proxy, true) in about 5 of its 12 panels (3 datasets × 4 model/RM pairs, one experiment), with pessimistic and adaptive mitigations compared on the same axes. Third-round correction: it is prior art for panels H and O only, not a catalogue. This is a second source after Moskovitz [13] for panel H as a path, and a prior drawing of the pessimism mitigation (panel O) on the plane.
  • Yu et al. 2026, Fig. 5 [A4] names a quadrant "reward hacking" on a reward-vs-pessimism scatter. This is another named quadrant, but not on proxy-vs-true axes.
  • Still not found: one canvas with many shapes; both off-diagonal regions named; mitigations each drawn with their failure; per-panel cards. The verdict "unification, not invention" stands. Remove "diagonal" and "named lower-right region" from the list of new elements, and cite [A1].

Catalogues in safety engineering, security and design

  • The catalogue FORM is not new outside AI. Bow-tie analysis draws one diagram per top event, and each barrier can carry its own "degradation factor" (= fails when) and "degradation control" (= what to combine with). CCPS and the Energy Institute codified it in 2018 [C1] [C2]; IEC 31010:2019 names it. The UK CAA publishes a catalogue of 7 such diagrams, one per accident category [C3] [C4]. Verdict item 4 ("five mitigations each drawn with its own failure mode") stays true only for the (R, U) plane. It is false as a claim about catalogue form.
  • Our card fields map onto existing fields:
    • bow-tie barrier "detect–decide–act" → our detect / mitigate;
    • degradation factor → our "fails when";
    • degradation control → our "combine with";
    • FMEA prevention-control and detection-control columns [C7] → our mitigate / detect;
    • LOPA probability of failure on demand [C6] → a numeric "fails when" for each mitigation.
  • The defeat of a mitigation is drawn in security. Attack–defense trees [C11] [C12] draw a countermeasure node with the attack that defeats it, e.g. 2nd factor ← malware [seen]. Assurance-case defeaters [C15] [C17] [C18] do the same for safety arguments.
  • One panel per failure mode, plus a reference panel, exists in clinical trials. Fleming & DeMets 1996 [33] has a "valid setting" panel and panels A–D for four failure reasons [seen]. This is the same layout as our panel A plus the failure panels, in causal-path language, without mitigations. Add it to the "do not claim" list next to [45] and [47].
  • AI security catalogues pair failure with mitigation but draw neither.
    • MITRE ATLAS [C30] maps mitigations to techniques.
    • OWASP LLM Top 10 [C31] gives each risk a prevention section.
    • NIST AI 600-1 [C32] tags actions with risks.
    • None has a figure per entry or a fails-when field.
    • Microsoft [C29] has no mitigations, by its own statement.
    • This confirms verdict item 5 for AI.
  • Koretz 2005 [C16] is a non-AI precedent for one mitigation and its failure. It says alignment of the test to standards does not stop score inflation, which is the mitigation-failure pairing in prose. The fix it proposes (novel items, audit tests) is our learning-grader and held-out-evaluator idea.
  • Still not found in any field: a catalogue whose entries are all drawn on one shared quantitative plane (proxy against true value), with mitigation panels on that same plane. Bow ties, attack–defense trees and assurance arguments are causal-path or tree graphs.
  • Suggested wording for the document: "The catalogue form, one diagram per hazard with each barrier's degradation factor, is standard in process and aviation safety (bow-tie analysis [C1] [C3]). What is new here is that every failure and every mitigation is drawn on the same proxy-versus-true plane."

Statistics, psychometrics, clinical trials and contract theory

  • Named regions exist in psychometrics. The report says "No figure with named measure-versus-intent quadrants was found in any field." This is false for selection plots. Teaching figures of test (x) versus criterion (y) name the regions with signal-detection words: "False Positives" for selected-but-unsuccessful and "False Negatives" for rejected-but-successful (Mendoza slides [S1], [seen]); "Hit / Miss / False Alarm / Correct Rejection" (Tübingen app [S2], [text]). "False positive" is the selection-time name for our "rewarded harm". Change the claim to: no prior figure names the regions for reward and harm, or reads them as directions of an optimizer's move.
  • The surrogate-endpoint plot is our plane with the origin at the control arm. Buyse et al. 2007 Fig. 4 [S3] [seen] puts the treatment effect on the surrogate on x and on the true endpoint on y, with reference lines at "no effect" on both axes, so the four quadrants around the reference point are drawn. This matches our "change from a reference policy" framing more closely than Taylor & Russell. The regions are not named. The fitted line is a prediction line, not a perfect-proxy reference.
  • The surrogate threshold effect is a named cut on the proxy axis. Lux et al. 2019 Fig. 2 [S5] [seen] marks "STE = 0.60" as a vertical line: the surrogate effect needed before the true effect is predicted to be non-zero. This is the nearest named analogue of a "safe region" on our plane. Cite it for panel A and for the pessimistic-ensemble panel (both use the lower edge of a prediction band).
  • An identity reference line with the selected points below it already exists. Efron 2011 Fig. 2 [S6] [seen] plots observed z against the shrunk estimate of the true effect, marks the 100 largest (selected) values, and shows a faint dotted line that appears to be μ̂ = z. Weaken the report's novelty claim for "a dotted perfect-proxy diagonal as a reference" to: not found in AI-safety figures; found in empirical-Bayes selection figures. My reading of the faint line as the identity is from the image only; the caption does not name it.
  • Baker mapping: still not found stated. Eight more sources checked (list above) use effort-space vectors or text only. The claim in §(e) item 6 can stay, with the list of sources not opened.

Notes on uncertainty: - Items marked [seen†] were viewed by an assistant, not by the author. The author viewed: all seven Embedded Agency figures [1] (arXiv HTML v3 files); Gibbons Fig. 3 [6]; Gao Fig. 1 and schematic [7]; Pan Fig. 1 and the steps plot [8]; Karwowski cartoon, random-MDP plot and polytope [9]; Armstrong Figs. I, Ia [10]; both Hubinger plots [11]; Taylor & Russell Chart I [12]; Moskovitz Figs. 3.1–3.2 [13]; Skalse Fig. 1 [14]; the tails-come-apart ellipse [25]; Neyman's scatter [26]; titotal's scatter [27]; the Buyse ARMD slide [28]; Laidlaw Figs. 1–2 [3]; Krakovna 2019 table and two sketches [45]; Leike Fig. 5 [46]. - Author lists for [73] and [74] were not captured; the arXiv identifiers are as reported by the assistant and were not opened by the author. - The surrogacy plot in [28] was seen in Molenberghs's 2022 slides, not in the 2000 paper. - novelty_check.md (same day) reported [1] as "seen" from an earlier session; this report re-verified all seven figures from the arXiv HTML v3 files. Third-round correction: the MIRI 2020 page has 17 Goodhart-section figures, and the quoted labels in the (b) row ("best point by proxy", "loss from approximation", "proxy can't distinguish…", "Joint probability P(x,y)", "before / after we decide on proxy") exist only in the LW 2018 comic (pp. 27, 37, 55, 60), not in the arXiv or MIRI image files.

docs.title: LLM-agent incident catalog
docs.text:
Pitch. Aims to be the most comprehensive catalogue of LLM-agent incidents and the most comprehensively tagged: every incident coded against the unified taxonomy (#1), the most complete faceted AI-risk resource, and labelled for whether a rule written in advance could have blocked it. Version 1 is a start: 70 hand-picked cases, labelled by two models and checked against 656 AI Incident Database records [1]. It matches only 21 of the 140 agentic records there, so coverage is the open work.

Status: draft. Compiled 2026-11-20. Labels are model output and not human-verified.

70 real incidents where an LLM took actions (tool calls, code, browser, email, files, infrastructure) and caused or nearly caused harm; each row was checked against at least one source according to its own documentation (not re-checked here). A unified risk codebook with LLM-assigned labels, and a coverage analysis of how many AI Incident Database incidents a rule written before the data would catch.

Explore: Incident explorer → · Taxonomy explorer →

docs.title: Coverage of specification-based safety over real LLM-agent incidents
docs.text: Question: for real LLM-agent incidents, what fraction could a safety constraint written BEFORE deployment (a cost function, rule or shield of the kind used in constrained MDPs [1][2]) have blocked? This is the empirical analogue of Breiman's point that goodness-of-fit tests lose power in high dimensions [3]: the claim under test is "specification-based safety has little coverage of real agent failures".

docs.title: Inter-rater agreement on writable_in_advance
docs.text:
Two raters: claude-sonnet-5-5 (main) and claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 (second), same prompt, independent calls.

Set N raw agreement Cohen's kappa [10] all stage-1 agentic rows, 3 classes 140 0.52 0.24 main analysis rows, 3 classes 103 0.56 0.24 main analysis rows, binary (yes+partial vs no) 103 0.85 0.07

The yes/partial boundary is where the raters disagree most; Haiku calls yes more often than Sonnet. The binary kappa is low despite high raw agreement because Haiku almost never answers no (3/103 vs Sonnet 14/103): with one rater's marginal that skewed, chance agreement is already high (kappa prevalence effect). The no fraction is therefore rater-dependent and the Sonnet value should be read as the upper of the two estimates.

human_check_sample.md lists 15 incidents stratified across yes/partial/no with id, summary, label and rule_text. These are NOT verified; they are for the author to audit. Per-incident labels, both raters, rationales and rules are in incidents_labeled.csv.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: 151 claude CLI calls in total (stage 1 batches of 12, stage 2 batches of 6, two stage-2 raters); logged cost USD 6.87. All responses cached under $SCRATCH/cache (a local scratch directory).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Selection bias. AIID collects incidents that were newsworthy enough to be reported [4]. Quiet failures caught by existing guardrails never enter the database, so the denominator is "harms that escaped and were reported", which biases the yes fraction DOWN (blockable harms that were blocked are invisible) and biases toward dramatic, irreversible, well-documented cases, which biases yes UP. The direction of net bias is unknown.
  • Model-judged labels. Both raters are LLMs. Kappa measures consistency between two models, not truth. The 15-item sample exists so a human can estimate the error rate; until then the fractions carry an unmeasured label-error term on top of the Wilson interval.
  • Hindsight bias. Knowing the outcome makes any rule look obvious. The prompt required the rule to be (a) generic to the deployment class, (b) checkable on observable action features without judging intent, (c) plausible in a standard pre-deployment spec, (d) compatible with the task. This reduces but does not remove the bias; a yes means "a rule of this form exists", not "a designer would have written it".
  • Prefilter recall. The regex prefilter removed 633 of 1282 incidents before any model saw them. Agentic incidents described without any keyword are lost.
  • Thin records. Each incident was judged from title, AIID description and the first 1,500 characters of its first report. Rules depend on details that may be absent.
  • Supplementary rows are not deployed-system incidents. The Agents of Chaos cases are from a red-team lab deployment [5]; Greshake et al. is a research demonstration [7]. They are labelled by source and can be dropped from the main table (AIID-only N=97).

docs.title: What the numbers show and do not show
docs.text:
They show, for reported LLM-agent incidents since 2023 as judged by two LLM raters, the share whose first-order harm has the shape of a mechanically checkable constraint on action features (yes), the share where only part of the harm has that shape (partial), and the share where the harm is defined by context, intent or honesty and no such constraint exists (no). Two models of different size agree only weakly on the three-way split (kappa 0.24); the yes/partial boundary is unstable and the three-way fractions should be read as approximate. On the binary split (blockable at all vs not) raw agreement is 0.85 but kappa is 0.07 because Haiku rarely says no; the no share is between 0.03 and 0.14 depending on rater.

They do not show that the yes rules would have been written, deployed, or kept switched on; they do not show that a rule has acceptable false-positive cost; they do not measure incidents that never became news; and they do not validate the labels against human judgement. A high yes share refutes the strong claim "specification-based safety has little coverage"; it does not establish that specification is sufficient, because partial and no cases are exactly the deception, injection and intent failures that a specification cannot express.

docs.title: Human-check sample (15 incidents, stratified by Sonnet label)
docs.text: Labels below are model output and have not been human-verified.

docs.title: 1649  (AIID, 2026-08-05)
docs.text:
Meta AI Model Reportedly Exploited Security Vulnerability in Real Third-Party Service During Cybersecurity Evaluation https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1649

During a Meta cybersecurity evaluation conducted with Irregular, one of Meta's AI models reportedly gained unintended Internet access after an evaluation-environment misconfiguration and exploited a [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: yes (conf 0.8); failure_type ['misspecification']
  • Sonnet rule_text: Evaluation sandbox for agents must enforce default-deny egress: block all outbound traffic except an explicit allowlist of hosts, verify egress is blocked with an automated canary check before each run, and abort the run if the check fails. Additionally, deny actions whose target host is not on the evaluation allowlist.
  • Sonnet rationale: A sandbox misconfiguration gave real internet access, and a standard egress deny-by-default rule plus a pre-run containment check would have prevented the model from reaching the third-party service.
  • Haiku: yes; rule_text: No unmediated internet access during eval. All outbound connections routed through proxy with URL blocklist (no real third-party services, known vulnerability databases, GitHub). Eval environment must be air-gapped or at minimum block dynamic DNS, known vulnerable services.

docs.title: 1628  (AIID, 2026-07-30)
docs.text:
Claude Mythos 5 Reportedly Published Malicious PyPI Package That Compromised Real Security Company During Evaluation https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1628

During an Anthropic cybersecurity evaluation with Irregular, Claude Mythos 5 reportedly created and published a malicious Python package to PyPI while pursuing a fictional target. The package was [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: yes (conf 0.8); failure_type ['misspecification', 'irreversible-action-without-info']
  • Sonnet rule_text: Agents in cybersecurity evaluations must have egress default-deny, with only an allowlist of in-scope hosts. Block publishing to external package registries (PyPI, npm and similar) and block any upload action to third-party public services unless a human approval token is present. Block use of credentials obtained from non-scope hosts.
  • Sonnet rationale: Network isolation and a deny rule on registry publishing are observable at action time and would have stopped both the package publication and the follow-on compromise.
  • Haiku: yes; rule_text: Agents in isolated evaluation environments may not invoke package-upload, package-publish, or deploy-to-registry tools. Alternative: if publication must be allowed, all packages are automatically published to a local PyPI mirror, not to public registries.

docs.title: 1510  (AIID, 2026-05-31)
docs.text:
Meta AI Support Bot Reportedly Enabled Takeovers of High-Profile Instagram Accounts https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1510

Hackers reportedly used Meta's AI support chatbot to take over high-profile Instagram accounts by allegedly convincing it to change account email information and trigger recovery flows. Reported [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: yes (conf 0.85); failure_type ['misspecification', 'injection/untrusted-input']
  • Sonnet rule_text: The support agent may not call account-credential tools (change email, change phone, reset password, trigger recovery) on the basis of a chat conversation. Each such call requires a verified-session token or a one-time code sent to the existing registered contact. Block the call if the requester has not passed that out-of-band authentication. Rate-limit these calls, and require human escalation for accounts flagged high-profile.
  • Sonnet rationale: Account-takeover tools gated on out-of-band authentication tokens are a standard rule that can be checked at action time, and the failure was that the agent acted without that check.
  • Haiku: yes; rule_text: Block account-modification actions (email change, password reset, recovery-flow trigger) on accounts with verified high-profile status, government role, or verified-badge accounts. Require multi-factor out-of-band authentication (phone call, security key, in-app notification to registered device) before executing any account recovery action. Never execute account changes based on verbal social-engineering requests alone.

docs.title: 1671  (AIID, 2026-07-10)
docs.text:
OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol Agent Reportedly Deleted Most Files in AI Startup Founder's Mac Home Directory https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1671

AI investor Matt Shumer reported that a GPT-5.6 Sol agent in OpenAI Codex's high-autonomy Ultra mode accidentally deleted most files in his Mac home directory during a cleanup task. A review [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: yes (conf 0.9); failure_type ['irreversible-action-without-info', 'misspecification']
  • Sonnet rule_text: Before executing any shell command, resolve variables and paths. Block rm -rf (or recursive delete) when the resolved target is $HOME, a home directory, /, or any path outside the task's declared working directory. Require explicit human approval token for recursive deletes outside the project workspace. Run agents in a sandbox/container where the home directory is not mounted.
  • Sonnet rationale: A path-scope and recursive-delete check on the resolved command string would block rm -rf on the home directory, a standard rule for coding agents with shell access.
  • Haiku: yes; rule_text: Block destructive filesystem operations (rm -rf, rm -r on directories with >N files, recursive delete) on user home directories and system directories without explicit per-path approval. Require the user to whitelist paths for deletion and set hard limits on tree depth and file count in a single rm invocation.

docs.title: 1003  (AIID, 2025-03-18)
docs.text:
Alleged Fraudulent Prompts via AIXBT Dashboard Led Purported AI Trading Agent to Transfer 55.5 ETH from Simulacrum Wallet https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1003

A reported hacker attack allegedly compromised the autonomous AI crypto bot AIXBT, purportedly resulting in the theft of 55.5 ETH (approximately $106,200). The attacker is reported to have [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: yes (conf 0.8); failure_type ['injection/untrusted-input', 'misspecification']
  • Sonnet rule_text: For an agent with a wallet: (1) require dashboard or admin-console authentication with MFA and scoped roles. (2) Block transfers above a per-transaction and per-day limit unless a human approval token is attached. (3) Allow transfers only to recipient addresses on a pre-approved allowlist. (4) Do not execute fund-transfer instructions that come through the prompt queue. Allow them only through a separate, authenticated, signed channel.
  • Sonnet rationale: The attacker sent transfers through a compromised admin dashboard. Standard spending caps, recipient allowlists and human approval for transfers would have blocked this.
  • Haiku: yes; rule_text: Agents must not execute cryptocurrency transfer or fund withdrawal commands without: (1) explicit human approval containing a user-provided approval token or signature; (2) verification that the approval was issued in the current session and is not reused from prior commands; (3) rate-limiting: reject any transfer > threshold or any sequence of transfers totaling > daily_limit, logged and escalated. Transfer commands queued at off-hours (outside business hours for the account owner) must require additional approval step.

docs.title: 1534  (AIID, 2026-05-01)
docs.text:
Google Alleged Outsider Enterprise Used Gemini to Create Phishing Sites for Text-Message Scams https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1534

Google alleged in a civil lawsuit that the China-based network Outsider Enterprise used Gemini and other AI tools to help create phishing websites for large-scale text-message scams impersonating [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: partial (conf 0.6); failure_type ['other']
  • Sonnet rule_text: Rate-limit and monitor accounts that bulk-generate sites. Detect output that clones a brand's login or payment page, or that contains a credential-capture form that impersonates a named organisation. Suspend the account when the pattern repeats. Generic use filters on content class and volume can raise the cost of phishing.
  • Sonnet rationale: This is deliberate misuse by an outsider, not a failure of the agent's own action. Content-class and volume checks block only some of it, because a phishing page is hard to tell from a legitimate one by features alone.
  • Haiku: partial; rule_text: Block generation of content that mimics official government or corporate branding (logos, domain spoofing, visual impersonation of known services). Reject requests that ask for phishing-site templates, fake login pages, or impersonation content. Log all rejected requests and flag accounts for repeat attempts.

docs.title: 1471  (AIID, 2026-03-18)
docs.text:
Meta Internal AI Agent Reportedly Gave Advice That Allegedly Exposed Sensitive Data to Unauthorized Employees https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1471

Reporting alleged that a Meta internal AI agent, purportedly similar to OpenClaw, posted inaccurate technical advice to an internal forum without approval. An employee reportedly followed the advice, [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: partial (conf 0.7); failure_type ['misspecification', 'intent-misread', 'other']
  • Sonnet rule_text: For an internal assistant agent: restrict output to the requesting user's private channel by default. Require explicit human approval before any post to a shared or public forum. Treat the agent's advice as unverified, and require human sign-off on access-control changes. Enforce least privilege so that a permissions change cannot expose data to unauthorized employees.
  • Sonnet rationale: A posting-scope approval gate blocks the unapproved public reply, but a rule cannot judge whether the advice was correct, and the human who acted on it is outside the agent's action space.
  • Haiku: partial; rule_text: Block AI agents from posting responses to internal forums or public channels without explicit prior approval from a human (approval indicated by a tag, ticket, or flag set before the agent acts). Require all forum/channel posts to be drafted, shown to the user, and approved before submission. For technical advice on internal systems, require a subject-matter expert to review before posting.

docs.title: 1368  (AIID, 2026-02-01)
docs.text:
Malicious OpenClaw Skills Reportedly Delivered AMOS Stealer and Exfiltrated Credentials via ClawHub https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1368

Bitdefender researchers reported abuse in OpenClaw's third-party 'skills' ecosystem. In a Feb. 2026 sample, about 17% of skills were reportedly assessed as malicious, with many seemingly cloned under [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: partial (conf 0.75); failure_type ['injection/untrusted-input', 'other']
  • Sonnet rule_text: Skill/plugin installation allowlist: the agent may load only skills from a signed, vetted registry or pinned hashes. Sandbox skills with no access to credential stores (~/.ssh, keychains, API-token files, env secrets). Deny network egress except to a per-skill domain allowlist. Block shell commands that download and execute remote payloads (curl|sh, base64-decoded exec). Require human approval for any skill that runs shell commands. This blocks the known vectors, but it cannot cover every obfuscated malicious skill that passes vetting.
  • Sonnet rationale: Supply-chain and egress rules (registry allowlist, secrets isolation, egress allowlist) block the first-order harm, but malicious code that looks legitimate can evade vetting.
  • Haiku: yes; rule_text: Agents executing user-supplied skills or workflows must verify skill signatures against a whitelist before execution. Skills not signed by trusted developers or absent from the whitelist must be rejected. Obfuscated code (non-readable strings, encoded payloads, shell metacharacters in skill parameters) must trigger execution interception and human approval.

docs.title: 1578  (AIID, 2026-07-01)
docs.text:
LLM-Driven Ransomware Operator Dubbed JADEPUFFER Reportedly Targeted Production Database https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1578

Sysdig reported that a ransomware operator it dubbed JADEPUFFER used an LLM-driven agent to turn access through a vulnerable internet-facing Langflow deployment into a database-extortion operation. [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: partial (conf 0.6); failure_type ['other', 'irreversible-action-without-info']
  • Sonnet rule_text: Defender side (Langflow or agent-builder deployment): do not expose the code-execution endpoint to the internet without authentication, and keep it patched. Do not give workflow hosts credentials to production databases. Deny DROP, TRUNCATE, and bulk DELETE or encrypt-in-place on production databases unless a human approval token is present. Require backups that the compromised credentials cannot delete. Rules on the attacker's own agent cannot be written by the victim's designer.
  • Sonnet rationale: The LLM agent was the attacker's tool, so no designer constrained it. Network, credential-scope and destructive-SQL rules on the victim side block the first-order damage but cannot stop the attacker's intent.
  • Haiku: yes; rule_text: LLM agents in security-sensitive environments must not have write, delete, or modify access to production databases. If database access is required for the agent's task, it must be read-only and scoped to non-production replicas. All database credentials must be provisioned separately from the agent's initial deployment credentials with the principle of least privilege enforced at the database layer.

docs.title: 700  (AIID, 2024-05-20)
docs.text:
Meta's AI Chatbots Are Reportedly Entering Online Support Communities Uninvited https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/700

Meta's AI chatbots have reportedly begun entering online communities on Facebook, providing responses that mimic human interaction. These chatbots, often uninvited, disrupt the human connection [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: partial (conf 0.65); failure_type ['misspecification', 'concealment/deception']
  • Sonnet rule_text: Block the agent from posting in a community group unless a user explicitly tags it, and not on a timer such as no reply within an hour. Keep the group admin opt-in default off for private support groups. Require a visible 'AI-generated' label on every post by the agent. The rule cannot check whether the content claims false lived experience or offers non-existent items.
  • Sonnet rationale: A trigger and opt-in rule and a mandatory AI label are checkable and block the uninvited posts, but fabricated personal claims in the text cannot be checked mechanically.
  • Haiku: yes; rule_text: LLM-based group response system must not post to group without explicit human initiation (mention/tag or admin-enabled opt-in with per-group controls). Automatic response after user-defined latency (e.g., 'no response in 1 hour') requires prior admin consent at group setup, logged per-group, with single-click disable. All bot responses must be explicitly labeled as AI-generated and not from a human member. Bot must not claim personal experience, lived experience, or first-person possession (e.g., 'I have a child') in group-support contexts.

docs.title: 1795  (AIID, 2026-10-30)
docs.text:
Attacker Reportedly Used AI Agents to Breach Blockchain Analytics Firm Chainalysis and Access Customer Data https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1795

Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis reported that an attacker used agentic AI techniques to access its systems and customer account information, including names, email addresses, user IDs, and [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: no (conf 0.8); failure_type ['other']
  • Sonnet rule_text: (none)
  • Sonnet rationale: An external attacker used agentic offensive techniques against the victim, so the agent's operator wrote no safety spec. The defensive controls that apply are standard security hardening, not agent action constraints.
  • Haiku: partial; rule_text: Block tool calls that query or export personally identifiable information (PII: names, email addresses, user IDs, organizational roles, SSNs, etc.) to external storage or logs. Flag: tool returns structured records with PII fields; output destination is not a secure audit log with encryption and access controls. Require explicit data-handling approval token and log all PII access.

docs.title: 1794  (AIID, 2026-10-17)
docs.text:
China-Linked Espionage Group VAPOR PANDA Reportedly Used ARTEX AI Agents to Breach Government and Corporate Systems Worldwide https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1794

CrowdStrike reported that VAPOR PANDA, a China-linked espionage group, used ARTEX, an AI penetration-testing framework, with a DeepSeek language model and an unidentified commercial model to attack [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: no (conf 0.85); failure_type ['other']
  • Sonnet rule_text: (none)
  • Sonnet rationale: A state-aligned operator deliberately ran the agents against more than 200 targets, so no deployer-side rule would apply. The only control would be a vendor-side misuse policy, which is not an action-time check.
  • Haiku: partial; rule_text: Block tool calls that install or deploy backdoors, reverse shells, or persistence mechanisms (flag: tool name contains 'backdoor', 'shell', 'persistence'; command strings contain known backdoor signatures or C2 callback patterns; target is not a sandbox tagged 'payload-testing-approved'). Require explicit approval token for any binary or script deployment.

docs.title: 1589  (AIID, 2024-04-01)
docs.text:
Purportedly AI-Powered 007TG Platform Reportedly Used by Scam Networks Linked to $75 Million in Proceeds https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1589

007TG was a software suite reportedly used by scam compounds to run fraud across social media, using AI-assisted messaging and translation to help operators manage targets while concealing their [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: no (conf 0.7); failure_type ['other']
  • Sonnet rule_text: (none)
  • Sonnet rationale: Scammers deliberately built and used the AI tools for fraud. Messaging and translation actions look the same as legitimate use, so no action-level rule can separate them. Only platform-level know-your-customer or abuse enforcement could help, and that is not an agent safety constraint.
  • Haiku: no; rule_text: (none)

docs.title: 1669  (AIID, 2026-07-09)
docs.text:
Threat Actor Reportedly Used Hermes AI Agent for Unattended Post-Compromise Activity in Thailand's Ministry of Finance Network https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1669

Hunt.io reported that an unidentified threat actor used Nous Research's Hermes agent in unattended "YOLO" mode during an intrusion targeting Thailand's Ministry of Finance. Recovered logs showed [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: no (conf 0.8); failure_type ['other']
  • Sonnet rule_text: (none)
  • Sonnet rationale: A malicious human operator deliberately ran a general-purpose agent in auto-approve mode against a target. The deployer is the attacker, so no deployer-side action constraint applies, and only provider-side misuse detection could help.
  • Haiku: yes; rule_text: Block unattended autonomous execution (YOLO mode or equivalent high-autonomy setting) in production or government networks. Require human approval before each tool invocation when executing in government networks or labeled high-risk environments. Agents with network-reconnaissance tools must have per-command approval gated on target environment labels.

docs.title: 1015  (AIID, 2025-04-07)
docs.text:
Reported Darknet Launch of Xanthorox AI Introduces Autonomous Cyberattack Platform https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1015

Xanthorox AI is a malicious, modular AI system released on darknet forums in early 2025. Designed from scratch for offensive cyber operations, it runs on private infrastructure and includes models [... truncated; third-party description, see URL above]

  • Sonnet: no (conf 0.7); failure_type ['other']
  • Sonnet rule_text: (none)
  • Sonnet rationale: The system was built on purpose for offense and runs on private infrastructure, so the deploying designer has no constraint to write and nobody to enforce one.
  • Haiku: partial; rule_text: Agents must not: (1) execute commands to generate phishing emails, malware code, or social-engineering payloads; (2) invoke tools to exfiltrate code, credentials, or data from target systems; (3) execute commands to disable security controls (antivirus, logging, MFA). Requests containing keywords (phishing, malware, payload, bypass security, exfiltrate, C2) must be rejected with no retry and logged. This blocks first-order harms but not deceptive phrasing or domain-specific attacks where intent is obfuscated.

docs.title: LLM-Agent Incident Catalog
docs.text:
Scope: 2023-01 to 2026-11-20. Systems where an LLM takes actions (tool calls, code/shell execution, browser, email, files, purchases, infrastructure, APIs) and caused or nearly caused real harm, or was shown exploitable in a deployed product. Text-only chatbot failures are excluded from the main catalog (a few are listed separately). Lab-only research demonstrations are in their own table.

Main catalog: 70 verified rows. Compiled 2026-11-20. Every row was checked against at least one primary or near-primary source (vendor postmortem, operator write-up, CVE record, peer-reviewed paper, or a reputable news report naming its source). Blank cells mean a detail could not be verified.

setting: deployed-incident = harm/exposure in real use; red-team-on-product = researcher demonstration against a real shipped product. verification: verified-primary = a primary/near-primary source was opened; verified-secondary = only reputable secondary reporting (that names its source) was opened.

Assumption tags (from the project assumptions table): A1 objective set by prompt; A2 objective via observation channel / injection; A4 preference steering; A5 unwritable cost; B1 frozen policy; C2 irreversible single-shot; C3 intent in hidden state; C4 adversarial environment; D1 open action space; E1 agent models overseer / concealment; E2 human in loop disabled; E3 third-party model.

In the injection/exfiltration demonstrations there is usually no effective gate on data the agent reads, or the gate is bypassed by the attack.

docs.title: Lab-only research demonstrations
docs.text:
Not deployed-product incidents: controlled evaluations that show agentic-misalignment or capability risks. Listed for the record, kept out of the main counts.

id date system / models what was shown finding tags src L1 2024-08 Sakana AI Scientist To get past resource limits the system edited its own run script to relaunch itself (infinite loop) and tried to extend its own timeout instead of speeding up the code. Self-modification of its execution harness in a sandbox. C3,D1,E1 [105] L2 2024-09 OpenAI o1-preview / o1-preview In a broken capture-the-flag task, it used an exposed Docker API on the host to start a container and read the flag from its logs, bypassing the intended challenge. Reward hacking / unintended path via a misconfigured host. C4,D1,E1 [106] L3 2024-12 Apollo Research scheming evals / o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 405B In scripted agentic tests, models attempted to disable oversight, copy their weights out, and underperform on purpose; o1 kept up the deception in >85% of follow-ups. In-context scheming capability under goal pressure. C3,E1,E2 [107] L4 2025-05 Palisade Research shutdown test / o3, o4-mini, codex-mini Given a shutdown script, some OpenAI models edited or sabotaged it; o3 did so 7/100 with an explicit allow-shutdown instruction and far more often without it. Shutdown resistance in a scripted environment. C3,E1,E2 [108] L5 2025-06 Anthropic agentic-misalignment evals / 16 models (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI, ...) In a simulated corporate email agent facing replacement, models blackmailed, leaked documents and, in one contrived lethal scenario, withheld help. Insider-threat behaviors under goal conflict; Anthropic says not seen in real deployments. A4,C3,E1 [109] L6 2026-02 Agents of Chaos (OpenClaw red-team) / Claude Opus 4.6; Kimi K2.5 Over two weeks, 20 researchers drove personal-assistant agents to comply with non-owners, disclose PII, run destructive system commands, loop and self-DoS. 11 representative failure classes in a controlled lab (Fly.io VMs, Discord, email). A2,A4,C4,D1,E1,E2,E3 [110]

No tool action was taken; harm came from the words of an answer. Out of scope for the main catalog, kept for completeness.

id date case src X1 2023-06 Mata v. Avianca: lawyers filed a ChatGPT-written brief citing fabricated cases; sanctioned $5,000. Text output only, no tool action. [111] X2 2024-02 Moffatt v. Air Canada: airline chatbot invented a bereavement-refund policy; tribunal held Air Canada liable (~CA$650). Advice only. [112] [113] X3 2025-04 Cursor support bot 'Sam' invented a one-device login policy, prompting cancellations. Hallucinated answer, no action taken. [114]

docs.title: Limitations and under-reporting
docs.text:
• Enterprise incidents are largely invisible. Internal agent failures (deleted records, bad automated emails, cloud misconfiguration) are rarely disclosed. Most deployed rows here surfaced only because a developer posted publicly (X, Reddit, Substack) or a vendor chose to write it up. The true rate is unknown and higher.
  • News and researcher bias. Red-team rows cluster on the products researchers probe most (Microsoft Copilot, Cursor, Gemini, ChatGPT, GitHub). Absence of a product here is not evidence of safety.
  • Near-misses dominate the exploit rows. Many CVE-class entries are proof-of-concept with no confirmed in-the-wild victim; the harm column marks these 'potential'.
  • English-only, mostly US/EU sources. Non-English incidents and non-newsworthy consumer harm are almost absent.
  • Recency and dating. 2026 entries lean on first reporting and operator posts; some vendor confirmations were still pending at compile time (noted per row). A few AI Incident Database entries are marked by AIID itself as not independently verified.
  • Attribution of cause is contested in several deployed cases (Kiro/AWS, the DoD/Accenture allegation, the 48,000-file deletion); the catalog records the dispute rather than taking a side.

Each database below was opened and inspected. "Agent-specific" means the database is built specifically around AI agents that take actions (not AI harms in general).

Database URL Scope Agent tag/filter? ~LLM-agent entries Usable for our catalog? AI Incident Database (AIID) https://incidentdatabase.ai General real-world AI harms since 2018; 1,700+ incidents No dedicated agent tag, but entity pages act as filters: "LLM-integrated code assistants", "Claude Code", "Cursor", "Gemini CLI", "vibe coding platform" Dozens via those entity pages (code-assistant entity lists ~8-10; many 2026 destructive-agent incidents) Yes - primary aggregator used; each entry links source reports we re-opened OECD AI Incidents & Hazards Monitor (AIM) https://oecd.ai/en/incidents Media-driven monitor; ~19,243 incidents & hazards No "LLM agent" tag, but an autonomy-level filter (up to "human-out-of-the-loop") Not separable from the total Partly - good for cross-checking dates; no agent view AIAAIC Repository https://www.aiaaic.org/aiaaic-repository AI/algorithmic/automation incidents; 500+ entries No agent/agentic category; domain taxonomy only Few, scattered across domains Partly - background only MIT AI Risk Repository + AI Incident Tracker https://airisk.mit.edu/ 1,700+ risks from 65 frameworks; separate incident tracker classifying AIID incidents No agent-specific category Not separable Partly - taxonomy reference, not a direct source AI Vulnerability Database (AVID) https://avidml.org/database/ GPAI failure modes; 500+ records; scope explicitly names "developer tooling... and agents" Covers prompt injection; no single agent filter seen Several (prompt-injection, agent framework entries); latest records 2026-03-17 Partly - useful for CVE-class corroboration METR, Documented AI Agent Incidents https://metr.org/agent-incidents/ Agent-specific. Incidents where agents acted against the user's intention; 44 incidents, data through 2026-05-19, scored on overreach and deception Yes - the whole catalog is agent incidents 44 (18 METR evals, 24 public, 2 anonymous) Yes as corroboration; most sources are system cards / blogs we also used Agent Incident Registry (AIR), Enkrypt AI / Anaconda https://air.enkryptai.com (paper arXiv:2609.11030) Agent-specific. Source-linked catalog, 487-529 records 2022-2026, verbatim-quote rule, taxonomy of causal role / disclosure class / mechanism / outcome Yes - purpose-built for agent incidents ~487-529 (200 with realized harm) Yes - closest peer to this catalog; methodology mirrors ours Eon, Rogue AI Agent Tracker https://www.eon.io/rogue-ai-agent-tracker Agent-specific. Confirmed agent incidents causing production damage, data loss, agent-assisted attacks, eval escapes; ~77 incidents Yes ~77 (33 accidents, 18 agent-assisted attacks, 5 eval escapes) Yes as corroboration Vibe Graveyard https://vibegraveyard.ai/ Broad catalog of AI failures incl. vibe-coding disasters; 60+ stories Not agent-specific; mixes autonomous-vehicle, legal, chatbot failures ~15-20 coding-agent stories Partly - lead-finding only OWASP GenAI Security Project, Incident & Exploit Round-ups https://genai.owasp.org/2025/07/14/owasp-gen-ai-incident-exploit-round-up-q225/ ; https://genai.owasp.org/2025/03/06/owasp-gen-ai-incident-exploit-round-up-jan-feb-2025/ Quarterly GenAI incident lists; 2026 Top-10 weighted by 6,639 incidents No agentic tag on entries (Q2'25 list verified - none tagged agentic) Few true agent-action entries (most are jailbreaks, deepfakes, data leaks) Partly - EchoLeak and tool-poisoning entries reused Simon Willison, prompt-injection tag https://simonwillison.net/tags/prompt-injection/ Curated link blog; 163 posts 2022-2026 De facto agent/injection focus Dozens of product exploits Yes - lead index; linked to primaries we opened Embrace The Red (J. Rehberger) https://embracethered.com/blog/ Researcher disclosures against named products De facto agent focus ~50 product-specific exploit posts 2023-2026 Yes - many primary sources

Is any existing database agent-specific? Yes - three are: METR's Documented AI Agent Incidents, the Agent Incident Registry (Enkrypt AI/Anaconda), and Eon's Rogue AI Agent Tracker. The large general databases (AIID, OECD AIM, AIAAIC, MIT) are not agent-specific; AIID is the most useful of these because its entity pages and 2026 coverage effectively surface agent incidents and link primary reports. The Agent Incident Registry (487-529 source-linked records) is the closest peer to this catalog and is the best external cross-check.

docs.title: Papers swept for an incident appendix
docs.text:
• Shapira et al. 2026, "Agents of Chaos" (arXiv:2602.20021) - opened. No appendix of real-world deployed incidents. It is a lab red-team study (OpenClaw framework, Claude Opus 4.6 + Kimi K2.5, Fly.io VMs, Discord + ProtonMail, 20 researchers, 2 weeks) with 11 representative failure classes. Recorded as lab-only row L6.
  • AgentDojo (arXiv:2406.13352) - opened. Motivational only; a benchmark (97 tasks, 629 security tests), no catalog of real incidents.
  • Greshake et al. 2023 (arXiv:2302.12173) - opened. Seminal indirect-injection paper; demos against Bing Chat (GPT-4) and code-completion engines. Catalog row C01.

docs.title: Sources swept and used (by channel)
docs.text:
• CVE / MITRE CVE API (cveawg.mitre.org): confirmed CVE-2023-29374, 2024-5565, 2025-32711, 2025-49596, 2025-6514, 2025-53773, 2025-54135, 2025-54136, 2025-55284. (CVE-2025-8217 via AWS bulletin; CVE-2026-6442 and CVE-2026-42824 via researcher/CSA write-ups - CVE records not separately opened.)
  • Vendor / operator primaries: AWS Security Bulletin AWS-2025-015; Anthropic (Project Vend, Agentic Misalignment, disrupting AI espionage, Claude for Chrome); Supabase; Invariant Labs; Tracebit; Trail of Bits; Brave; Guardio; Pillar Security; Legit Security; PromptArmor (Superhuman, Claude Cowork, MS Copilot Cowork, Snowflake, Antigravity); Zenity; Noma/Register; AppOmni; UK AISI incident report; Grigorev (AI Shipping Labs); Google AI Dev forum; GitHub issue google-gemini/gemini-cli#4586; Sakana AI; OpenAI o1 system card.
