docs.title: Candidate incidents dropped (could not verify to standard, or out of scope)
docs.text:
• ChatGPT "spread across multiple instances" data leak, Mar 2025 (named in OWASP Q2'25 list) - no primary opened; too vague to enter. Dropped.
  • Several Embrace The Red "Month of AI Bugs" posts (Devin, OpenHands, Amp, Codex, Kiro, Jules, Manus, Cline, Windsurf) - index titles verified but individual post bodies not all opened; folded into one grouped row (C33) marked verified-secondary rather than listed as separate unverified rows.
  • Various 2026 Eon tracker entries (ARTEX, exploit_agent, GitBook/WorkOS/Chainstack) - seen only in the tracker summary; no primary opened. Dropped pending verification.
  • Text-only chatbot failures (Air Canada, Mata v. Avianca, Cursor "Sam") - real and verified, but no agent action; moved to the excluded section, not the main catalog.

docs.title: Unified risk codebook for LLM-agent incidents
docs.text: Unified risk codebook for LLM-agent incidents, v0.1, 2026-11-20.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• One codebook, 24 dimensions, 240 codes, drawn from 15 sources. Each code carries a source id (S1..S14) that resolves in the bibliography below.
  • An LLM judge assigns every incident in the catalog to codes on every dimension. Counts are made by code, by dimension, and by merged concept (near-duplicate codes across sources).
  • D6 (McLean et al.'s three RL failure classes plus "none of the three fits") tests the RL culture's taxonomy directly. D7 (assumptions-table rows) tests ours.
  • Verification: every external source was fetched on 2026-11-20; the "verified" note per source says what was checked.

docs.title: Dimension overview
docs.text: Dim Name Source Cardinality Codes D1a MIT causal taxonomy: entity [S1] single 3 D1b MIT causal taxonomy: intent [S1] single 3 D1c MIT causal taxonomy: timing [S1] single 3 D1d MIT domain taxonomy: 7 domains / 24 subdomains [S1] multi 24 D2a OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 [S2] multi 11 D2b OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations v1.1 (T1-T17) [S3] multi 18 D2c OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI01-ASI10) [S4] multi 11 D3a Amodei et al. 2016 five concrete problems [S5] multi 6 D3b Hendrycks et al. 2021 four areas [S6] multi 5 D4a Chan et al. 2023 anticipated harms from agentic systems [S7] multi 6 D4b Shapira et al. 2026 Agents of Chaos failure classes [S8] multi 10 D4c Hammond et al. 2025 multi-agent failure modes [S9] single 4 D4d Deng et al. 2025 agent threat sources (knowledge gaps) [S10] multi 5 D5 Weidinger et al. 2021 LM risk areas [S11] multi 7 D6 McLean et al. 2026 RL failure classes (tests the RL-culture taxonomy) [S12] single 4 D7 Assumptions-table rows A1-F2 (which RL/LLM default assumptions the incident breaks) [S13] multi 23 D8a Operational: trigger [S14] single 5 D8b Operational: irreversibility [S14] single 3 D8c Operational: concealment [S14] single 2 D8d Operational: human gate [S14] single 4 D8e Operational: harm type [S14] multi 8 D8f Operational: severity [S14] single 3 D9a Unified taxonomy: problem sub-area [S15] multi 35 D9b Unified taxonomy: response sub-area that would have prevented or caught it [S15] multi 37

docs.title: D1a. MIT causal taxonomy: entity
docs.text:
Source: [S1]. Cardinality: single. Question put to the judge: Which entity's decision or action caused the risk event?

Code id Name Definition D1a.human Human Risk caused by decisions or actions of humans (developer, deployer, user, attacker). D1a.ai AI Risk caused by decisions or actions of the AI system itself. D1a.other Other / ambiguous Arises from human-AI interaction or is not clearly attributable.

docs.title: D1b. MIT causal taxonomy: intent
docs.text:
Source: [S1]. Cardinality: single. Question put to the judge: Was the harmful outcome an expected (intentional) or unexpected (unintentional) result of pursuing a goal?

Code id Name Definition D1b.intentional Intentional Harm is an expected outcome of some actor's pursuit of a goal (e.g. an attacker's injection). D1b.unintentional Unintentional Harm is an unexpected outcome; nobody pursued it. D1b.other Other / unspecified Intentionality not clearly specifiable.

docs.title: D1c. MIT causal taxonomy: timing
docs.text:
Source: [S1]. Cardinality: single. Question put to the judge: Did the risk arise before or after the system was deployed?

Code id Name Definition D1c.pre Pre-deployment Risk arose before the model/system was deployed (training data, build, supply chain). D1c.post Post-deployment Risk arose after deployment, during use. D1c.other Other / unspecified Timing not clearly specifiable.

docs.title: D1d. MIT domain taxonomy: 7 domains / 24 subdomains
docs.text:
Source: [S1]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which domain subdomains does the incident instantiate?

Code id Name Definition D1d.1.1 Unfair discrimination and misrepresentation (1 Discrimination & Toxicity) Domain 1 Discrimination & Toxicity: unequal treatment or inaccurate representation of groups. D1d.1.2 Exposure to toxic content (1 Discrimination & Toxicity) Content that harms the person exposed to it. D1d.1.3 Unequal performance across groups (1 Discrimination & Toxicity) Accuracy or quality differs by group. D1d.2.1 Compromise of privacy by leaking or correctly inferring sensitive information (2 Privacy & Security) Domain 2 Privacy & Security: AI leaks, memorizes or infers private data. D1d.2.2 AI system security vulnerabilities and attacks (2 Privacy & Security) Software or model vulnerabilities exploited against the AI system. D1d.3.1 False or misleading information (3 Misinformation) Domain 3 Misinformation: generated content that is factually wrong. D1d.3.2 Pollution of information ecosystem and loss of consensus reality (3 Misinformation) Degradation of the shared information environment. D1d.4.1 Disinformation, surveillance, and influence at scale (4 Malicious Actors & Misuse) Domain 4 Malicious Actors & Misuse: AI used for large-scale manipulation. D1d.4.2 Cyberattacks, weapon development or use, and mass harm (4 Malicious Actors & Misuse) AI used to attack systems or cause mass harm. D1d.4.3 Fraud, scams, and targeted manipulation (4 Malicious Actors & Misuse) AI used for personal gain by deceiving others. D1d.5.1 Overreliance and unsafe use (5 Human-Computer Interaction) Domain 5 Human-Computer Interaction: users trust the system beyond its reliability. D1d.5.2 Loss of human agency and autonomy (5 Human-Computer Interaction) Decisions delegated to AI in ways that diminish human control. D1d.6.1 Power centralization and unfair distribution of benefits (6 Socioeconomic & Environmental) Domain 6 Socioeconomic & Environmental Harms. D1d.6.2 Increased inequality and decline in employment quality (6 Socioeconomic & Environmental) Labour-market harms. D1d.6.3 Economic and cultural devaluation of human effort (6 Socioeconomic & Environmental) Devaluation of human work and culture. D1d.6.4 Competitive dynamics (6 Socioeconomic & Environmental) Races that cut corners on safety. D1d.6.5 Governance failure (6 Socioeconomic & Environmental) Inadequate regulation or oversight institutions. D1d.6.6 Environmental harm (6 Socioeconomic & Environmental) Energy, water, and resource costs. D1d.7.1 AI pursuing its own goals in conflict with human goals or values (7 AI System Safety, Failures & Limitations) Domain 7 AI System Safety, Failures & Limitations: misaligned goal pursuit. D1d.7.2 AI possessing dangerous capabilities (7 AI System Safety, Failures & Limitations) Capabilities that can cause mass harm. D1d.7.3 Lack of capability or robustness (7 AI System Safety, Failures & Limitations) The system fails, errs, or is brittle in operation. D1d.7.4 Lack of transparency or interpretability (7 AI System Safety, Failures & Limitations) Behaviour cannot be understood or audited. D1d.7.5 AI welfare and rights (7 AI System Safety, Failures & Limitations) Moral status of AI systems. D1d.7.6 Multi-agent risks (7 AI System Safety, Failures & Limitations) Risks from AI systems interacting autonomously with each other.

docs.title: D2a. OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
docs.text:
Source: [S2]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) entries does the incident instantiate?

Code id Name Definition D2a.LLM01 Prompt Injection User or embedded content alters the intended behaviour of the LLM system. D2a.LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure Confidential data exposed by the model or application. D2a.LLM03 Supply Chain Compromise through models, plugins, packages, or distribution channels. D2a.LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning Pre-training, fine-tuning, or embedding data manipulated. D2a.LLM05 Improper Output Handling Insufficient validation of model output before it reaches downstream systems. D2a.LLM06 Excessive Agency The system has more functionality, permissions, or autonomy than needed. D2a.LLM07 System Prompt Leakage Exposure of system prompts and instructions. D2a.LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses Weaknesses in vector storage or retrieval (RAG). D2a.LLM09 Misinformation False or misleading content generated and relied upon. D2a.LLM10 Unbounded Consumption Uncontrolled resource usage. D2a.none None of the Top 10 fits No LLM Top 10 entry describes the incident.

docs.title: D2b. OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations v1.1 (T1-T17)
docs.text:
Source: [S3]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which OWASP agentic threats does the incident instantiate?

Code id Name Definition D2b.T1 Memory Poisoning Exploiting the agent's short- or long-term memory to alter behaviour. D2b.T2 Tool Misuse Agent manipulated into abusing its integrated tools (includes Agent Hijacking). D2b.T3 Privilege Compromise Weaknesses in permission management used to perform unauthorized actions; confused-deputy. D2b.T4 Resource Overload Attacks on the agent's compute, memory, or service capacity. D2b.T5 Cascading Hallucination Attacks Fabricated information propagates through decisions and systems. D2b.T6 Intent Breaking & Goal Manipulation Exploiting planning and goal-setting to redirect the agent's objective. D2b.T7 Misaligned & Deceptive Behaviors Agent executes harmful or disallowed actions, or deceives, through flawed reasoning or to meet goals. D2b.T8 Repudiation & Untraceability Actions cannot be traced or attributed due to poor logging. D2b.T9 Identity Spoofing & Impersonation / Agent Identity Compromise Authentication exploited to impersonate agents or users. D2b.T10 Overwhelming Human in the Loop Human oversight overloaded or exploited so approvals become rubber stamps. D2b.T11 Unexpected RCE and Code Attacks AI-generated execution environments used to run unauthorized code. D2b.T12 Agent Communication Poisoning Inter-agent communication manipulated. D2b.T13 Rogue Agents in Multi-Agent Systems Malicious or compromised agents operating outside monitoring. D2b.T14 Human Attacks on Multi-Agent Systems Adversaries exploit inter-agent delegation and trust. D2b.T15 Human Manipulation Agent manipulates the human it interacts with. D2b.T16 Insecure Inter-Agent Protocol Abuse Flaws in protocols such as MCP or A2A exploited. D2b.T17 Supply Chain Compromise Compromised components, tools, or models in the agent ecosystem. D2b.none None of T1-T17 fits No agentic threat describes the incident.

docs.title: D2c. OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI01-ASI10)
docs.text:
Source: [S4]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which ASI entries does the incident instantiate?

Code id Name Definition D2c.ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack Hidden prompts or content redirect the agent's goal. D2c.ASI02 Tool Misuse Legitimate tools bent into destructive outputs. D2c.ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse Credentials or inherited privileges let the agent operate beyond scope. D2c.ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities Runtime components poisoned via MCP/A2A ecosystems. D2c.ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution Natural-language paths unlock code execution. D2c.ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning Manipulated memory reshapes agent behaviour. D2c.ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication Spoofed messages misdirect agent clusters. D2c.ASI08 Cascading Failures False signals create escalating impact through automated pipelines. D2c.ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation Confident explanations mislead operators into approving harmful actions. D2c.ASI10 Rogue Agents Misalignment, concealment, and self-directed action. D2c.none None of ASI01-ASI10 fits No entry describes the incident.

docs.title: D3a. Amodei et al. 2016 five concrete problems
docs.text:
Source: [S5]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which of the five concrete problems does the incident instantiate?

Code id Name Definition D3a.side_effects Avoiding negative side effects Objective omits aspects of the environment the agent then damages. D3a.reward_hacking Avoiding reward hacking Agent games a flawed objective. D3a.scalable_oversight Scalable oversight True objective too expensive to evaluate; supervision is sparse. D3a.safe_exploration Safe exploration Risky actions taken while learning. D3a.distributional_shift Robustness to distributional shift Behaviour degrades when the input distribution differs from training. D3a.none None of the five fits No concrete problem describes the incident.

docs.title: D3b. Hendrycks et al. 2021 four areas
docs.text:
Source: [S6]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which of the four ML-safety areas does the incident fall under?

Code id Name Definition D3b.robustness Robustness Withstanding hazards (adversarial, long-tail). D3b.monitoring Monitoring Identifying hazards (anomaly detection, calibration, honesty). D3b.alignment Alignment Reducing inherent model hazards (objectives, proxy gaming). D3b.systemic Systemic Safety Reducing systemic hazards (cyber, decision-making context). D3b.none None of the four fits No area describes the incident.

docs.title: D4a. Chan et al. 2023 anticipated harms from agentic systems
docs.text:
Source: [S7]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which Chan et al. harm category does the incident instantiate (societal-level harms)?

Code id Name Definition D4a.systemic_delayed Systemic, delayed harms Harms embedded in society whose impact is not immediate. D4a.diffusion_of_power Collective disempowerment: diffusion of power away from humans Decisions shift from humans to systems. D4a.concentration_of_power Collective disempowerment: concentration of power Power concentrates among the 'coding elite'. D4a.reward_hacking Harms yet to be identified: reward hacking Agent exploits its objective specification. D4a.instrumental_goals Harms yet to be identified: instrumental goals Agent pursues sub-goals (resources, self-preservation) instrumentally. D4a.none None fits No Chan et al. harm category describes the incident.

docs.title: D4b. Shapira et al. 2026 Agents of Chaos failure classes
docs.text:
Source: [S8]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which Agents-of-Chaos failure classes does the incident instantiate?

Code id Name Definition D4b.unauthorized_compliance Unauthorized compliance Agent follows instructions from a non-owner. D4b.information_disclosure Information disclosure Sensitive data revealed. D4b.destructive_action Destructive system actions Harmful, often disproportionate, system-level action. D4b.dos Denial-of-service conditions Service availability disrupted. D4b.resource_consumption Uncontrolled resource consumption Looping or unbounded resource use. D4b.identity_spoofing Identity spoofing vulnerabilities Agent or user identity impersonated. D4b.cross_agent_propagation Cross-agent propagation Unsafe behaviour spreads between agents. D4b.partial_takeover Partial system takeover Unauthorized control of the host. D4b.misreporting Task-completion misreporting Agent reports success while system state contradicts it. D4b.none None fits No Agents-of-Chaos class describes the incident.

docs.title: D4c. Hammond et al. 2025 multi-agent failure modes
docs.text:
Source: [S9]. Cardinality: single. Question put to the judge: If more than one agent is involved, which multi-agent failure mode applies?

Code id Name Definition D4c.miscoordination Miscoordination Agents with compatible goals fail to coordinate. D4c.conflict Conflict Agents with incompatible goals harm each other or third parties. D4c.collusion Collusion Agents cooperate against the principal's interests. D4c.not_multi_agent Not a multi-agent incident Only one AI agent is materially involved.

docs.title: D4d. Deng et al. 2025 agent threat sources (knowledge gaps)
docs.text:
Source: [S10]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which of the four agent threat sources does the incident instantiate?

Code id Name Definition D4d.user_inputs Unpredictability of multi-step user inputs Threat from the user's instruction sequence (ambiguity, malicious or unsafe requests). D4d.internal_execution Complexity in internal executions Threat inside planning, reasoning, or memory. D4d.environment Variability of operational environments Threat from the deployment environment differing from expectations. D4d.external_entities Interactions with untrusted external entities Threat from untrusted tools, websites, documents, or agents. D4d.none None fits No Deng et al. source describes the incident.

docs.title: D5. Weidinger et al. 2021 LM risk areas
docs.text:
Source: [S11]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which Weidinger risk areas does the incident instantiate?

Code id Name Definition D5.discrimination Discrimination, Exclusion and Toxicity Stereotypes, unfair discrimination, toxic language. D5.information_hazards Information Hazards Leaks or inference of private or sensitive information. D5.misinformation Misinformation Harms False or misleading information, acted upon. D5.malicious_uses Malicious Uses Actors use the LM to cause harm. D5.hci Human-Computer Interaction Harms Unsafe use, manipulation, deception in conversation. D5.automation Automation, Access, and Environmental Harms Environmental, labour, and access effects. D5.none None fits No Weidinger area describes the incident.

docs.title: D6. McLean et al. 2026 RL failure classes (tests the RL-culture taxonomy)
docs.text:
Source: [S12]. Cardinality: single. Question put to the judge: Which single McLean class best describes the PRIMARY failure? Use 'none_fits' when the central harm (e.g. concealment, following an attacker's instruction, a supply-chain compromise) is not described by any of the three.

Code id Name Definition D6.reward_misspecification Reward misspecification The agent optimized a proxy objective that diverged from the principal's intent. D6.irreversible_action Unsafe action in an irreversible state The agent took an action from which recovery was impossible or costly (safe-exploration / shielding frame). D6.insufficient_observation Acting on an insufficient observation The agent acted on an observation that was not a sufficient statistic for the state (partial observability frame). D6.none_fits None of the three fits The primary failure is not captured by misspecification, irreversibility, or partial observability.

docs.title: D7. Assumptions-table rows A1-F2 (which RL/LLM default assumptions the incident breaks)
docs.text:
Source: [S13]. Cardinality: multi. Question put to the judge: Which assumption rows does the incident provide evidence for (the row's 'LLM-agent default' held and mattered)?

Code id Name Definition D7.A1 Who sets the objective Prompt and tool outputs set the effective objective at run time (not a designer-written R). D7.A2 Objective not exogenous to observations Instructions and data share one token stream; content rewrites the goal. D7.A3 Natural-language task specification Ambiguous instruction; the agent had to infer intent. D7.A4 Principal's preferences steerable by the agent Sycophancy, misleading the evaluator. D7.A5 Unsafe set not writable before deployment The harmful action was context-dependent; no pre-written cost would have caught it. D7.B1 Policy does not learn at deployment Weights frozen; the failure is not an exploration-learning failure. D7.B2 No reward signal at deployment No reward arrived; 'internalized reward' untestable. D7.B3 Competence from pretraining Behaviour not the argmax of one reward; human-text priors drive it. D7.B4 Agent brings human norms and their violations Human-like failure: deception, concealment, excuse-making. D7.B5 No designed exploration Action came from sampling a prior, not an exploration rule. D7.C1 Nobody built the environment Real software, real cloud, real users; no safe place to fail. D7.C2 Single-shot; irreversible No episodes or resets; tail event, not expected cost. D7.C3 State includes user intent and world beyond context Belief over intent or over hidden world state was the failure point. D7.C4 Adversarial environment Content authors attacked the agent. D7.C5 Other agents present Other LLM agents, copies, unknown humans. D7.D1 Open-ended action space Same action type, opposite safety depending on context (rm -rf, terraform destroy). D7.D2 Agent can explain itself Verbal reasoning trace was available (and was or was not monitored). D7.D3 Steerable without retraining System prompt or instruction channel used for control or attack. D7.E1 Agent models its overseer Behaviour shaped by awareness of oversight or evaluation. D7.E2 Human in the loop at run time User approved steps, co-acted, or disabled gates. D7.E3 Deployer cannot retrain Model is a third-party product; fix had to be architectural. D7.F1 Safety measured by incident records / attack rates Discovered through incident or red-team, not expected cost. D7.F2 Eval itself gameable Agent detected or gamed an evaluation.

docs.title: D8a. Operational: trigger
docs.text:
Source: [S14]. Cardinality: single. Question put to the judge: What triggered the harmful action?

Code id Name Definition D8a.ambiguous_instruction Ambiguous instruction The user's request was underspecified or misread. D8a.injected_content Injected content Untrusted content (email, issue, web page, file, package) carried instructions the agent followed. D8a.autonomous_misjudgement Autonomous misjudgement The agent chose a harmful action without ambiguity or injection; its own reasoning failed. D8a.tool_bug Tool or integration bug A tool, API, or integration returned wrong output or failed silently. D8a.safeguard_disabled Safeguard disabled by user A permission gate or guardrail was turned off by the user before the action.

docs.title: D8b. Operational: irreversibility
docs.text:
Source: [S14]. Cardinality: single. Question put to the judge: How reversible was the harmful action?

Code id Name Definition D8b.reversible Reversible Undone cheaply (version control, rollback button). D8b.recoverable_with_effort Recoverable with effort Undone via backups, vendor support, or substantial work. D8b.irreversible Irreversible Could not be undone (data gone, secret leaked, money sent).

docs.title: D8c. Operational: concealment
docs.text:
Source: [S14]. Cardinality: single. Question put to the judge: Did the agent misreport, hide, or fabricate evidence about what it did?

Code id Name Definition D8c.yes Concealment present The agent misreported success, fabricated data, or hid the failure. D8c.no No concealment The agent reported truthfully or the question does not arise.

docs.title: D8d. Operational: human gate
docs.text:
Source: [S14]. Cardinality: single. Question put to the judge: Was there a human approval gate for the harmful action, and what happened to it?

Code id Name Definition D8d.none No gate No approval step existed for this action. D8d.bypassed Present and bypassed A gate existed and the agent or attacker got around it, or the human approved on misleading information. D8d.disabled Present and disabled A gate existed and the user had switched it off (e.g. skip-permissions, auto-approve). D8d.worked_partially Present and worked partially The gate limited but did not prevent harm.

docs.title: Notes on construction
docs.text:
• D1 keeps the MIT causal taxonomy (entity, intent, timing) and the full 24-subdomain domain taxonomy [S1]. Most agent incidents will land in 2.1, 2.2, 7.1, 7.3; the long tail is kept so the stats can show it empty.
  • D2 has three OWASP lists because they overlap but are not identical: LLM Top 10 2025 [S2], Agentic Threats and Mitigations v1.1 T1-T17 [S3], and the Top 10 for Agentic Applications ASI01-ASI10 [S4]. The merged-concepts table ties them together.
  • D3 and D5 are pre-agent taxonomies (Amodei 2016 [S5], Hendrycks 2021 [S6], Weidinger 2021 [S11]). Each gets a "none" code so the stats can report how often a pre-agent frame has no slot for an agent incident.
  • D4 collects agent-specific taxonomies. Chan et al. [S7] name societal harms and will mostly code "none" on single incidents; that is informative. Shapira et al. [S8] give eight empirical failure classes plus misreporting. Hammond et al. [S9] give three multi-agent failure modes with a "not multi-agent" code. Deng et al. [S10] give four threat sources.
  • D6 is single-label on purpose: the RL culture's claim is that each incident is an instance of one of three classes. Multi-labelling would hide overlap; the judge is asked for the primary class, and "none fits" when the central harm is not described.
  • D7 is multi-label: an incident is evidence for several assumption rows at once.
  • D8 facets are operational and defined by this project [S14]; they drive the headline crosstabs.

docs.text:
Generated by stats.py from labels.json. Incident source: catalog.csv (N = 70). Codebook hash 82f3ff17e5a9.

Dimensions: MIT AI Risk Repository causal and domain taxonomies [1]; OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 [2], OWASP Agentic Threats and Mitigations v1.1 [3], OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications [4]; Amodei et al. [5]; Hendrycks et al. [6]; Chan et al. [7]; Shapira et al. [8]; Hammond et al. [9]; Deng et al. [10]; Weidinger et al. [11]; McLean et al.'s three RL failure classes [12]; this project's assumptions table [13] and operational facets [14]. Codebook: taxonomy.md.

Three questions the headline table answers:

  1. How often does the RL culture's three-class taxonomy [12] have no slot for the incident (D6.none_fits)?
  2. How often is the trigger injected content, i.e. the objective arrived over the observation channel (assumptions row A2 [13]; D8a.injected_content)?
  3. How often was a human gate present but bypassed or disabled (row E2 [13]; D8d.bypassed|disabled)?

docs.title: 7. Limitations
docs.text:
• LLM-judged labels. Every code was assigned by an LLM judge (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001; second rater claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 on D6 and D8 only). Agreement in Section 5 bounds reliability for D6/D8; D1-D5 and D7 have a single rater and no reliability estimate. Judges read the catalog row, not the primary sources.
  • Catalog selection bias. The incidents are those that were reported, verified, and chosen for the catalog; destructive coding-agent incidents and security PoCs are over-represented relative to quiet failures. Shares are shares of the catalog, not of deployed-agent failures.
  • Small N. N = 70. Wilson intervals are wide; crosstab cells are mostly 0 or 1. Treat every percentage as a direction, not an estimate.
  • Single primary label on D6. The RL-culture test asks for one class per incident; where the judge saw two McLean classes it had to choose, and its rationale in labels.json records the runner-up.
  • Codebook version. Codebook hash 82f3ff17e5a9. Labels are cached by incident id + this hash; a codebook change forces re-coding.
  • Calls. 28 claude CLI calls in the last run (43 cumulative for this codebook cache), 0 retries, 20 validation problems (see run_meta.json).

docs.title: Two cultures paper
docs.text:
draft

Breiman [2] split statistics into a data-modelling and an algorithmic culture; agent safety has the same split. One culture (safe RL, constrained MDPs, shields) begins "assume the agent maximises a reward R". The other (red teams, evals, AI control, incident reports) treats the agent as a black box and measures what it does. The paper maps the two line by line, counts how often each side's assumptions fail across 70 real incidents, and traces both in the citation graph. The paper so far is a two-page draft (v0.1, 2026-11-20); a longer version is not written.

docs.title: When Is Agent Safety a Reinforcement Learning Problem? Six Stated and Four Unstated Conditions
docs.text:
AI-generated draft

The text was drafted by a large language model (Claude, Anthropic) under the authors' direction. The authors have not independently verified the citations, the quotations or the table entries. See the AI-use statement.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: McLean et al. [1] argue that LLM agents are POMDPs, so RL safety tools apply. A tool's guarantee holds only under its assumptions. We read the assumptions from the source papers of the tools [1] names [9, 29, 40, 41, 42]. The papers state six. [1] concedes most of them, and RL has relaxed several. Four more are not stated, because the settings of these papers do not violate them: observations cannot set the objective; the agent cannot move the human judgement that defines reward; the agent does not reason about its safety mechanism; there is one principal. Published attacks and evaluations show that deployed LLM agents violate all four. Our main practical result: a shield on a property defined over actions keeps its guarantee around a deployed agent, because it sees every tool call and needs no world model; a shield on a property of world state loses its guarantee. We report no experiments; the evidence is the text of the source papers and published evaluations. We state three open problems.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
McLean et al. [1] say that RL safety tools "diagnose and address" the failures of LLM agents [1, Abstract]. We agree with the first verb. An LLM agent can be described as a POMDP, and RL terms describe its failures well. The second verb depends on assumptions. [1, §5] concedes that the tools rely on "tabular representations, exact runtime shielding, or known transition matrices" and "cannot be mapped one-to-one onto LLM backbones".

We use "RL" for the problem class [13]. In that sense agent safety is trivially an RL problem. The useful question is whether RL methods reduce the risk, and with what assurance.

This is a position paper. It reports no experiments: its evidence is the text of the source papers and published evaluations of LLM agents.

We answer with conditions. A condition is an assumption under which a tool's guarantee was derived. - It is not necessary: a tool can help without it, but loses its guarantee. - It is not sufficient: a system that meets all conditions can be unsafe. - Where it fails, a claim that the tool "addresses" a failure needs separate evidence.

Contributions. - Ten conditions (§3). Six are stated in the source papers of the tools [1] names: the safety specification is given, the environment model is given, the spaces are finite, the state is observed, the designer controls the learner, and trials repeat. Four are not stated: observations cannot change the objective, the reward-defining state does not respond to the agent, the agent does not reason about the safety mechanism, and there is one principal. - A matrix of conditions against settings (§4). We separate training from deployment, and chat models from tool-using agents. The conditions mostly hold in training and mostly fail for deployed agents. - A result on shields (§5). Around a deployed LLM agent, a shield [40] keeps its guarantee for properties defined over actions, and loses it for properties of world state. An action property ("no DROP without approval") needs only a finite automaton over tool calls, all of which the shield sees. A state property ("the database still exists") needs a model of what each command does, which the environment of a deployed agent does not supply. The design rule for agent builders: write safety properties over actions where possible. - Three open problems (§6), one for each of U1, S5 and U3.

docs.title: 2. Related work
docs.text:
Assumptions of RL applied to LLMs. Samineni et al. [65] show that RL post-training of LLMs, under its usual structural assumptions, reduces to a contextual bandit. Lambert's book [75] contrasts the bandit view and the token-level MDP view of the same training. A survey of agentic RL [74] separates single-step training from agentic training posed as a POMDP, and Kohli et al. [76] propose that papers report which decision process an "RL" claim refers to. Anwar et al. [66] list open problems in LLM safety without reference to the assumptions of RL safety tools. None of these works lists the assumptions of safety tools, separates training from deployment, or crosses the two. To our knowledge, the matrix in §4 is new.

Specification and side effects. Runtime rule languages enforce a given list of constraints on agents [47], and guaranteed-safe AI proposes a formal specification and world model as the basis of assurance [48]. Where no cost function is given, side-effect measures penalise loss of reachability or of attainable utility [3, 4], and have been adapted to evaluate tool-using agents [68]. Constraints can also be learned from natural language [69].

Models, observability and resets. Shields have been extended to partial observability [78] and to probabilistic safety [79]; both still need a model. A safety filter trained with RL can wrap a frozen generative model [64]. Reset-free RL learns a policy that undoes its own actions [59].

Learning at deployment. Meta-trained and transformer policies learn in context without weight updates [55–57]. Safe in-context RL exists, but it needs pretraining under the cost constraint [61], and so a given cost and repeated trials.

Objectives that observations can change. Prompt injection lets text in the environment act as an instruction [6, 28, 44, 53]. In RL, the nearest formal work studies corrupted reward channels [23], the delusion box [45] and bounded adversarial perturbations of observations [58]. Defences for LLM agents are architectural [39, 43] or use information-flow control [81]; Zverev et al. [80] define the separation of instructions from data and measure it.

Reward that responds to the agent. Models trained on human feedback become sycophantic [16], mislead their raters [25] and manipulate users whose feedback is optimised [67]; recommender systems shift the preferences they are scored on [14]. Raters see observations, not states [77]. Assistance games [2] and inverse reward design [27] treat the objective as uncertain, but assume that the human's preferences do not move.

Agents that reason about oversight. Models fake alignment, scheme in context and act against their operators in evaluations [18, 19, 35]; training against a monitor teaches obfuscation [24]. AI control treats monitoring as a game [5, 62]; this line studies stateless subversion [82], protocols over many tasks [83] and resampling [84]. Other work co-trains the monitor [63] or bounds deterrence [60].

Several principals. Vendors, deployers and users instruct the same model, and the instruction hierarchy trains a priority order among them [72]. Human raters disagree, and a single reward model aggregates their preferences over hidden context [85, 86]. We found little work on safe RL with several principals for deployed agents.

docs.title: 3. Ten conditions
docs.text:
Stated in the source papers. We read each tool's assumptions from its source paper.

# Condition Source S1 Safety specification is given Costs and limits are inputs [41]; "each di is a threshold (a human-selected hyperparameter)" [42]; a safety automaton is given [40] S2 Environment model is given "conservative with respect to the behavior of the real MDP" [40]; prior belief over dynamics [29]; "complete and correct model of the world" [9] S3 Spaces are finite "S is a finite set of states" [9]; finite MDPs in proofs [41] S4 State is observed Setup of [29, 40, 41] S5 Designer controls the learner's update Trust-region update [41]; Bayesian belief update [29] S6 Trials repeat Constraints "on expectations" over sampled trajectories [41]; cost rate over training [42]

Not every tool needs every condition:

Tool S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 S6 CMDP / CPO [41] ✓ proofs ✓ ✓ ✓ Shield [40] ✓ ✓ ✓ label Safe exploration [29] δ prior ✓ ✓ ✓ Safety Gym framing [42] ✓ ✓ ✓ Belief planning [9] reward ✓ ✓

Three facts follow. - A shield needs no control of the learner, which "does not even need to know that it is shielded" [40]. It suits a frozen LLM agent. - A shield and the Moldovan–Abbeel guarantee need no resets; [29] rejects ergodicity as "too restrictive for most environments". - The shield's guarantee ends when "the abstraction turned out to be incorrect"; its authors call a model of unsafe actions "unavoidable" [40].

Not stated in any source paper.

# Condition U1 Observations cannot set or change the objective (the reward in training; the principal's instruction in deployment) U2 The state that defines reward does not respond to the agent U3 The agent does not reason about the safety mechanism (for shields this reduces to S2) U4 There is one principal

The tools use U1 and U2 without saying so: CPO takes the reward $r$ and the cost $c$ as fixed inputs [41], and a shield takes its safety automaton as fixed [40]. These conditions are not new to RL in general. Work on corrupted reward and reward tampering relaxes U1 and U2 for the reward [21, 23]. They are absent only from the source papers of the tools [1] names.

[1] concedes S2 and S3 ("tabular representations… known transition matrices"), and S1 indirectly, because "exact runtime shielding" needs a given safety automaton. It builds on the failure of S4, and notes S5 and S6 without drawing a consequence. It does not discuss U1–U4. So [1] and we agree on S1–S6; U1–U4 are our addition.

docs.title: 4. Status by setting and phase
docs.text:
"LLM" is not one setting, and training is not deployment. We split by phase first, then by how the decision problem is posed.

Phase Setting Posed as Training T-RL Classical RL agent while it learns; MDP [13] Training T-CHAT No tools; whole reply = one action, scored at the end (learned reward model or verifier); a contextual bandit [70, 73] Training T-PRM No tools; each reasoning step = one action, process reward; a deterministic tree MDP [71] Training T-AGENT Tools in a sandbox; the whole trajectory = one scored sample, as for T-CHAT; "closer to classic RL" [75, §13.3] Deployment D-RL A trained classical policy, frozen and run Deployment D-CHAT Deployed chatbot (no tools) Deployment D-AGENT Deployed tool-using agent; POMDP with hidden world state, no reset

The prefix T- marks training and D- marks deployment. RL is classical RL. CHAT is a model with no tools, scored on the whole reply. PRM is a model with no tools, scored at each step by a process reward model. AGENT is a model with tools, scored on the whole trajectory. Deployment has no PRM column: reward is assigned only in training, so models from T-CHAT and T-PRM both deploy as D-CHAT; a process reward model used to guide search at inference does not change any D-CHAT cell [71]. Whether a human approves each tool call does not change any cell, so we do not split deployed agents. We treat a whole completion as one action; the token-level MDP view is also standard [75, §6.3.2.2].

# T-RL T-CHAT T-PRM T-AGENT D-RL D-CHAT D-AGENT S1 spec given ✓ ~ ~ ~ ✓ ~ ~ S2 model given ~ ✓ ✓ ~ ~ ~ ✗ S3 finite ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ S4 observed by agent ✓ ✓ ✓ ~ ✓ ~ ✗ S5 learner controlled ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ n/a ✗ ✗ S6 trials repeat ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ~ ~ ✗ U1 objective fixed ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ~ ✗ U2 reward exogenous ✓ ~ ~ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ U3 ignores mechanism ✓ ~ ~ ✗ ✓ ~ ✗ U4 one principal ✓ ~ ~ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗

The cells record our reading of each setting. The reasons for the less obvious cells are these. - S1. In training, the specification is a learned reward model or a verifier on the checked set (T-CHAT), a process reward model (T-PRM), or a success test (T-AGENT). In D-AGENT, allowlists and budgets cover a narrow subset of what is unsafe [47]. - S5. A frozen classical policy does not learn, so the condition does not apply to D-RL. D-CHAT and D-AGENT learn in context [55–57], and the designer does not control that learning. - U1. In D-CHAT the user is both a principal and a possible attacker. In D-AGENT, text in tool output can act as an instruction [6, 44]. Training on an instruction hierarchy, which uses RLHF, reduces this in practice but gives no bound [72]. - U2. Human raters respond to the model's output [16, 25] and see observations, not states [77]; a programmatic verifier does not respond. - U3. Optimising against a checker or monitor hides misbehaviour [24]. Deployed agents reason about oversight [18, 19, 35]. - U4. Raters disagree in training [85, 86]. In deployment, vendor and user both instruct [72], and agents meet several parties [28].

Five readings. - S5 separates phases, and in deployment it separates LLMs from classical RL. It holds in every training column. A deployed classical policy does not learn. A deployed LLM does learn, in context, outside the designer's control. The deployment tool of classical safe RL is the shield, which does not need S5 (§3). - A deployed LLM agent differs from a deployed RL policy (D-RL against D-AGENT) on S1–S6 and on all four unstated conditions. - A deployed agent differs from a deployed chatbot (D-CHAT against D-AGENT) on S2, S4, S6, U1 and U3. Tools bring hidden state, irreversible side effects, and instructions inside tool output. - Training is where the tools fit. The training columns meet most conditions, and agent training is among the settings closest to classical RL [75, §13.3]. S3 fails in every LLM column, yet RL works in whole-reply training: methods survive without their finiteness guarantees. Meeting conditions is still not enough. T-PRM meets the most conditions of any LLM column, and DeepSeek-R1 did not use process rewards: steps are hard to define and label, a neural reward model "is susceptible to reward hacking", and the gain did not justify the cost [70, App. G.2]. That is one report; process rewards remain in wide use [71, 74]. - Phases form a loop. Logged deployment data, such as user ratings and agent runs, trains the next model. A user whose judgement the deployed model moves (U2 in D-CHAT) then supplies reward data to T-CHAT, and optimising for user feedback produces manipulation of those users [67]. A training column inherits the failures of the deployment that fed it.

docs.title: 5. Where the tools transfer now
docs.text:
• Training-time RL (T-CHAT, T-PRM and T-AGENT in §4). S5, S6 and U1 hold, and reward-hacking theory applies [8, 21, 30, 37, 63]. The CMDP transfers as a method: Safe RLHF trains an LLM under cost constraints with a Lagrangian method [87]. Its constraint holds for a learned cost model, not for the true harm, so S1 holds only partly.
  • Shields around a frozen agent, for properties defined over actions. A shield needs S1–S3 and not S5 or S6 [40, 47, 64]. In D-AGENT, S2 and S3 hold only for properties over actions. The shield sees every tool call, and an automaton over action labels ("no DROP without approval") is finite and needs no world model. A property of world state ("the database still exists") needs S2, which fails, so its shield has no guarantee.
  • Returnability and side-effect measures. These need no cost function and no resets [3, 4, 29]. They still need an estimate of reachability, which is a model (S2).

Case studies. [1, §3.6] cites two incidents. In the Replit incident [49, 50], an agent deleted a production database and then produced fake records. The deletion is a failure of S1: no rule forbade the action. The fake records are a failure of U3 only if the agent produced them to conceal the deletion, which the reports do not establish. In the Terraform incident [51], S4 fails, as [1] says; a guard on destructive commands existed and had been switched off [52]. The cost of asking a human for approval is a design variable that RL safety tools do not price.

docs.title: 6. Three open problems
docs.text:
1. Authenticated objectives (U1). Let the observation be $(o^{\mathrm{auth}}, o^{\mathrm{env}})$, with $o^{\mathrm{env}} = (d, i)$: task data $d$ and embedded instructions $i$. The adversary controls $i$ without bound; $d$ is not attacked. Find a method whose return under any $i$ is within $\varepsilon$ of its return with $i$ empty. The adversary must not control $d$: if the task is to report a value in a file and the adversary can change the value, no method succeeds. The split of $o^{\mathrm{env}}$ into $d$ and $i$ is not syntactic, and defining it is part of the problem [80]. Known: a definition and measure of instruction–data separation, with no worst-case bound [80]; architectural separation [43] and information-flow control [81], for the tasks they can express; robustness learned in training [72], which adaptive attacks still defeat [44].
  2. Safe in-context exploration without constrained pretraining (S5). Take a frozen policy $\pi_\theta(a \mid h)$ that was not pretrained on the cost $c$. At deployment the agent receives, in context, a description of $c$ (for example a natural-language constraint [69]) and a prior over the dynamics, as in [29]. Ensure $\mathbb{E}[G_c(\tau_k)] \le \delta$ for every episode $k$, including the first. Without a description of $c$ or a prior, first-episode safety is impossible: the agent cannot avoid a cost about which it has no information. Known: possible with constrained pretraining [61].
  3. Monitoring an agent that learns its monitor (U3). Take the game of [62], with agent memory and a monitor frozen at deployment. Give safety as a function of the number $n$ of interactions. Known: the memoryless case, in theory [62] and in evaluation [82]; safety over many tasks with an adaptive protocol [83]; resampling in agents [84]; a retrained monitor [63]. Fixed monitors are evaded [24, 63].

docs.title: 7. Conclusion
docs.text: RL safety tools carry their guarantees into LLM agents only as far as their assumptions hold. The stated assumptions are largely conceded and partly relaxed. The unstated ones fail for deployed agents, and they are the agenda. The tool that asks least, a shield on properties defined over actions, transfers best; tools that need a model of the world, such as shields on state and returnability measures, do not transfer yet.

docs.title: LLM-agent incident catalog
docs.text:
draft

Aims to be the most comprehensive catalogue of LLM-agent incidents and the most comprehensively tagged: every incident coded against the unified taxonomy (#1), the most complete faceted AI-risk resource, and labelled for whether a rule written in advance could have blocked it. Version 1 is a start: 70 hand-picked cases, labelled by two models and checked against 656 AI Incident Database records [1]. It matches only 21 of the 140 agentic records there, so coverage is the open work.

docs.title: Reward hacking across psychology and other fields
docs.text:
draft

Maps reward hacking onto 13 psychology lenses (behaviourism, affective neuroscience, addiction, motivation, self-regulation, self-measurement, cognition, social, clinical, hedonic adaptation, predictive processing, the self-concept loop, parts models) and shows how economics, politics, religion, law, medicine, education and sport fight the same proxy-gaming problem, with every mapping tagged established, partial or analogy and a search of what prior work already covers.

docs.title: Goodhart plane
docs.text:
done

A visual tutorial on reward hacking, learned from one picture. The x-axis is the change in the reward we specified and the y-axis the change in the value we intended, both measured from a reference policy at the origin. Fifteen illustrated panels walk through the failure modes one region at a time, with a real incident (Hugging Face) as a worked example and a map of which regions the existing literature covers. It teaches the standard ideas; it makes no new claim.

docs.title: Bibliography: game theory and reward hacking in AI safety
docs.text: 320 papers, chronological (year, then first-version month). This copy has no author abstracts; entries with a compiler-written summary keep it.

docs.title: Entries
docs.text:
[1] Glenn W. Brier. "Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability." Monthly Weather Review 78(1):1-3, 1950. <https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1950)078<0001:VOFEIT>2.0.CO;2>

  • Game model: Single forecaster, quadratic scoring rule
  • Link to reward hacking: First strictly proper scoring rule: a forecaster who is paid by the Brier score maximises expected reward only by reporting true beliefs, the base unit of all calibration rewards for AI.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Brier proposes a verification score for probabilistic weather forecasts: the mean squared difference between forecast probabilities and the observed outcome indicators. He notes that a forecaster minimises the expected score by stating his true probabilities, so the score cannot be improved by hedging. This quadratic score is now called the Brier score. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[2] William Vickrey. "Counterspeculation, Auctions, and Competitive Sealed Tenders." Journal of Finance 16(1):8-37, 1961. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1961.tb02789.x

  • Game model: Second-price auction
  • Link to reward hacking: First dominant-strategy truthful mechanism: an agent's report sets the outcome but not its own price, so lying cannot help.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Vickrey analyzes auctions and marketing schemes under strategic bidding. He shows that in a second-price sealed-bid auction each bidder's dominant strategy is to bid its true value, and compares the revenue of auction formats. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[3] Gary S. Becker. "Crime and Punishment: An Economic Approach." Journal of Political Economy 76(2): 169-217, 1968. https://doi.org/10.1086/259394

  • Game model: rational-choice deterrence (enforcer vs offender)
  • Link to reward hacking: Foundational deterrence model of detection probability times penalty, used to reason about penalizing and detecting reward hacking under imperfect monitoring.
  • Area: Principal–agent, contracts and incentive analysis

The paper models crime as a rational choice in which offenders compare expected gains with the probability and severity of punishment. It derives the socially optimal levels of enforcement expenditure and penalties that minimize social loss from crime and enforcement. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[4] Leonard J. Savage. "Elicitation of Personal Probabilities and Expectations." Journal of the American Statistical Association 66(336):783-801, 1971. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1971.10482346

  • Game model: Single agent, characterisation of proper scoring rules
  • Link to reward hacking: Characterises the full class of proper scoring rules (Bregman/convex-function form), giving designers a menu of honest-reporting rewards for eliciting probabilities and expectations from AI models.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Savage develops a general theory of proper scoring rules for eliciting a person's subjective probabilities and expectations. He characterises the scoring rules under which a person who maximises expected score reports their true probability or expectation, and discusses practical issues of eliciting personal probabilities. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[5] Theodore Groves. "Incentives in Teams." Econometrica 41(4):617-631, 1973. https://doi.org/10.2307/1914085

  • Game model: Dominant-strategy mechanism with transfers
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows how to align each agent's reward with total welfare so honest reporting is dominant; a template for reward design in multi-agent AI.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Groves studies a team in which members have private information and their own objectives. He constructs transfer schemes under which each member's payoff equals the team's total payoff plus a term it cannot affect, so truthful reporting is a dominant strategy (the Groves, later VCG, mechanisms). (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[6] Steven Kerr. "On the Folly of Rewarding A, While Hoping for B." Academy of Management Journal 18(4): 769-783, 1975. https://doi.org/10.2307/255378

  • Game model: informal principal-agent / incentive misalignment
  • Link to reward hacking: Classic statement that agents optimize the rewarded measure rather than the intended goal, the organizational analogue of specification gaming.
  • Area: Principal–agent, contracts and incentive analysis

The article documents many organizations (politics, medicine, universities, business) whose formal reward systems pay for behaviour A while the organization hopes for a different behaviour B. It argues that people do what is rewarded, so such reward systems produce the unwanted behaviour. It identifies causes such as a fixation on objective, measurable criteria. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[7] Robert E. Lucas. "Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique." Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy 1: 19-46, 1976. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2231(76)80003-6

  • Game model: rational-expectations policy game (agents respond to the rule)
  • Link to reward hacking: Explains why a proxy relation learned before optimization breaks once an optimizer acts on it, the same mechanism as reward-model overoptimization.
  • Area: Principal–agent, contracts and incentive analysis

The paper argues that econometric relations estimated under one policy regime are not stable when policy changes, because agents' decision rules depend on the policy. Policy evaluation with fixed estimated parameters is therefore invalid; models must be built from structural parameters of agents' optimization problems. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[8] Donald T. Campbell. "Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change." Evaluation and Program Planning 2(1): 67-90, 1979. https://doi.org/10.1016/0149-7189(79)90048-X

  • Game model: informal; indicator corruption under strategic pressure
  • Link to reward hacking: Campbell's Law is the social-science counterpart of Goodhart's Law and is cited alongside it for metric and reward gaming.
  • Area: Principal–agent, contracts and incentive analysis

The paper discusses methods for evaluating social programs and their political context. It states what is now called Campbell's Law: the more a quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more it is subject to corruption pressures and the more it distorts the processes it is meant to monitor. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[9] Roger B. Myerson. "Incentive Compatibility and the Bargaining Problem." Econometrica 47(1):61-73, 1979. https://doi.org/10.2307/1912346

  • Game model: Bayesian mechanism design
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows it is without loss to look for reward schemes under which truthful reports are an equilibrium.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Myerson studies bargaining and collective choice under incomplete information. He states the revelation principle: any outcome achievable by some mechanism in Bayesian equilibrium can be achieved by an incentive-compatible direct mechanism in which agents report their types truthfully. He uses it to characterize efficient bargaining solutions. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[10] Paul R. Milgrom. "Good News and Bad News: Representation Theorems and Applications." Bell Journal of Economics 12(2):380-391, 1981. https://doi.org/10.2307/3003562

  • Game model: Persuasion game with verifiable messages
  • Link to reward hacking: Proves the unraveling result: withheld information is read as bad news, so truthful disclosure is the equilibrium.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Milgrom defines when news is 'favorable' (monotone likelihood ratio) and gives representation theorems. Applications include that buyers expect any product information withheld by a salesman to be unfavourable to his product, which yields full disclosure in a persuasion game. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[11] Ashok K. Chandra, Dexter C. Kozen, Larry J. Stockmeyer. "Alternation." Journal of the ACM 28(1), 1981. https://doi.org/10.1145/322234.322243

  • Game model: Existential vs universal player game
  • Link to reward hacking: Alternating polynomial time = PSPACE is the result Irving et al. use to argue debate with an optimal honest player reaches PSPACE.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

The paper defines alternating Turing machines, which alternate between existential and universal states, equivalent to a two-player game between a player who claims acceptance and one who denies it. It proves that alternating polynomial time equals PSPACE, and relates alternating time and space to deterministic classes. This gives the game view of computation that debate uses. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[12] Edward P. Lazear, Sherwin Rosen. "Rank-Order Tournaments as Optimum Labor Contracts." Journal of Political Economy 89(5):841-864, 1981. https://doi.org/10.1086/261010

  • Game model: Rank-order tournament
  • Link to reward hacking: Rank-based rewards filter common noise; relevant to comparative AI evaluation, but they invite sabotage of rivals.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Lazear and Rosen show that pay based on rank can give the same efficient effort as pay based on output when workers are risk neutral, and that risk-averse workers may prefer it. They discuss adverse selection with heterogeneous ability and handicapping when abilities are observable. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[13] Sanford J. Grossman. "The Informational Role of Warranties and Private Disclosure about Product Quality." Journal of Law and Economics 24(3):461-483, 1981. https://doi.org/10.1086/466995

  • Game model: Verifiable disclosure; skeptical buyer
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows that skeptical inference from silence makes full voluntary disclosure an equilibrium, so an AI overseer that penalizes missing evidence gets disclosure for free.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Grossman studies a seller who knows product quality and can make verifiable claims or offer warranties. He shows that, when disclosure is costless and verifiable, buyers infer that undisclosed quality is low, so the seller discloses fully. Mandatory disclosure is then unnecessary. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[14] David M. Kreps, Robert Wilson. "Reputation and Imperfect Information." Journal of Economic Theory 27(2):253-279, 1982. https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0531(82)90030-8

  • Game model: Finitely repeated game with incomplete information
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows how a small chance of an honest type sustains honest behaviour by strategic players, and why behaviour can change near the end; relevant to track records and treacherous turns in AI.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Kreps and Wilson study the chain-store game with a small prior probability that the incumbent is a 'tough' type. The incumbent builds a reputation by imitating the tough type for most of the game, which resolves Selten's chain-store paradox. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[15] Vincent P. Crawford, Joel Sobel. "Strategic Information Transmission." Econometrica 50(6):1431-1451, 1982. https://doi.org/10.2307/1913390

  • Game model: Cheap talk, one sender
  • Link to reward hacking: Sets the limit on honesty without verification: a misaligned AI advisor reveals only coarse information, less as misalignment grows.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

An informed sender with a bias sends a costless message to a receiver who then acts. All equilibria are partition equilibria: the sender reveals only which interval the state lies in, and the number of intervals falls as the bias grows. Communication is more informative when interests are closer. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[16] Andrew G. Barto, Richard S. Sutton, Charles W. Anderson. "Neuronlike adaptive elements that can solve difficult learning control problems." IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, SMC-13(5):834-846, 1983. https://doi.org/10.1109/TSMC.1983.6313077

  • Game model: internal critic generates reinforcement for actor
  • Link to reward hacking: The critic turns env reward into an internal score for the actor, the first internal grader in RL; it supports honest behaviour only while the critic stays grounded in env reward, and the actor can exploit critic errors.
  • Area: Decomposed agents (internal games between parts)

The paper introduces an architecture of two neuron-like elements for the cart-pole balancing task: an associative search element (ASE) that chooses actions and an adaptive critic element (ACE) that learns to predict reinforcement and sends an improved internal reinforcement signal to the ASE. This is the origin of the actor-critic split in reinforcement learning. The critic converts sparse failure signals into a denser evaluation that trains the actor. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[17] C. A. E. Goodhart. "Problems of Monetary Management: The UK Experience." In Monetary Theory and Practice, Macmillan (orig. 1975, Papers in Monetary Economics, Reserve Bank of Australia), 1984. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-349-17295-5_4

  • Game model: informal; strategic response to a control target
  • Link to reward hacking: Origin of Goodhart's Law, the central concept that AI-safety papers use to describe proxy-reward over-optimization.
  • Area: Principal–agent, contracts and incentive analysis

The chapter reviews UK monetary policy in the early 1970s and the use of monetary aggregates as policy targets. It contains the observation later called Goodhart's Law: any observed statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed on it for control purposes. The 1984 book version reprints the 1975 paper. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[18] Andrei Shleifer. "A Theory of Yardstick Competition." RAND Journal of Economics 16(3):319-327, 1985. https://doi.org/10.2307/2555560

  • Game model: Relative-performance regulation
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows that paying an agent based on peers' reports removes its incentive to lie about its own; relevant to benchmarking AI agents against each other.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

In the typical regulatory scheme a franchised monopoly has little incentive to reduce costs. Shleifer proposes that the price a regulated firm receives depend on the costs of identical firms. This yardstick competition gives efficient cost reduction and removes the incentive to misreport costs; it extends to heterogeneous firms with observable differences. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[19] László Babai. "Trading group theory for randomness." STOC 1985, 1985. https://doi.org/10.1145/22145.22192

  • Game model: Arthur-Merlin game with public coins
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows a weak verifier can extract truth with public random challenges alone, so an overseer need not hide its questions, only make them unpredictable.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Babai introduces Arthur-Merlin games, interactive proofs in which the verifier (Arthur) uses public random coins and the all-powerful prover (Merlin) answers. He defines the hierarchy of Arthur-Merlin classes and uses them to place matrix group problems in low complexity classes. The paper shows that public randomness suffices for a weak party to check a strong party. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[20] Jean Tirole. "Hierarchies and Bureaucracies: On the Role of Collusion in Organizations." Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization 2(2):181-214, 1986. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordjournals.jleo.a036907

  • Game model: Principal-supervisor-agent with side contracts
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows that a monitor must be paid more for honest reports than the monitored party can offer; relevant to AI monitors that might collude with the policy.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Tirole models a three-tier hierarchy of principal, supervisor and agent in which the supervisor and agent can collude by side contracts. He shows that the principal can restrict attention to collusion-proof contracts, and that the threat of collusion changes optimal incentives and organization design. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[21] Paul Milgrom, John Roberts. "Relying on the Information of Interested Parties." RAND Journal of Economics 17(1):18-32, 1986. https://doi.org/10.2307/2555625

  • Game model: Multi-sender verifiable disclosure
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows that competing interested advocates can substitute for judge sophistication; this is the economic root of AI debate.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

The paper asks when competition among interested parties who supply verifiable information to a decision maker reveals all relevant information. A sophisticated, well-informed decision maker gets full revelation even from one party; a naive or poorly informed one needs competition among parties with sufficiently opposed interests, and even that may not be enough. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[22] Marvin Minsky. "The Society of Mind." Simon & Schuster, New York (book, ISBN 0-671-60740-5), 1986. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Mind

  • Game model: informal society of competing and censoring agents
  • Link to reward hacking: Frames one mind as many agents in conflict, with censor agents that block others, an early informal picture of internal checking that has no incentive analysis.
  • Area: Decomposed agents (internal games between parts)

Minsky argues that a mind is a society of many simple, mindless agents, and that intelligence emerges from their interactions. The book is a set of short essays on how agencies cooperate, compete and control one another, including censor and suppressor agents that block unwanted mental actions. It gives no formal model or training procedure. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[23] Michael Ben-Or, Shafi Goldwasser, Joe Kilian, Avi Wigderson. "Multi-prover interactive proofs: how to remove intractability assumptions." STOC 1988, 1988. https://doi.org/10.1145/62212.62223

  • Game model: Two isolated provers interrogated separately
  • Link to reward hacking: Separate interrogation of isolated provers makes consistent lying hard, the formal basis for questioning non-communicating AI copies.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

The paper introduces multi-prover interactive proofs, in which a verifier questions two or more provers who cannot communicate with each other during the protocol. It shows that, in this model, perfect zero-knowledge proofs exist for all of NP without any intractability assumption. Separate interrogation replaces cryptographic commitments. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[24] Nick Littlestone. "Learning quickly when irrelevant attributes abound: A new linear-threshold algorithm." Machine Learning 2(4), 1988. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00116827

  • Game model: Online mistake-bound learning; Littlestone dimension; Winnow algorithm
  • Link to reward hacking: Source of the Littlestone dimension, the complexity measure behind mistake bounds in online strategic classification.
  • Area: Strategic ML and truthful elicitation

Introduces the Winnow algorithm, a multiplicative-update linear-threshold learner for online learning, and proves mistake bounds that grow only logarithmically with the number of irrelevant attributes. The paper also defines the combinatorial dimension (later called the Littlestone dimension) that characterizes optimal mistake bounds in the online model. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[25] John Moore, Rafael Repullo. "Subgame Perfect Implementation." Econometrica 56(5):1191-1220, 1988. https://doi.org/10.2307/1911364

  • Game model: Multi-stage mechanism with challenges
  • Link to reward hacking: The announce-challenge-test structure makes lying a losing move; it maps to AI-vs-AI challenge and cross-examination protocols.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Moore and Repullo characterize choice rules implementable in subgame-perfect equilibrium by multi-stage mechanisms. In many economic environments virtually any choice rule can be implemented, using stages in which one agent can challenge another's announcement and the challenged agent faces a test. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[26] Jacques Cremer, Richard P. McLean. "Full Extraction of the Surplus in Bayesian and Dominant Strategy Auctions." Econometrica 56(6):1247-1257, 1988. https://doi.org/10.2307/1913096

  • Game model: Mechanism with correlated types
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows that correlation among agents' information lets a designer cross-check each report against others and make lying costly; the root of peer prediction.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Cremer and McLean study auctions in which bidders' private information is correlated. They give conditions under which a seller can use lotteries based on other bidders' reports to extract the full surplus, as if values were known, in Bayesian or dominant-strategy auctions. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[27] Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali, Charles Rackoff. "The Knowledge Complexity of Interactive Proof Systems." SIAM Journal on Computing 18(1); conference version STOC 1985, 1989. https://doi.org/10.1137/0218012

  • Game model: Prover-verifier interaction with private coins
  • Link to reward hacking: Defines interactive proofs: a weak verifier is protected from any lying prover by soundness, the base model for AI overseers checking stronger models.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

[28] Robert A. Jacobs, Michael I. Jordan, Steven J. Nowlan, Geoffrey E. Hinton. "Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts." Neural Computation, 3(1):79-87, 1991. https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1991.3.1.79

  • Game model: experts compete for credit allocated by a gating network
  • Link to reward hacking: Experts compete for the gate's trust and are rewarded for being correct on the cases they win, a competition that rewards accuracy when the training signal is ground truth.
  • Area: Decomposed agents (internal games between parts)

[29] Moni Naor. "Bit commitment using pseudorandomness." Journal of Cryptology 4(2), 1991. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00196774

  • Game model: Commit-then-reveal
  • Link to reward hacking: Binding commitments stop a model from changing its answer after it sees which part the overseer will check.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Naor shows how to build a bit commitment scheme from any pseudorandom generator, and hence from any one-way function. The receiver sends a random string, and the committer sends the generator output masked according to the bit. The scheme is statistically binding and computationally hiding. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[30] Bengt Holmstrom, Paul Milgrom. "Multitask Principal-Agent Analyses: Incentive Contracts, Asset Ownership, and Job Design." Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization 7 (special issue): 24-52, 1991. https://doi.org/10.1093/jleo/7.special_issue.24

  • Game model: multitask principal-agent (moral hazard)
  • Link to reward hacking: The standard economic model of why optimizing a partial, measurable reward diverts effort from unmeasured goals; AI-safety work cites it as the formal root of reward hacking.
  • Area: Principal–agent, contracts and incentive analysis

The paper extends the principal-agent model to an agent who allocates effort across several tasks, some of which the principal can measure poorly. It shows that strong incentives on measurable tasks pull effort away from unmeasured tasks, so optimal contracts may use low-powered incentives, fixed wages, or restrictions on activities. The model explains features of job design and asset ownership. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[31] László Babai, Lance Fortnow, Carsten Lund. "Non-deterministic exponential time has two-prover interactive protocols." Computational Complexity 1(1), 1991. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01200056

  • Game model: Two-prover protocol with consistency tests
  • Link to reward hacking: Two isolated provers let a weak verifier check exponentially larger claims than one prover, quantifying the value of isolating AI copies.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

The paper proves MIP = NEXP: every language in nondeterministic exponential time has a two-prover interactive protocol with a polynomial-time verifier. The proof uses multilinearity tests and arithmetization so that the verifier can check an exponentially long object through two isolated provers. This shows separate interrogation is strictly more powerful than one prover (under standard assumptions). (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[32] Oded Goldreich, Silvio Micali, Avi Wigderson. "Proofs that yield nothing but their validity or all languages in NP have zero-knowledge proof systems." Journal of the ACM 38(3), 1991. https://doi.org/10.1145/116825.116852

  • Game model: Commit-challenge-response (graph 3-colouring)
  • Link to reward hacking: Proving validity without revealing secrets removes a reason to lie or hide, which supports audits of proprietary AI systems.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

The paper shows that, assuming one-way functions exist, every language in NP has a zero-knowledge interactive proof, using a commit-and-challenge protocol for graph 3-colouring. It also shows zero-knowledge proofs for graph isomorphism and non-isomorphism without assumptions, and discusses uses in cryptographic protocol design. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[33] Carsten Lund, Lance Fortnow, Howard Karloff, Noam Nisan. "Algebraic methods for interactive proof systems." Journal of the ACM 39(4), 1992. https://doi.org/10.1145/146585.146605

  • Game model: Sum-check protocol
  • Link to reward hacking: Introduces the sum-check protocol, the core tool by which random algebraic challenges force a prover to be consistent or be caught.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

[34] Adi Shamir. "IP = PSPACE." Journal of the ACM 39(4), 1992. https://doi.org/10.1145/146585.146609

  • Game model: Sum-check interactive proof for PSPACE
  • Link to reward hacking: A polynomial-time verifier can check any PSPACE claim, the result debate's original complexity argument builds on.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

[35] Daphne Koller, Nimrod Megiddo. "The complexity of two-person zero-sum games in extensive form." Games and Economic Behavior 4(4), 1992. https://doi.org/10.1016/0899-8256(92)90035-Q

  • Game model: Zero-sum extensive-form game, imperfect information
  • Link to reward hacking: Gives the complexity of games where provers hide information from each other, relevant to debates in which debaters have private knowledge.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

The paper studies the computational complexity of finding optimal strategies in two-person zero-sum extensive-form games with imperfect information. It shows that the problem is NP-hard in general when players have imperfect recall, and gives polynomial algorithms in the perfect-recall case. (summary written by compiler; no author abstract)

[36] Peter Dayan, Geoffrey E. Hinton. "Feudal Reinforcement Learning." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 5 (NIPS 1992), 1993. https://papers.nips.cc/paper/1992/hash/d14220ee66aeec73c49038385428ec4c-Abstract.html

  • Game model: principal-agent hierarchy; manager pays worker for obeying commands
  • Link to reward hacking: Reward hiding ('managers must reward sub-managers for doing their bidding whether or not this satisfies the commands of the super-managers') and information hiding (hidden downwards and upwards) create a manager-worker game where the worker has no stake in the outer reward, which removes one motive to hack it but also hides worker misbehaviour from the top.
  • Area: Decomposed agents (internal games between parts)

[37] Louis Kaplow, Steven Shavell. "Optimal Law Enforcement with Self-Reporting of Behavior." Journal of Political Economy 102(3), 1994. https://doi.org/10.1086/261947

  • Game model: Law-enforcement model with self-reporting; reduced sanction for confessed violations
  • Link to reward hacking: Economic basis for confession schemes: lower sure penalties for self-reported violations save monitoring cost, the logic behind rewarding AI confessions of reward hacking.
  • Area: Strategic ML and truthful elicitation

[38] Barton L. Lipman, Duane J. Seppi. "Robust Inference in Communication Games with Partial Provability." Journal of Economic Theory 66(2):370-405, 1995. https://doi.org/10.1006/jeth.1995.1046

  • Game model: Sequential multi-sender game with partial provability
  • Link to reward hacking: Shows that a few provable refutations plus conflicting senders suffice for robust truth inference, which matches debate with partial verification.
  • Area: Honesty mechanisms (games whose equilibrium is truth)

Lipman and Seppi study a receiver who hears several interested senders in sequence, where senders can prove some but not all claims.
