docs.title: Risk vocabulary
docs.text:
Pitch. A source-grounded glossary of risk, hazard, harm, safety and related terms: 195 verbatim definitions of 102 terms from 38 risk-management, safety-engineering, security and AI-safety sources (ISO 31000, the Society for Risk Analysis glossary, NIST, Leveson, Kaplan and Garrick and others), with a comparison of where the fields conflict and which usage the taxonomy adopts.

Status: done. Compiled 2026-11-21. Complete for the sources listed; not proofread end to end; not human-reviewed.

AI use. Most text was generated by Claude (Anthropic) under Robin Chauhan's direction; not fully human-reviewed.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Paywalled texts were not read: ISO 31000 clause 3 proper, ISO Guide 73, ISO/IEC 23894 and 22989, IEC 60812. ISO wording comes from secondary reproductions (EU Agency for Railways, NIST glossary, Wikipedia).
  • 18 requested items were unavailable. They are listed under "Not obtained" at the end of Definitions by source.
  • Quotes are shortened: any quoted span over 250 characters is cut to its start and marked [...]. Follow the clause and URL for the full text.
  • Some AI-safety definitions come from abstracts only, and a few quotes may differ slightly from the page text. Details are in section 5 of the analysis.

docs.title: How to read
docs.text:
• Every definition is the source's own wording in quotes, with the source number, the clause or section, and a field tag: risk_safety_eng (risk management and safety engineering), security or ai_safety.
  • Source numbers such as [6] are listed in the bibliography, with year, how much of each text was read, and a URL.
  • Definitions by source is the reference: one section per term, one line per definition.
  • The analysis compares the definitions, shows where the fields use one word for different things, and says which usage the AI-risk taxonomy adopts.
  • The interactive explorer shows every source's definition of a term side by side, with search, filters by field and source, and a clickable diagram of the chain below.

docs.title: The core chain
docs.text:
Risk management, safety engineering and security all describe the same chain, with different words at each link.

risk source / hazard / threat  -->  event (top event, accident)  -->  consequence / harm / loss
        |                                   |                                |
   vulnerability, exposure             likelihood                       severity
                                  risk = f(likelihood, severity)   over the set of scenarios
   controls / barriers / mitigations act on any link
  • Risk source, hazard, threat. The thing with potential to cause harm. "Hazard" is a source in most sources and a system state in Leveson's STPA.
  • Event. What happens: an occurrence or change of circumstances, the top event of a bow-tie, an accident.
  • Consequence, harm, loss. What results. Consequence is neutral, harm is people-centred, loss is relative to what stakeholders value.
  • Risk. Three families of definition are in use: likelihood times severity; the effect of uncertainty on objectives; a set of scenarios with their likelihoods and consequences.
  • Controls. Measures that modify risk, acting on any link.

Explore: Vocabulary explorer → · Taxonomy explorer →

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
• Definitions by source: 102 terms, 195 definitions, with clause and URL.
  • Analysis: the chain in detail, where the fields conflict, and the vocabulary adopted.
  • Bibliography: the 38 sources.
  • Interactive explorer: side-by-side definitions and the clickable chain.

docs.title: Risk vocabulary: how the standards define the terms, where they conflict, and what an AI-risk taxonomy should adopt
docs.text: 2026-11-21 (v1). Sources are numbered as in biblio.md; every quoted definition is in terms.md with clause and URL (quotes over 250 characters are shortened there and here; follow the URL for the full text). 38 sources, 195 definitions, 102 terms. Paywalled texts (ISO 31000 clause 3 proper, ISO Guide 73, ISO/IEC 23894 and 22989, IEC 60812) were not read; ISO wording comes via the EU Agency for Railways reproduction [5] and the NIST glossary [26], FMEA wording via Wikipedia [38]. Most text was generated by Claude (Anthropic) under Robin Chauhan's direction; not fully human-reviewed.

docs.title: 1. The core chain
docs.text:
Risk management, safety engineering and security all describe the same chain, with different words at each link:

risk source / hazard / threat  -->  event (top event, accident)  -->  consequence / harm / loss
        |                                   |                                |
   vulnerability, exposure             likelihood                       severity
                                  risk = f(likelihood, severity)   over the set of scenarios
   controls / barriers / mitigations act on any link
  • Risk source: "Element (action, sub-activity, component, system, event, etc.) which alone or in combination with other elements has the potential to give rise to some specified consequences" (SRA [6] 1.14).
  • Hazard: "A risk source where the potential consequences relate to harm" (SRA [6] 1.9); "Hazard, therefore, simply exists as a source. Risk includes the likelihood of conversion of that source into actual delivery of loss" (Kaplan and Garrick [1] 2.2); Def Stan: "An item, event, activity, or situation with the potential to cause: injury, ill-health, or death; damage..." [19].
  • Event: "Occurrence or change of a particular set of circumstances" (ISO 31000 [5]). Bow-tie top event: the moment the hazard is released [28]. Accident: "any undesired or unplanned event or condition that results in what stakeholders consider to be a loss" (Leveson [7]).
  • Consequence / harm / loss: consequence is neutral, "Outcome of an event affecting objectives" (ISO [5]); harm is people-centred, "Physical or psychological injury or damage" (SRA [6] 1.8), "Adverse impact on people" (Def Stan [19]); loss is stakeholder-relative, "something of value to stakeholders ... any other loss that is unacceptable" (Leveson [7]). NIST AI RMF widens harm to "individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment, and the planet" [22].
  • Likelihood "Chance of something happening" (ISO [5]); severity "A measure of the degree of harm" (Def Stan [19]).
  • Risk, three families of definition (section 2).
  • Control "Measure that maintains and/or modifies risk" (ISO [5]); mitigation "A decision, action, or practice intended to reduce the level of risk" (NIST [26]); barrier prevention or recovery control on the bow-tie [28]; countermeasure (security) [32].

docs.title: 2.1 "Risk" has three definitions in use
docs.text:
1. Likelihood times severity. "Combination of the likelihood of harm and the severity of that harm" (Def Stan 00-56 [19]); "the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm" (EU AI Act Art. 3(2) [25]); "composite measure of an event's probability of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences" (NIST AI RMF [22]); SP 800-30's "function of (i) the adverse impacts ... and (ii) the likelihood" [26].
  2. Effect of uncertainty on objectives (ISO 31000 [5], Guide 73 via [26]). Direction-neutral; the SRA glossary lists seven qualitative variants and treats the ISO form as one of them [6] 1.1.
  3. A set of scenarios. Kaplan and Garrick: risk "is" the set of triplets (scenario, likelihood, consequence) [1] 3.1. Leveson goes further and defines risk by "the effectiveness of the controls used to enforce safe system behavior" [7].

For AI the regulatory texts (EU, NIST) use family 1. The AI-risk taxonomy proposed here (seven facets, section 3) is a family-3 object: the facets are the components of the triplet, and a risk is a row.

docs.title: 2.2 "Hazard": a source or a state
docs.text: Most sources make a hazard a source of harm ([1] [6] [19] [26] [28]). Leveson makes it a system state: "a system state or set of conditions that, together with a particular set of worst-case environmental conditions, will lead to a loss" [7]. The AI-safety papers that borrow the word, Hendrycks 2021 [12] and 2023 [20], use it without defining it; "inherent model hazards" and "systemic hazards" [12] fit the source reading, while a misaligned model in deployment would be a Leveson-hazard (a state).

docs.title: 2.3 "Threat": three senses
docs.text:
• Safety: a synonym for risk source, "commonly used in relation to security applications" (SRA [6] 1.18).
  • Security: "Any circumstance or event with the potential to adversely impact organizational operations ... through an information system via unauthorized access, destruction, disclosure..." (NIST SP 800-30 [26] [33]); also an adversary's intent (SRA second sense [6]).
  • Bow-tie: "A possible direct cause that will potentially release a hazard by producing a top event" [28], a cause on the left of the diagram.

docs.title: 2.4 "Threat model": the AI-safety sense is not the security sense
docs.text:
• Security: "a structured representation of all the information that affects the security of an application" (OWASP [37]); threat modeling is "a form of risk assessment that models aspects of the attack and defense sides" (NIST SP 800-53 [35]) and answers four questions, "What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job?" (Manifesto [10]). It is a whole-system analysis, not one story.
  • AI safety: Kenton et al.'s review [14] builds each threat model from a "development model" and a "risk model" but gives no definition sentence; usage in the field is one path from a cause to a catastrophe. The standards' word for that object is scenario (Kaplan and Garrick [1]), loss scenario (Leveson [7]) or a bow-tie pathway [28].
  • Consequence for the taxonomy: the threat_models facet is a set of loss scenarios. The name is kept because the field uses it, but the facet must say which sense is meant, and must not be read as a security threat model.

docs.title: 2.5 "Failure mode": FMEA fits the AI-safety usage
docs.text: FMEA: "The specific manner or way by which a failure occurs in terms of failure of the part, component, function, equipment, subsystem, or system under investigation" [38]; failure is "The loss of a function under stated conditions" [38]. Def Stan: "An unintended behaviour of a product, service or system which could be hazardous in the broader system context" [19]. AI-safety terms fit this well: specification gaming "satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome" [9]; reward hacking, "optimizing an imperfect proxy reward function leads to poor performance according to the true reward function" [17]; goal misgeneralization, "a specific form of robustness failure ... competently pursues an undesired goal" [16]. Scheming is defined by motive, "perform well in training ... in order to gain power later" [18], which is a failure mode of the training process in Def Stan's "unintended behaviour" sense. Under Leveson, several of these would instead be hazards (states) and the failure mode would be the unsafe control action that produced them [7].

docs.title: 2.6 "Mitigation", "control", "countermeasure": all act on risk; research does not
docs.text: Every definition requires the thing to modify risk ([5] [26] [28] [32]). Interpretability research, agent-foundations theory and lists of organisations do not modify risk; they are enablers or inputs to controls. A facet that holds them cannot be called mitigations without stretching every standard. The ISO-neutral word for the whole response side is risk treatment, "process to modify risk" (Guide 73 via [26]); the bow-tie splits controls into prevention (left of the top event) and recovery (right) [28], which maps onto the AI distinction between training-time methods and deployment-time control.

docs.title: 2.7 "Harm" versus "consequence" versus "loss"
docs.text: Safety standards reserve harm for people ([6] [19]); consequence is neutral and can be positive ([5]); loss is anything stakeholders value ([7]). The AI literature says harm for all of these, and NIST AI RMF endorses the wide use [22]. The EU AI Act's serious incident [25] Art. 3(49) and systemic risk [25] Art. 3(65) are consequence-side legal terms with specific triggers (death, infrastructure disruption, fundamental rights; reach in the Union market).

docs.title: 2.8 Terms with no standard equivalent
docs.text:
• Dangerous capability: only a fragment in Shevlane et al. [23]; no standard defines it. Nearest standard notion: the energy or material in a hazard (SRA's hazard note: "energy (e.g., explosion, fire), material (toxic or eco-toxic)" [6] 1.9). A capability is what a hazard is made of.
  • Propensity: "the propensity of models to apply their capabilities for harm" [23]. Nearest standard notion: the likelihood component conditional on the capability existing, or vulnerability in the SRA sense, "risk conditional on the occurrence of a risk source" [6] 1.19.
  • Alignment / misalignment: "A is trying to do what H wants it to do" (Christiano [4]); systems that "pursue unintended goals" [16]; goals "in conflict ... with human interests" [15]. These are safety properties and their absence; the STPA word for the property is system-level constraint, "the system conditions or behaviors that need to be satisfied to prevent hazards" [7].
  • Safety case is the one AI term that matches its standard exactly: Def Stan "A structured argument, supported by a body of evidence that provides a compelling, comprehensible and valid case that a [system] is safe for a given application in a given environment" [19]; Clymer et al. "a structured rationale that a system is unlikely to cause significant harm if it is deployed to a particular setting" [24].

docs.title: 3. Mapping to the seven facets of the taxonomy
docs.text: Facet Standard term adopted Source Note harms harm / consequence [6] 1.8, [19], [5] people-centred "harm" in the standards; this facet uses the NIST AI RMF wide sense [22] and states so risk_sources risk source; hazard when the consequence is harm [6] 1.14, 1.9 the misuse / misalignment / mistakes / structural split is a classification of risk sources by agent and intent failure_modes failure mode (FMEA) [38], [19] Leveson would call several of these hazards (states); noted, not adopted threat_models scenario; loss scenario [1] 3.1, [7] not the security sense of threat model [37] [35]; the facet must state this capabilities (none); component of a hazard [6] 1.9 note field term "dangerous capability" kept [23] safety_properties system-level constraint; safety requirement [7], [19] alignment [4] is one such property responses (was mitigations) risk treatment; control; risk assessment; barrier [26], [5], [6] 2.6, [28] mitigations is a misnomer for research content; the facet is named responses and each node is tagged control, assessment or enabler (section 4) risk (not a facet) set of (scenario, likelihood, consequence) [1]; family 1 for regulators [19] [25] [22] a risk register row

docs.title: 4. Vocabulary adopted
docs.text:
• Risk: a triplet (scenario, likelihood, consequence) after Kaplan and Garrick [1]; reported to regulators as likelihood times severity [25] [22]. Never a facet or a tree node.
  • Harm: adverse effect on people, groups, society, environment (wide sense, [22]); the harms facet.
  • Risk source: SRA 1.14 [6]; hazard when harm is the consequence.
  • Failure mode: FMEA sense [38].
  • Threat model: used in the AI-safety sense of a loss scenario [7] [1]; flagged wherever used.
  • Dangerous capability: field term [23]; a hazard component.
  • Safety property: a system-level constraint [7].
  • Response (replacing mitigation as the facet name): anything on the response side, the standards' risk treatment [26] widened to include assessment and enabling work. Within it, control = modifies risk ([5]); assessment = risk identification, analysis and evaluation ([6] 2.6, [26]); enabler = research or infrastructure that does not itself modify risk (no standard term).
  • Safety case: Def Stan [19] and Clymer [24], which agree.

docs.title: 5. Limits
docs.text:
• ISO text is second-hand ([5] via the EU Agency for Railways; Guide 73 via NIST [26]); IEC 60812 via Wikipedia [38]; GSN v3 was not read, so no GSN definition.
  • Several AI-safety definitions are from abstracts only (Hubinger [8], Hendrycks 2023 [20], International Report [29]); Kenton [14] has no definition sentence; the Bostrom quote [2] lacks its subject.
  • A few quotes may differ slightly from the page text, because some pages were read in summarised form. Clause numbers were recorded where visible.
  • Not covered: actuarial and financial risk vocabulary; ISO/IEC 23894 (AI risk management) and 22989 (AI concepts), both paywalled; MITRE ATT&CK/ATLAS (not obtained).

docs.title: Numbered list (academic form)
docs.text:
1. S. Kaplan and B. J. Garrick, Risk Analysis 1(1):11-27 (1981). On the Quantitative Definition of Risk. https://www.risksciences.ucla.edu/s/On-the-Quantitative-Definition-of-Risk.pdf Note: DOI 10.1111/j.1539-6924.1981.tb01350.x. Free PDF from the UCLA Garrick Institute. Mathematical symbols (the triplets and braces) are omitted from the quoted text.
  2. Bostrom (2002). Existential Risks: Analyzing Human Extinction Scenarios. https://nickbostrom.com/existential/risks Note: Section 1.2.
  3. Microsoft (2017). Threats - Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/develop/threat-modeling-tool-threats Note: Section: STRIDE model.
  4. Christiano (2018). Clarifying AI alignment. https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/ZeE7EKHTFMBs8eMxn/clarifying-ai-alignment
  5. ISO (reproduced by ERA) (2018). ISO 31000:2018 clause 3 terms, as reproduced by the EU Agency for Railways terminology collection. https://www.era.europa.eu/era-railway-terminology-collection/risk/term_2/sms_safety_culture_human_and_organisational_factor Note: ISO 31000:2018 itself was not read (paywalled). ERA pages reproduce entries for risk, event, consequence, likelihood and control; risk source and risk treatment were not available. Clause numbers 3.1 to 3.7 are inferred from cross-references in the notes.
  6. Society for Risk Analysis (expert group led by Terje Aven) (2018). Society for Risk Analysis Glossary. https://www.sra.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/SRA-Glossary-FINAL.pdf Note: Updated August 2018. Clause numbers as printed.
  7. Nancy G. Leveson and John P. Thomas (MIT PSAS) (2018). STPA Handbook. https://psas.scripts.mit.edu/home/get_file.php?name=STPA_handbook.pdf Note: Section names given instead of page numbers.
  8. Hubinger et al. (2019). Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems. https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01820 Note: Abstract only; definitions of deceptive alignment and mesa-optimizer from the paper body are not recorded.
  9. Krakovna et al. (DeepMind) (2020). Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity. https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/specification-gaming-the-flip-side-of-ai-ingenuity/ Note: Blog post.
  10. Threat Modeling Manifesto authors (2020). Threat Modeling Manifesto. https://www.threatmodelingmanifesto.org/
  11. Assurance Case Working Group, Safety-Critical Systems Club (2021). GSN Community Standard Version 3 (SCSC-141C). https://scsc.uk/scsc-141c Note: The standard was not read; no GSN definition is recorded.
  12. Hendrycks et al. (2021). Unsolved Problems in ML Safety. https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13916 Note: Abstract.
  13. Hendrycks, Mazeika (2022). X-Risk Analysis for AI Research. https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.05862 Note: Abstract.
  14. Kenton et al. (DeepMind) (2022). Threat Model Literature Review. https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/wnnkD6P2k2TfHnNmt/threat-model-literature-review Note: No explicit definition sentence of 'threat model' found; the post structures each threat model as a development model plus a risk model, by example only. Not verbatim-confirmed.
  15. Ngo, Chan, Mindermann (2022). The Alignment Problem from a Deep Learning Perspective. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00626 Note: Revised abstract (includes early-2025 update); no definition of situational awareness in the abstract.
  16. Shah et al. (2022). Goal Misgeneralization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01790 Note: Abstract.
  17. Skalse et al. (2022). Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13085 Note: Abstract.
  18. Carlsmith (2023). Scheming AIs: Will AIs fake alignment during training in order to get power?. https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.08379 Note: Abstract.
  19. UK Ministry of Defence (DStan) (2023). Defence Standard 00-056 Part 01 Issue 8, Safety Management Requirements for Defence Systems. https://www.contractsfinder.service.gov.uk/Notice/Attachment/c8604aaa-d62e-4283-a94d-63283324da61 Note: Issue 8 (14 October 2023), not Issue 7. Definitions are in the Definitions section (pp. 3-2 to 3-6).
  20. Hendrycks, Mazeika, Woodside (2023). An Overview of Catastrophic AI Risks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.12001 Note: Abstract.
  21. ISO/IEC (2023). ISO/IEC 23894:2023 and ISO/IEC 22989. https://www.iso.org/obp/ui/ Note: Paywalled; not read.
  22. NIST (2023). Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1. https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf
  23. Shevlane et al. (2023). Model evaluation for extreme risks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15324 Note: Abstract.
  24. Clymer et al. (2024). Safety Cases: How to Justify the Safety of Advanced AI Systems. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10462 Note: Abstract and HTML introduction.
  25. European Union (2024). Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 3 Definitions. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202401689 Note: Text from the Official Journal HTML version.
  26. NIST Computer Security Resource Center (2024). NIST CSRC Glossary. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary Note: Each term page lists definitions by originating document; only SP 800-30 Rev. 1, ISO Guide 73 (via SP 800-160v1r1) and a few others are recorded. Pages for accident, failure, fault, mishap, risk source, risk acceptance and safeguard were not found.
  27. Anthropic (2025). Responsible Scaling Policy. https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy Note: The web page has no standalone definitions; they are in linked documents that were not read.
  28. UK Civil Aviation Authority (2025). UK CAA Bowtie guidance (bowtie elements pages). https://www.caa.co.uk/safety-initiatives/working-with-industry/bowtie/bowtie-elements/ Note: Used instead of a commercial bow-tie page and the CCPS book (paywalled). Definitions are in boxes labelled Definition on each element page.
  29. Bengio et al. (2025). International AI Safety Report 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17805 Note: Abstract only; it has no definition of risk or of the three-way split.
  30. NIST (2025). NIST CSRC Glossary: adversary. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/adversary
  31. NIST (2025). NIST CSRC Glossary: attack surface. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/attack_surface
  32. NIST (2025). NIST CSRC Glossary: countermeasure(s). https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/countermeasures Note: The singular URL does not exist; the plural URL is cited.
  33. NIST (2025). NIST CSRC Glossary: threat. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/threat
  34. NIST (2025). NIST CSRC Glossary: threat model. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/threat_model Note: Page not found.
  35. NIST (2025). NIST CSRC Glossary: threat modeling. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/threat_modeling Note: Only the SP 800-53 Rev. 5 definition is on the page (SP 800-154 is not).
  36. NIST (2025). NIST CSRC Glossary: vulnerability. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/vulnerability
  37. OWASP (2025). Threat Modeling. https://owasp.org/www-community/Threat_Modeling Note: Now at https://community.owasp.org/Threat_Modeling
  38. Wikipedia contributors (2026). Failure mode and effects analysis (Wikipedia). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Failure_mode_and_effects_analysis Note: Secondary source, used because IEC 60812 is paywalled. The article carries an unsourced-material banner; its text is not verified as a verbatim quote of IEC 60812.

docs.title: Risk vocabulary: definitions by source
docs.text: Compiled 2026-11-21 (v1). 195 definitions of 102 terms from 38 sources (numbers: biblio.md). Text in quotes is the source's wording; a quote longer than 250 characters is cut to its start and marked [...], so follow the clause and URL for the full text. Short notes in italics give context. Most text was generated by Claude (Anthropic) under Robin Chauhan's direction; not fully human-reviewed. Field tags: risk_safety_eng = risk management and safety engineering; security; ai_safety.

docs.title: risk
docs.text:
• [1, Section 3.1 'Set of Triplets Idea'] (risk_safety_eng) "If this table contains all the scenarios we can think of, we can then say that it (the table) is the answer to the question and therefore is the risk. More formally, using braces, { }, to denote “set of” we can say that the risk [...]"
  • [5, ISO 31000:2018 term Risk (3.1 per cross-references)] (risk_safety_eng) "Effect of uncertainty on objectives"
  • [5, ISO/IEC management-system common term (ERA term_5 page, cross-referencing ISO 31000 and ISO Guide 73)] (risk_safety_eng) "Effect of uncertainty on objectives (3.20)"
  • [6, 1.1 Risk, comment on ISO] (risk_safety_eng) "ISO defines risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives. It is possible to interpret this definition in different ways; one as a special case of those considered above (e.g., d) or g)), with the consequences seen in relation to the objectives."
  • [6, 1.1 Risk, overall qualitative definitions (item 2)] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk is the potential for realization of unwanted, negative consequences of an event"
  • [6, 1.1 Risk, overall qualitative definitions (item 3)] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk is exposure to a proposition (e.g., the occurrence of a loss) of which one is uncertain"
  • [6, 1.1 Risk, overall qualitative definitions (item 4)] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk is the consequences of the activity and associated uncertainties"
  • [6, 1.1 Risk, overall qualitative definitions (item 5)] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk is uncertainty about and severity of the consequences of an activity with respect to something that humans value"
  • [6, 1.1 Risk, overall qualitative definitions (item 6)] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk is the occurrences of some specified consequences of the activity and associated uncertainties"
  • [6, 1.1 Risk, overall qualitative definitions (item 7)] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk is the deviation from a reference value and associated uncertainties"
  • [6, 1.1 Risk, overall qualitative definitions (list item 1)] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk is the possibility of an unfortunate occurrence" — One of seven overall qualitative definitions the glossary allows.
  • [6, 1.1 Risk, preamble] (risk_safety_eng) "We consider a future activity [interpreted in a wide sense to also cover, for example, natural phenomena], for example the operation of a system, and define risk in relation to the consequences (effects, implications) of this [...]"
  • [7, Chapter 7 Designing an Effective Safety Management System, STAMP risk discussion] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk is defined in terms of the effectiveness of the controls used to enforce safe system behavior, i.e., the design and operation of the safety control structure."
  • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-4] (risk_safety_eng) "Combination of the likelihood of harm and the severity of that harm."
  • [22, Section 1.1 Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms, para 1] (risk_safety_eng) "In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event. The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can [...]" — Hyphenation removed.
  • [22, Section 1.1, para 1] (risk_safety_eng) "When considering the negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of occurrence (Adapted [...]"
  • [25, Article 3(2)] (risk_safety_eng) "‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;"
  • [26, csrc term 'risk'; source NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "Effect of uncertainty on objectives." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk
  • [26, csrc term 'risk'; source NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 (via NIST SP 1800-11B etc.)] (risk_safety_eng) "A measure of the extent to which an entity is threatened by a potential circumstance or event, and typically a function of: (i) the adverse impacts that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs; and (ii) the likelihood of occurrence." — URL https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk . Another variant from CNSSI 4009-2022 / OMB A-130: '...a function of: (i) the adverse impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs; and (ii) the likelihood of occurrence.'

docs.title: risk source
docs.text: • [6, 1.14 Risk source or risk agent] (risk_safety_eng) "Element (action, sub-activity, component, system, event, etc.) which alone or in combination with other elements has the potential to give rise to some specified consequences (typically undesirable consequences)."

docs.title: hazard
docs.text:
• [1, Section 2.2 The Distinction Between Risk and Hazard] (risk_safety_eng) "Hazard, therefore, simply exists as a source. Risk includes the likelihood of conversion of that source into actual delivery of loss, injury, or some form of damage." — Authors quote the dictionary: hazard is 'a source of danger'. Risk is the 'possibility of loss or injury' and the 'degree of probability of such loss.'
  • [1, Section 3.2, footnote 3] (risk_safety_eng) "Having defined risk as a set of triplets, we may now, in line with Section 2.2, define hazard as a set of doublets" — The doublet formula is omitted.
  • [6, 1.9 Hazard] (risk_safety_eng) "A risk source where the potential consequences relate to harm. Hazards could, for example, be associated with energy (e.g., explosion, fire), material (toxic or eco-toxic), biota (pathogens) and information (panic communication)."
  • [7, Chapter 2, Identifying system-level hazards] (risk_safety_eng) "A hazard is a system state or set of conditions that, together with a particular set of worst-case environmental conditions, will lead to a loss." — Leveson hazard differs from most sources: it is a system state, defined relative to the system boundary, not a source of danger.
  • [7, Chapter 3 Integrating STPA, discussion of hazards] (risk_safety_eng) "So for practical reasons, hazards are defined as precursor states to an accident that the system designers never want to occur and thus should be eliminated or controlled in the design process." — Preceded by text rejecting the definition 'a condition that could lead to an accident or a precondition for an accident'.
  • [12, abstract] (ai_safety) "We present four problems ready for research, namely withstanding hazards ("Robustness"), identifying hazards ("Monitoring"), reducing inherent model hazards ("Alignment"), and reducing systemic hazards ("Systemic Safety")." — hazard undefined; inherent model hazards vs systemic hazards
  • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-3] (risk_safety_eng) "An item, event, activity, or situation with the potential to cause: injury, ill-health, or death; damage to or loss of equipment or property; or damage to the environment - (An intermediate state where potential for harm exists)" — Bullets joined.
  • [20, abstract] (ai_safety) "For each category of risk, we describe specific hazards, present illustrative stories, envision ideal scenarios, and propose practical suggestions for mitigating these dangers." — hazard undefined; specific instance within a risk category
  • [26, csrc term 'hazard'; CNSSI 4009-2022 from DoD Dictionary of Military and Associated Terms] (risk_safety_eng) "A condition with the potential to cause injury, illness, or death of personnel; damage to or loss of equipment or property; or mission degradation." — Only one definition on the page. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/hazard
  • [28, Bowtie element Step 1: Define the Hazard, Definition box] (risk_safety_eng) "A condition, situation, activity or object that could cause or contribute to an aircraft incident or accident." — Aviation-specific wording. URL https://www.caa.co.uk/safety-initiatives/working-with-industry/bowtie/bowtie-elements/hazard/
  • [28, How does bowtie work] (risk_safety_eng) "something in, around or part of an organisation or activity which has the potential to cause damage or harm" — Quoted from the parenthesis in the sentence 'The safety risk picture revolves around the hazard (...)'. URL https://www.caa.co.uk/safety-initiatives/working-with-industry/bowtie/about-bowtie/how-does-bowtie-work/

docs.title: threat
docs.text:
• [6, 1.18 Threat] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk source, commonly used in relation to security applications (but also in relation to other applications, for example the threat of an earthquake)"
  • [6, 1.18 Threat] (risk_safety_eng) "Threat in relation to an attack: A stated or inferred intention to initiate an attack with the intention to inflict harm, fear, pain or misery"
  • [26, csrc term 'threat'; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 under Threat from CNSSI 4009] (risk_safety_eng) "Any circumstance or event with the potential to adversely impact organizational operations (including mission, functions, image, or reputation), organizational assets, individuals, other organizations, or the Nation through an [...]" — Information-security sense. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/threat
  • [28, Bowtie element Step 3: Identify Threats, Definition box] (risk_safety_eng) "A possible direct cause that will potentially release a hazard by producing a top event." — URL https://www.caa.co.uk/safety-initiatives/working-with-industry/bowtie/bowtie-elements/threats/
  • [33, NIST SP 800-160v1r1] (security) "Potential cause of unacceptable asset loss and the undesirable consequences or impact of such a loss."
  • [33, NIST SP 800-221] (security) "Any circumstance or event with the potential to adversely impact organizational operations."
  • [33, NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1] (security) "Any circumstance or event with the potential to adversely impact organizational operations (including mission, functions, image, or reputation), organizational assets, individuals, other organizations, or the Nation through an [...]"
  • [33, NISTIR 8053] (security) "potential cause of an unwanted incident, which may result in harm to a system or organization"

docs.title: threat model
docs.text: • [37, intro] (security) "A threat model is a structured representation of all the information that affects the security of an application."

docs.title: threat modeling
docs.text:
• [10, definition] (security) "Threat modeling is analyzing representations of a system to highlight concerns about security and privacy characteristics."
  • [10, key questions] (security) "What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job?" — four questions joined; original is a numbered list
  • [35, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5] (security) "A form of risk assessment that models aspects of the attack and defense sides of a logical entity, such as a piece of data, an application, a host, a system, or an environment."
  • [37, intro] (security) "Threat modeling works to identify, communicate, and understand threats and mitigations within the context of protecting something of value."

docs.title: vulnerability
docs.text:
• [6, 1.19 Vulnerability, overall qualitative definitions] (risk_safety_eng) "The degree to which a system is affected by a risk source or agent"
  • [6, 1.19 Vulnerability, overall qualitative definitions (item 2)] (risk_safety_eng) "The degree to which a system is able to withstand specific loads"
  • [6, 1.19 Vulnerability, overall qualitative definitions (item 3)] (risk_safety_eng) "Vulnerability is risk conditional on the occurrence of a risk source/agent. If, for example, risk is interpreted in line with Section 1.1e), vulnerability is uncertainty about and severity of the consequences, given the occurrence of a risk source"
  • [26, csrc term 'vulnerability'; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 under Vulnerability from CNSSI 4009] (risk_safety_eng) "Weakness in an information system, system security procedures, internal controls, or implementation that could be exploited or triggered by a threat source." — Information-security sense. The page attributes this text to FIPS 200 from CNSSI 4009 - Adapted, and to SP 800-30 Rev. 1 and SP 800-53 Rev. 5. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/vulnerability
  • [36, CNSSI 4009-2022] (security) "A known weakness in a system, system security procedures, internal controls, or implementation by which an actor or event may intentionally exploit or accidentally trigger the weakness to access, modify, or disrupt normal operations of a system."
  • [36, FIPS 200 / CNSSI 4009] (security) "Weakness in an information system, system security procedures, internal controls, or implementation that could be exploited or triggered by a threat source."
  • [36, NIST SP 800-160v1r1] (security) "A weakness that can be exploited or triggered to produce an adverse effect."
  • [36, NISTIR 7435] (security) "a bug, flaw, weakness, or exposure of an application, system, device, or service that could lead to a failure of confidentiality, integrity, or availability"

docs.title: exposure
docs.text:
• [6, 1.6 Exposure] (risk_safety_eng) "Exposure of something: being subject to a risk source/agent (for example, exposure of asbestos)"
  • [26, csrc term 'exposure'; NIST SP 800-161r1-upd1 from ISO Guide 73 - adapted] (risk_safety_eng) "Extent to which an organization and/or stakeholder is subject to a risk." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/exposure

docs.title: event
docs.text:
• [5, ISO 31000:2018 term Event] (risk_safety_eng) "Occurrence or change of a particular set of circumstances"
  • [6, 1.7 Event, Consequences] (risk_safety_eng) "Event: the occurrence or change of a particular set of circumstances such as a system failure, an earthquake, an explosion or an outbreak of a pandemic; a specified change of the states of the world/affairs" — Two bullets joined with a semicolon ; they are separate bullets in the source.
  • [26, csrc term 'event'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "Occurrence or change of a particular set of circumstances." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/event

docs.title: scenario
docs.text: • [1, Section 3.1] (risk_safety_eng) "To answer these questions we would make a list of outcomes or “scenarios” as suggested in Table I." — Scenario = line in the scenario list (Table I) with likelihood and consequence.

docs.title: top event
docs.text:
• [28, Bowtie element Step 2: Define the Top Event, Definition box] (risk_safety_eng) "A Top Event in a BowTie diagram, is the point in time which describes the release or loss of control over a Hazard." — URL https://www.caa.co.uk/safety-initiatives/working-with-industry/bowtie/bowtie-elements/top-events/
  • [28, How does bowtie work] (risk_safety_eng) "the release or loss of control over a hazard known as the undesired system state" — Parenthesis in the intro paragraph.

docs.title: harm
docs.text:
• [6, 1.8 Harm, damage, adverse consequences, impacts, severity] (risk_safety_eng) "Harm: Physical or psychological injury or damage"
  • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-3] (risk_safety_eng) "Adverse impact on people, including fatality, physical or psychological injury, or short or long term damage to health."
  • [22, Section 1.1, para 1 (context, no stand-alone definition)] (risk_safety_eng) "Negative impact or harm can be experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment, and the planet." — AI RMF 1.0 gives no formal definition of 'harm'; this is the closest sentence.
  • [26, csrc term 'harm'; NIST SP 800-122 (privacy sense)] (risk_safety_eng) "Any adverse effects that would be experienced by an individual (i.e., that may be socially, physically, or financially damaging) or an organization if the confidentiality of PII were breached." — Narrow privacy sense, not general harm. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/harm

docs.title: consequence
docs.text:
• [5, ISO 31000:2018 term Consequence] (risk_safety_eng) "Outcome of an event (3.5) affecting objectives"
  • [6, 1.7 Event, Consequences] (risk_safety_eng) "Consequences: The effects of the activity with respect to the values defined (such as human life and health, environment and economic assets), covering the totality of states, events, barriers and outcomes. The consequences are [...]"
  • [26, csrc term 'consequence'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO/IEC 15026-1:2019] (risk_safety_eng) "Effect (change or non-change), usually associated with an event or condition or with the system and usually allowed, facilitated, caused, prevented, changed, or contributed to by the event, condition, or system." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/consequence
  • [28, Bowtie element Step 4: Identify Consequences, Definition box] (risk_safety_eng) "A potential event resulting from the release of a Hazard, which directly results in loss or damage." — URL https://www.caa.co.uk/safety-initiatives/working-with-industry/bowtie/bowtie-elements/consequences/ . Guiding principle: 'Consequences are events not the actual loss or damage.'

docs.title: impact
docs.text: • [26, csrc term 'impact'; NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 / SP 800-60] (risk_safety_eng) "The magnitude of harm that can be expected to result from the consequences of unauthorized disclosure of information, unauthorized modification of information, unauthorized destruction of information, or loss of information or [...]" — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/impact

docs.title: loss
docs.text: • [7, Chapter 2, Identifying losses] (risk_safety_eng) "A loss involves something of value to stakeholders. Losses may include a loss of human life or human injury, property damage, environmental pollution, loss of mission, loss of reputation, loss or leak of sensitive information, or [...]" — Printed as 'Definition:'.

docs.title: accident
docs.text:
• [7, Chapter 3 Integrating STPA, Identification of Losses to be Considered] (risk_safety_eng) "Formally, an accident (or mishap, which is the term used by the military) is any undesired or unplanned event or condition that results in what stakeholders consider to be a loss."
  • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-2] (risk_safety_eng) "An event, or sequence of events, that: causes unintended harm, such that a person is killed or suffers an injury. An accident sequence will need to consider the functional safety of equipments/systems involved."

docs.title: incident
docs.text:
• [19, Definitions section, p. 3-3] (risk_safety_eng) "The occurrence of an event that might have progressed to an accident but did not cause injury or damage but had the potential to do so." — Closest free definition of 'near miss'; the standard does not define near miss.
  • [26, csrc term 'incident'; FIPS 200] (risk_safety_eng) "An occurrence that actually or potentially jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system or the information the system processes, stores, or transmits or that constitutes a violation or [...]" — Information-security sense. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/incident

docs.title: serious incident
docs.text: • [25, Article 3(49)] (risk_safety_eng) "‘serious incident’ means an incident or malfunctioning of an AI system that directly or indirectly leads to any of the following: (a) the death of a person, or serious harm to a person’s health; (b) a serious and irreversible [...]"

docs.title: likelihood
docs.text:
• [5, ISO 31000:2018 term Likelihood] (risk_safety_eng) "Chance of something happening"
  • [6, 1.3 Probability, Likelihood entry] (risk_safety_eng) "Likelihood: The same as probability."
  • [26, csrc term 'likelihood'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "Chance of something happening." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/likelihood
  • [26, csrc term 'likelihood'; NISTIR 7621 Rev. 1 from NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1] (risk_safety_eng) "A weighted factor based on a subjective analysis of the probability that a given threat is capable of exploiting a given vulnerability or a set of vulnerabilities." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/likelihood

docs.title: probability
docs.text: • [6, 1.3 Probability (likelihood, chance, frequency), overall definition] (risk_safety_eng) "A measure for representing or expressing uncertainty, variation or beliefs, following the rules of probability calculus."

docs.title: severity
docs.text:
• [6, 1.8] (risk_safety_eng) "Severity: The magnitude of the damage, harm, etc."
  • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-5] (risk_safety_eng) "A measure of the degree of harm."

docs.title: failure
docs.text: • [38, Section 'Basic terms' (glossary list)] (risk_safety_eng) "The loss of a function under stated conditions." — Secondary source. Not verified as verbatim IEC 60812.

docs.title: failure mode
docs.text:
• [19, Definitions section, p. 3-3] (risk_safety_eng) "An unintended behaviour of a product, service or system which could be hazardous in the broader system context, eg when the product or service is integrated into a system, or system as part of a system of systems."
  • [38, Section 'Basic terms' (glossary list)] (risk_safety_eng) "The specific manner or way by which a failure occurs in terms of failure of the part, component, function, equipment, subsystem, or system under investigation. Depending on the type of FMEA performed, failure mode may be [...]" — Secondary source. Following sentences give piece-part, functional and process examples.

docs.title: failure effect
docs.text: • [38, Section 'Basic terms' (glossary list)] (risk_safety_eng) "Immediate consequences of a failure on operation, or more generally on the needs for the customer / user that should be fulfilled by the function but now is not, or not fully, fulfilled." — Secondary source.

docs.title: failure cause
docs.text: • [38, Section 'Basic terms' (glossary list), entry 'Failure cause and/or mechanism'] (risk_safety_eng) "Defects in requirements, design, process, quality control, handling or part application, which are the underlying cause or sequence of causes that initiate a process (mechanism) that leads to a failure mode over a certain time. A [...]" — Secondary source.

docs.title: error
docs.text: • [26, csrc term 'error'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1] (risk_safety_eng) "The difference between desired and actual performance or behavior of a system or system element." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/error

docs.title: unsafe control action
docs.text: • [7, Chapter 2, Identifying unsafe control actions] (risk_safety_eng) "An Unsafe Control Action (UCA) is a control action that, in a particular context and worst-case environment, will lead to a hazard." — Footnote 9 on the page. Handbook states a UCA has five parts: source, type (provided, not provided, too early or too late, stopped too soon or applied too long), control action, context, link to hazards.

docs.title: risk assessment
docs.text:
• [6, 2.6 Risk assessment] (risk_safety_eng) "Systematic process to comprehend the nature of risk, express and evaluate risk, with the available knowledge"
  • [26, csrc term 'risk assessment'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "Overall process of risk identification, risk analysis, and risk evaluation." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_assessment
  • [26, csrc term 'risk assessment'; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1] (risk_safety_eng) "The process of identifying risks to organizational operations (including mission, functions, image, reputation), organizational assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation, resulting from the operation of an [...]" — Sources listed: NIST SP 1800-11B, 1800-30B, 1800-34B from NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_assessment
  • [26, csrc term 'risk assessment'; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 from NIST SP 800-39] (risk_safety_eng) "A systematic examination of risk using disciplined processes, methods, and tools. A risk assessment provides an environment for decision makers to evaluate and prioritize risks continuously and to recommend strategies to [...]" — The csrc page lists this text with source 'CNSSI 4009-2022 from DoDD 3020.40; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 under Risk Assessment from NIST SP 800-39'. URL https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_assessment

docs.title: risk analysis
docs.text:
• [6, 2.4 Risk analysis] (risk_safety_eng) "Systematic process to comprehend the nature of risk and to express the risk, with the available knowledge (1.10)"
  • [6, 2.4 Risk analysis, second paragraph] (risk_safety_eng) "Risk analysis is often also understood in a broader way, in particular in the Society for Risk Analysis (SRA) community: risk analysis is defined to include risk assessment, risk characterization, risk communication, risk [...]"
  • [26, csrc term 'risk analysis'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "Process to comprehend the nature of risk and to determine the level of risk." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_analysis

docs.title: risk identification
docs.text: • [26, csrc term 'risk identification'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "Process of finding, recognizing, and describing risks." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_identification

docs.title: risk evaluation
docs.text:
• [6, 2.11 Risk evaluation] (risk_safety_eng) "Process of comparing the result of risk analysis (see Risk analysis (2.4)) against risk (and often benefit) criteria to determine the significance and acceptability of the risk"
  • [26, csrc term 'risk evaluation'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "Process of comparing the results of risk analysis with risk criteria to determine whether the risk and/or its magnitude is/are acceptable or tolerable." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_evaluation

docs.title: risk treatment
docs.text:
• [6, 3.15 Risk treatment] (risk_safety_eng) "Process of actions to modify risk"
  • [26, csrc term 'risk treatment'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "Process to modify risk." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_treatment

docs.title: mitigation
docs.text: • [26, csrc term 'mitigation'; NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1] (risk_safety_eng) "A decision, action, or practice intended to reduce the level of risk associated with one or more threat events, threat scenarios, or vulnerabilities." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/mitigation

docs.title: control
docs.text:
• [5, ISO 31000:2018 term Control] (risk_safety_eng) "Measure that maintains and/or modifies risk (3.1)"
  • [26, csrc term 'control'; NIST SP 1800-15B from NISTIR 8053] (risk_safety_eng) "A measure that is modifying risk. (Note: controls include any process, policy, device, practice, or other actions that modify risk.)" — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/control

docs.title: countermeasure
docs.text:
• [32, CNSSI 4009-2022] (security) "Any action, device, procedure, technique, or other measure that reduces the vulnerability of or threat to a system."
  • [32, FIPS 200] (security) "Actions, devices, procedures, techniques, or other measures that reduce the vulnerability of an information system." — glossary lists synonyms: safeguards, security controls

docs.title: residual risk
docs.text:
• [22, Section 1.2.2 Risk Tolerance] (risk_safety_eng) "Residual risk – defined as risk remaining after risk treatment (Source: ISO GUIDE 73) – directly impacts end users or affected individuals and communities."
  • [26, csrc term 'residual risk'; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 under Residual Risk from CNSSI 4009] (risk_safety_eng) "Portion of risk remaining after security measures have been applied." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/residual_risk . Also: 'Risk that remains after risk responses have been documented and performed.' (NISTIR 8286).

docs.title: risk tolerance
docs.text:
• [6, 3.12 Risk tolerance] (risk_safety_eng) "An attitude expressing that the risk is judged tolerable"
  • [26, csrc term 'risk tolerance'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "The organization or stakeholder’s readiness to bear the risk after risk treatment in order to achieve its objectives." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_tolerance
  • [26, csrc term 'risk tolerance'; NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 from NIST SP 800-39] (risk_safety_eng) "The level of risk or the degree of uncertainty that is acceptable to an organization." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_tolerance

docs.title: risk acceptance
docs.text: • [6, 3.2 Risk acceptance] (risk_safety_eng) "An attitude expressing that the risk is judged acceptable by a particular individual or group"

docs.title: safety
docs.text:
• [6, 1.16 Safe, safety] (risk_safety_eng) "Safe: Without unacceptable risk. Safety: Interpreted in the same way as safe (for example when saying that safety is achieved); The antonym of risk (the safety level is linked to the risk level; a high safety means a low risk and [...]" — Bullets and the trailing sentence concatenated.
  • [26, csrc term 'safety'; NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1 from MIL-STD-882E] (risk_safety_eng) "Freedom from conditions that can cause death, injury, occupational illness, damage to or loss of equipment or property, or damage to the environment." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/safety
  • [26, csrc term 'safety'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017] (risk_safety_eng) "Expectation that a system does not, under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life, health, property, or the environment is endangered." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/safety

docs.title: assurance
docs.text: • [26, csrc term 'assurance'; NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 from ISO/IEC 15026-1:2019 - adapted] (risk_safety_eng) "Grounds for justified confidence that a [security or privacy] claim has been or will be achieved." — Text as printed on the page. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/assurance

docs.title: assurance case
docs.text:
• [26, csrc term 'assurance case'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO/IEC 15026-1:2019] (risk_safety_eng) "A reasoned, auditable artifact created that supports the contention that its top-level claim (or set of claims), is satisfied, including systematic argumentation and its underlying evidence and explicit assumptions that support the claim(s)." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/assurance_case
  • [26, csrc term 'assurance case'; NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5 from SEI] (risk_safety_eng) "A structured set of arguments and a body of evidence showing that a system satisfies specific claims with respect to a given quality attribute." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/assurance_case

docs.title: safety case
docs.text:
• [19, Definitions section, p. 3-5] (risk_safety_eng) "A structured argument, supported by a body of evidence that provides a compelling, comprehensible and valid case that a PSS is safe for a given application in a given environment. It is through-life, pan-Defence Lines of [...]" — PSS = Products, Services and/or Systems.
  • [19, Part 01 clause on safety case, para 3] (risk_safety_eng) "A safety case is a sub-set of the information set and consists of a structured argument, supported by a body of evidence that provides a case that a system is safe for a given application in a given environment."
  • [24, Introduction] (ai_safety) "A safety case is a structured rationale that a system is unlikely to cause significant harm if it is deployed to a particular setting."
  • [24, abstract] (ai_safety) "a structured rationale that AI systems are unlikely to cause a catastrophe"

docs.title: attack surface
docs.text:
• [31, NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1] (security) "The set of points on the boundary of a system, a system element, or an environment where an attacker can try to enter, cause an effect on, or extract data from."
  • [31, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5] (security) "The set of points on the boundary of a system, a system component, or an environment where an attacker can try to enter, cause an effect on, or extract data from, that system, component, or environment."

docs.title: adversary
docs.text:
• [30, CNSSI 4009-2022] (security) "Person, group, organization, or government that conducts or has the intent to conduct detrimental activities."
  • [30, NIST SP 800-107 Rev. 1] (security) "An entity that is not authorized to access or modify information, or who works to defeat any protections afforded the information."

docs.title: dangerous capability
docs.text: • [23, abstract] (ai_safety) "Developers must be able to identify dangerous capabilities (through "dangerous capability evaluations")" — fragment; no formal definition

docs.title: alignment
docs.text:
• [4, opening definition] (ai_safety) "When I say an AI A is aligned with an operator H, I mean: A is trying to do what H wants it to do." — Italics removed.
  • [16, abstract] (ai_safety) "The field of AI alignment is concerned with AI systems that pursue unintended goals."
  • [23, abstract] (ai_safety) "the propensity of models to apply their capabilities for harm (through "alignment evaluations")." — fragment

docs.title: misalignment
docs.text: • [15, abstract] (ai_safety) "We argue that, without substantial effort to prevent it, AGIs could learn to pursue goals that are in conflict (i.e. misaligned) with human interests." — situational awareness not defined in abstract

docs.title: specification gaming
docs.text:
• [9, opening definition] (ai_safety) "Specification gaming is a behaviour that satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome."
  • [16, abstract] (ai_safety) "One commonly studied mechanism by which an unintended goal might arise is specification gaming, in which the designer-provided specification is flawed in a way that the designers did not foresee."

docs.title: reward hacking
docs.text: • [17, abstract] (ai_safety) "We provide the first formal definition of reward hacking, a phenomenon where optimizing an imperfect proxy reward function leads to poor performance according to the true reward function."

docs.title: goal misgeneralization
docs.text: • [16, abstract] (ai_safety) "Goal misgeneralization is a specific form of robustness failure for learning algorithms in which the learned program competently pursues an undesired goal that leads to good performance in training situations but bad performance [...]"

docs.title: scheming
docs.text:
• [18, abstract] (ai_safety) "This report examines whether advanced AIs that perform well in training will be doing so in order to gain power later -- a behavior I call 'scheming' (also sometimes called 'deceptive alignment')." — schemer: AI that does so; abstract also says schemers pretend to be aligned on tests designed to reveal their motivations
  • [18, abstract] (ai_safety) "because schemers pretend to be aligned on tests designed to reveal their motivations, it may be quite difficult to tell whether this has occurred."

docs.title: catastrophic risk
docs.text: • [20, abstract] (ai_safety) "Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have sparked growing concerns among experts, policymakers, and world leaders regarding the potential for increasingly advanced AI systems to pose catastrophic risks." — framing, no formal definition

docs.title: existential risk
docs.text:
• [2, 1.2 Existential risks] (ai_safety) "One where an adverse outcome would either annihilate Earth-originating intelligent life or permanently and drastically curtail its potential." — Leading 'An existential risk is' is elided
  • [13, abstract] (ai_safety) "there is some concern that building ever more intelligent and powerful AI systems could eventually result in systems that are more powerful than us; some say this is like playing with fire and speculate that this could create [...]" — not a definition

docs.title: systemic risk
docs.text: • [25, Article 3(65)] (risk_safety_eng) "‘systemic risk’ means a risk that is specific to the high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models, having a significant impact on the Union market due to their reach, or due to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative [...]"

docs.title: reasonably foreseeable misuse
docs.text: • [25, Article 3(13)] (risk_safety_eng) "‘reasonably foreseeable misuse’ means the use of an AI system in a way that is not in accordance with its intended purpose, but which may result from reasonably foreseeable human behaviour or interaction with other systems [...]"

docs.title: STRIDE: denial of service
docs.text: • [3, STRIDE model] (security) "Denial of service (DoS) attacks deny service to valid users—for example, by making a Web server temporarily unavailable or unusable."

docs.title: STRIDE: elevation of privilege
docs.text: • [3, STRIDE model] (security) "An unprivileged user gains privileged access and thereby has sufficient access to compromise or destroy the entire system."

docs.title: STRIDE: information disclosure
docs.text: • [3, STRIDE model] (security) "Involves the exposure of information to individuals who are not supposed to have access to it—for example, the ability of users to read a file that they were not granted access to, or the ability of an intruder to read data in [...]"

docs.title: STRIDE: repudiation
docs.text: • [3, STRIDE model] (security) "Associated with users who deny performing an action without other parties having any way to prove otherwise—for example, a user performs an illegal operation in a system that lacks the ability to trace the prohibited operations."

docs.title: STRIDE: spoofing
docs.text: • [3, STRIDE model] (security) "Involves illegally accessing and then using another user's authentication information, such as username and password"

docs.title: STRIDE: tampering
docs.text: • [3, STRIDE model] (security) "Involves the malicious modification of data. Examples include unauthorized changes made to persistent data, such as that held in a database, and the alteration of data as it flows between two computers over an open network, such as the Internet"

docs.title: AI system
docs.text: • [25, Article 3(1)] (risk_safety_eng) "‘AI system’ means a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it [...]"

docs.title: ALARP
docs.text: • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-2] (risk_safety_eng) ""ALARP" is short for "as low as reasonably practicable". "SFAIRP" is short for "so far as is reasonably practicable". The two terms mean essentially the same thing and at their core is the concept of "reasonably practicable" [...]"

docs.title: barrier / control
docs.text: • [28, Bowtie element Prevention Controls, Definition box] (risk_safety_eng) "Any measure taken which acts against some undesirable force or intention, in order to maintain a desired state." — CAA uses 'control' where CCPS uses 'barrier'. URL https://www.caa.co.uk/safety-initiatives/working-with-industry/bowtie/bowtie-elements/prevention-controls/

docs.title: controller constraint
docs.text: • [7, Chapter 2, Defining Controller Constraints] (risk_safety_eng) "A controller constraint specifies the controller behaviors that need to be satisfied to prevent UCAs"

docs.title: damage
docs.text: • [6, 1.8] (risk_safety_eng) "Damage: Loss of something desirable"

docs.title: escalation factor
docs.text: • [28, How does bowtie work] (risk_safety_eng) "the reasoning to why a control may be defeated or less effective" — Parenthesis in the sentence on escalation factors.

docs.title: FMEA
docs.text: • [38, Lead paragraph] (risk_safety_eng) "Failure mode and effects analysis ( FMEA ; often written with "failure modes" in plural) is the process of reviewing as many components, assemblies, and subsystems as possible to identify potential failure modes in a system and [...]" — Secondary source.

docs.title: hazard analysis
docs.text:
• [13, abstract] (ai_safety) "First, we review how systems can be made safer today, drawing on time-tested concepts from hazard analysis and systems safety that have been designed to steer large processes in safer directions." — safety-engineering vocabulary; x-risk framed as long-tail risk
  • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-3] (risk_safety_eng) "The process of describing in detail the hazards and accidents associated with a system, and defining accident sequences."

docs.title: hazard identification
docs.text: • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-3] (risk_safety_eng) "The process of identifying and listing the hazards and accidents associated with a system."

docs.title: intended purpose
docs.text: • [25, Article 3(12)] (risk_safety_eng) "‘intended purpose’ means the use for which an AI system is intended by the provider, including the specific context and conditions of use, as specified in the information supplied by the provider in the instructions for use [...]"

docs.title: loss scenario / causal factor
docs.text: • [7, Chapter 2, Identifying loss scenarios] (risk_safety_eng) "A loss scenario describes the causal factors that can lead to the unsafe control actions and to hazards." — Used for 'scenario' and 'causal factor' in the STPA sense. The handbook also warns: 'The most common mistake is to identify individual causal factors rather than a scenario.'

docs.title: mesa-optimizer
docs.text: • [8, abstract] (ai_safety) "We analyze the type of learned optimization that occurs when a learned model (such as a neural network) is itself an optimizer - a situation we refer to as mesa-optimization, a neologism we introduce in this paper."

docs.title: mishap
docs.text: • [7, Chapter 3 Integrating STPA, Identification of Losses to be Considered] (risk_safety_eng) "an accident (or mishap, which is the term used by the military)" — Same sentence as accident; mishap is treated as a synonym.

docs.title: mitigation strategies
docs.text: • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-4] (risk_safety_eng) "Measures that, when implemented, reduce risk."

docs.title: prevention control
docs.text: • [28, How does bowtie work, table, left side] (risk_safety_eng) "Preventative measures which eliminate the threat entirely or prevent the threat from causing the top event" — Table text; the label 'recovery' belongs to the next row.

docs.title: recovery control
docs.text: • [28, How does bowtie work, table, right side] (risk_safety_eng) "Measures which reduce the likelihood of the consequence owing to the top event being "live" or mitigate the severity of the consequence"

docs.title: resilience
docs.text: • [6, 1.13 Resilience, first overall qualitative definition] (risk_safety_eng) "Resilience is the ability of the system to sustain or restore its basic functionality following a risk source or an event (even unknown)."

docs.title: risk avoidance
docs.text: • [6, 3.3 Risk avoidances] (risk_safety_eng) "Process of actions to avoid risk, for example, not be involved in, or withdraw from an activity in order not to be exposed to any risk source"

docs.title: risk characterization
docs.text: • [6, 2.9 Risk characterization, risk description] (risk_safety_eng) "A qualitative and/or quantitative picture of the risk; i.e., a structured statement of risk usually containing the elements: risk sources, causes, events, consequences, uncertainty representations/measurements (for example [...]"

docs.title: risk criteria
docs.text: • [26, csrc term 'risk criteria'; NIST SP 800-160v1r1 from ISO Guide 73] (risk_safety_eng) "Terms of reference against which the significance of a risk is evaluated." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_criteria

docs.title: risk estimation
docs.text: • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-4] (risk_safety_eng) "The systematic use of available information to estimate risk."

docs.title: risk management
docs.text:
• [6, 2.14 Risk management] (risk_safety_eng) "Activities to handle risk such as prevention, mitigation, adaptation or sharing"
  • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-4] (risk_safety_eng) "Process that encompasses systematic hazard identification; risk assessment; hazard risk matrix; risk reduction and risk monitoring, evaluation, and review."
  • [26, csrc term 'risk management'; ISO Guide 73 wording] (risk_safety_eng) "Coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk." — Wording is the ISO Guide 73 / ISO 31000 definition. https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_management

docs.title: risk metric: (C′,Q,K)
docs.text: • [6, 1.1 Risk metrics/descriptions (examples) item 4] (risk_safety_eng) "The triplet (C’,Q,K), where C’ is some specified consequences, Q a measure of uncertainty associated with C’ (typically probability), and K the background knowledge that supports C’ and Q (which includes a judgment of the strength of this knowledge)"

docs.title: risk metric: combination of probability and severity
docs.text: • [6, 1.1 Risk metrics/descriptions (examples) item 1] (risk_safety_eng) "The combination of probability and magnitude/ severity of consequences" — Metric, not the definition of risk: the glossary states 'None of these examples can be viewed as risk itself'.

docs.title: risk metric: hazard and vulnerability
docs.text: • [6, 1.1 Risk metrics/descriptions (examples) item 2] (risk_safety_eng) "The combination of the probability of a hazard occurring and a vulnerability metric given the occurrence of the hazard"

docs.title: risk metric: scenario triplet
docs.text: • [6, 1.1 Risk metrics/descriptions (examples) item 3] (risk_safety_eng) "The triplet (si,pi,ci), where si is the ith scenario, pi is the probability of that scenario, and ci is the consequence of the ith scenario, i =1,2,…N."

docs.title: risk mitigation
docs.text:
• [6, 3.5 Risk mitigation] (risk_safety_eng) "Process of actions to reduce risk"
  • [26, csrc term 'risk mitigation'; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 under Risk Mitigation from CNSSI 4009] (risk_safety_eng) "Prioritizing, evaluating, and implementing the appropriate risk-reducing controls/countermeasures recommended from the risk management process. A subset of Risk Response." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_mitigation

docs.title: risk prevention
docs.text: • [6, 3.7 Risk prevention] (risk_safety_eng) "Process of actions to avoid a risk source or to intercept the risk source pathway to the realization of damage with the effect that none of the targets are affected by the risk source"

docs.title: risk response
docs.text: • [26, csrc term 'risk response'; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 under Risk Response from NIST SP 800-39] (risk_safety_eng) "Accepting, avoiding, mitigating, sharing, or transferring risk to organizational operations (i.e., mission, functions, image, or reputation), organizational assets, individuals, other organizations, or the Nation." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/risk_response

docs.title: risk vs probability times consequence
docs.text: • [1, Section 3.3 Comments on the Definition] (risk_safety_eng) "One often hears it said that “risk is probability times consequence.” We find this definition misleading and prefer instead, in keeping with the set of triplets idea, to say that “risk is probability and consequence.”"

docs.title: safe
docs.text: • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-4] (risk_safety_eng) "Freedom from unacceptable or intolerable levels of harm."

docs.title: safety analysis
docs.text:
• [6, 2.16 Safety analysis] (risk_safety_eng) "Systematic process to comprehend the nature of the safety of a system and to express the safety level; Systematic process to determine the degree of risk reduction that is sufficient to obtain a “safe system”" — Two bullets joined with a semicolon.
  • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-4] (risk_safety_eng) "The systematic identification of potential causes of hazards or failure modes that contribute to a hazard."

docs.title: safety component
docs.text: • [25, Article 3(14)] (risk_safety_eng) "‘safety component’ means a component of a product or of an AI system which fulfils a safety function for that product or AI system, or the failure or malfunctioning of which endangers the health and safety of persons or property;"

docs.title: safety engineering
docs.text: • [19, Definitions section, p. 3-5] (risk_safety_eng) "The development of products, services or systems which are safe, informed by hazard identification, hazard analysis, risk analysis, safety analysis and knowledge of failure modes that contribute to a hazard."

docs.title: scenario triplet components
docs.text: • [1, Section 3.1] (risk_safety_eng) "where [s_i] is a scenario identification or description; [p_i] is the probability of that scenario; and [x_i] is the consequence or evaluation measure of that scenario, i.e., the measure of damage." — Symbols in brackets omitted; the descriptive words are verbatim.

docs.title: system
docs.text: • [7, Chapter 2, Identifying system-level hazards] (risk_safety_eng) "A system is a set of components that act together as a whole to achieve some common goal, objective, or end. A system may contain subsystems and may also be part of a larger system."

docs.title: system-level constraint
docs.text: • [7, Chapter 2, Defining system-level constraints] (risk_safety_eng) "A system-level constraint specifies system conditions or behaviors that need to be satisfied to prevent hazards (and ultimately prevent losses)"

docs.title: threat event
docs.text: • [26, csrc term 'threat event'; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1] (risk_safety_eng) "An event or situation that has the potential for causing undesirable consequences or impact." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/threat_event

docs.title: threat scenario
docs.text: • [26, csrc term 'threat scenario'; NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1] (risk_safety_eng) "A set of discrete threat events, associated with a specific threat source or multiple threat sources, partially ordered in time." — https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/threat_scenario

docs.title: uncertainty
docs.text:
• [6, 1.2 Uncertainty, overall qualitative definitions] (risk_safety_eng) "For a person or a group of persons, not knowing the true value of a quantity or the future consequences of an activity"
  • [6, 1.2 Uncertainty, overall qualitative definitions (second bullet)] (risk_safety_eng) "Imperfect or incomplete information/knowledge about a hypothesis, a quantity, or the occurrence of an event"

docs.title: unhackable proxy
docs.text: • [17, abstract] (ai_safety) "We say that a proxy is unhackable if increasing the expected proxy return can never decrease the expected true return."

docs.title: Not obtained
docs.text:
These were requested and could not be read or were not found:

  • Terms with no verbatim definition found in any source read: fault; near miss (Def Stan 'incident' is the closest); risk factor; causal factor (only STPA 'loss scenario' text); contributing factor; assurance argument (only assurance case and safety case); scenario in the general sense (only Kaplan and NIST threat scenario).
  • ISO 31000:2018 and ISO Guide 73:2009 full text: paywalled, not read. Only risk, event, consequence, likelihood and control were obtained, via the ERA reproduction; risk source and risk treatment of ISO 31000:2018 were not available. ISO Guide 73 wording for risk treatment, risk analysis, risk evaluation, risk identification, tolerance and residual risk comes only through NIST CSRC citations.
  • ISO/IEC 23894:2023 and ISO/IEC 22989: paywalled, not read.
  • GSN Community Standard Version 3 (SCSC-141C): the standard was not read, so no GSN definition of assurance case or assurance argument is recorded. A secondary summary attributed to GSN v3 was not verified against the standard and is deliberately omitted. NIST CSRC assurance case entries (from ISO/IEC 15026-1 and SEI) and the Def Stan safety case definition are given instead.
  • Def Stan 00-56 Issue 7 Part 1: not read. Issue 8 (2023) Part 01 is used instead.
  • IEC 60812 (FMEA): paywalled, not read. Wikipedia is used instead.
  • Bow-tie: a commercial bow-tie page was not available and the CCPS book 'Bow Ties in Risk Management' is paywalled. UK CAA bow-tie pages are used instead; they use 'control' for what CCPS calls 'barrier'.
  • Leveson, 'Engineering a Safer World': not read; the STPA Handbook is used instead.
  • EU AI Act: the text is taken from the Official Journal HTML version (the EUR-Lex ELI URL returned no content).
  • Aven 2012/2016: not read; the SRA glossary (Aven-led) is used for the uncertainty-based definitions.
  • NIST CSRC pages not found: accident, failure, fault, mishap, risk source, risk acceptance, safeguard, risk level.
  • Kenton et al.: no explicit definition sentence of 'threat model' found in the post.
  • Hubinger et al.: definitions of deceptive alignment and mesa-optimizer from the paper body not obtained (abstract only).
  • International AI Safety Report 2025: definition of risk and the three-way split not found in the abstract; full text not read.
  • Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy: definitions of capability threshold and required safeguards are in linked documents not read.
  • NIST CSRC glossary page for 'threat model': not found.
  • NIST SP 800-154 definition of threat modeling: not obtained.
  • Ngo et al.: definition of situational awareness not in the abstract.

docs.title: Safety environments catalog
docs.text:
Pitch. 87 safety environments and benchmarks mapped onto the taxonomy, with licence and access checked, so a researcher can see at a glance which risks have tests and which have none (32 of 70 sub-areas have no entry).

Status: draft. Version 0. Mappings are model-assigned and not human-reviewed.

87 environments and benchmarks mapped to the unified taxonomy, with metadata and one-line own-word descriptions only. 83 entries were checked against a primary page (often only the abstract page); 4 are the author's own local environments and are unverified. 32 of 70 taxonomy sub-areas have no entry. Licence, access and release status are weak for many entries. Area 7 is over-represented because the catalog is mostly evaluations.

Explore: Environments explorer → · Taxonomy explorer →

docs.title: Catalog of AI-safety environments and benchmarks (v0 draft)
docs.text:
Mappings are model-assigned, not human-reviewed. Numbers in brackets point to the bibliography. Full fields, including repository URLs and the licence evidence URL for each entry, are in catalog.csv.

Licence and access columns were checked on 2026-11-22: one Sonnet agent opened each entry's repository, LICENSE file or dataset card, and a second agent tried to refute the result. ✓ = confirmed by both; ⚠ = corrected after the second check; (low) = only the paper page could be read. 'none stated' means no licence file was found, not that reuse is allowed. This is not legal advice.

AI-use: most text in this catalog was generated by Claude (Anthropic) under the direction of Robin Chauhan. Entries were checked against primary pages by the model; mappings are model-assigned and not human-reviewed.
