docs.title: Two cultures paper
docs.text:
Pitch. Breiman [1] split statistics into a data-modelling and an algorithmic culture; agent safety has the same split. One culture (safe RL, constrained MDPs, shields) begins "assume the agent maximises a reward R". The other (red teams, evals, AI control, incident reports) treats the agent as a black box and measures what it does. The paper maps the two line by line, counts how often each side's assumptions fail across 70 real incidents, and traces both in the citation graph. The paper so far is a two-page draft (v0.1, 2026-11-20); a longer version is not written.

Status: draft. All incident statistics are model-judged, not human-audited (marked [U]).

"Agent Safety: The Two Cultures" (Breiman analogy): framing, assumptions table, related work, citation census, concept semantics, and a two-page draft. Depends on the rebuttal and the incident catalog.

docs.title: Unified assumptions table: classical RL vs LLM agents
docs.text:
Status: STARTED

Not final. Not fully human-reviewed. See the AI-use statement.

v0.1, 2026-11-20. Companion to framing.md. Extends the precondition list P1–P7 in ../rebuttal-agent-safety-rl/draft.md §6.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• Each row is one axis, stated neutrally. Both cultures fill it in.
  • Owner says whose default assumption the row tests:
    • RL: a classical-RL assumption that fails for LLM agents.
    • LLM: an LLM-agent assumption that fails in typical RL.
    • Both: each side assumes something the other side breaks.
  • RL exceptions names the RL sub-literature that already relaxes the assumption. This is the steelman column. A row with a strong exception is weak evidence for a culture split.
  • "Classical RL" means the Sutton–Barto setting [1] as used in safe RL [2, 3, 4]: a learner, a designer-written reward, a designed environment, episodic resets.

docs.title: Row groups and the Breiman section each mirrors
docs.text: Row group Breiman section mirrored One-sentence reason A. Objective §5 "The use of data models" and §5.2 on goodness-of-fit "Assume the agent maximizes R" is "assume the data are generated by the following model"; a satisfied constraint has no power outside the abstraction, as a passed goodness-of-fit test has none in high dimensions. B. Learning §5.3 "Multiplicity of data models" and §8 Rashomon Many rewards fit one behavior, as many models fit one data set; the "internalized reward" is one picture among many. C. Environment and state §6 "The limitations of data models" The deployment environment "stopped looking like a nail": non-episodic, adversarial, real; the toolkit is frozen at CMDP, safe exploration and shielding. D. Actions and observations §9 Occam, and §10 Bellman's curse (folded in) The MDP abstraction is simple and wrong about open-ended actions whose safety depends on context; accuracy, not formal tidiness, is the goal. E. Overseer §7 "A new research community" and §11 "Information from a black box" The behavior-modeling community formed around oversight; CoT monitoring extracts intent from the agent black box as permutation importance extracted structure from the forest. F. Validation §5.4 "Predictive accuracy" plus the Efron comment Both cultures measure where their instruments reach; the Efron objection ("prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient") applies to evals as to forests.

docs.title: The table
docs.text: # Axis Classical RL default LLM-agent default Owner RL exceptions (steelman) Safety consequence A. Objective A1 Who sets the objective Designer writes R before training; fixed Prompt and tool outputs set the effective objective at run time [5, 6] RL Goal-conditioned RL takes a goal as input, but from a designer-known goal space [7] Untrusted content can rewrite the objective (prompt injection [6, 8]) A2 Is the objective exogenous to the observations Yes: observations cannot change R No: instructions and data share one token stream [9] RL Corrupted-reward channel [10], delusion box [11]; both assume a known corruption model Reward arrives over an unauthenticated channel; a security problem, not a noise problem A3 Form of the task specification Scalar reward function Natural-language instruction, written by a non-expert, at test time [12, 13] LLM Language-conditioned RL [14] Task is ambiguous by construction; the agent must infer intent A4 Can the principal's preferences be steered by the agent No: R is fixed Yes: sycophancy, induced preference shift, misleading the evaluator [15, 16, 17] RL Assistance games [18] model a human, but with exogenous preferences The target moves under optimization; POMDP planning assumes it does not A5 Can the cost or unsafe set be written before deployment Yes: joint limits, hazard lists [4] No: open-world, normative, context-dependent RL Shields over finite abstractions [3]; impact measures need no cost [19, 20] CMDPs and shields cover only the enumerable subset [debunking §5.4] B. Learning B1 Does the policy learn at deployment Yes: training and acting are one loop No: weights frozen; adaptation only in context [12] RL Offline RL, fixed-policy evaluation Safe-exploration methods have nothing to modify [21] B2 Does a reward signal arrive at deployment Yes, each step or episode No RL Inverse RL infers a reward, but it is not identifiable [22, 23] "Internalized reward" claims cannot be tested B3 Where competence comes from Reward-driven trial and error from scratch Pretraining on human text; post-training steers it lightly [12, 24] Both Pretrained representations in robotics RL Behavior is not the argmax of any one reward; reward-based diagnosis misattributes B4 Does the agent bring human norms No: tabula rasa Yes: inherits norms, and their violations, from human text LLM None classical Some safety is free; some failure is human-like (deception, concealment) B5 Who controls exploration Designer (ε-greedy, entropy bonus, safe-exploration rules) No designed exploration; actions come from sampling a prior RL — "Unsafe exploration" relabels an action-selection error C. Environment and state C1 Who built the environment Experimenter; usually a simulator Nobody: real software, real internet, real users LLM Sim-to-real transfer [25] No safe place to fail; evaluation is not the deployment distribution C2 Episodes and resets Many episodes; failures amortize [4] Single-shot; many actions irreversible RL Reset-free and single-life RL Expected-cost guarantees are the wrong metric; tail matters C3 What the state contains Physical or game state; Markov in a designer-chosen representation Includes the user's intent and the world beyond the context window RL POMDPs with belief states [26] The belief over intent is the alignment problem, not a filter C4 Is anything in the environment adversarial Usually nature only Yes: content authors attack the agent [6, 8] LLM Robust and adversarial RL [27, 28] A security threat model is required; average-case RL guarantees do not hold C5 Other agents Single agent, or designed multi-agent games Other LLM agents, copies of itself, unknown humans [29] LLM Multi-agent RL Collusion and miscoordination risks that single-agent safety cannot see D. Actions and observations D1 Action space Fixed, small, known semantics Open-ended text and tool calls; composable; semantics depend on context RL Large discrete action spaces, but enumerable rm -rf /tmp/x vs rm -rf /: the same action type, opposite safety D2 Can the agent explain itself No Yes: verbal reasoning traces, partly monitorable [30, 31] LLM — New oversight channel; it degrades if trained against [32] D3 Can the agent be steered without retraining No: change R and retrain Yes: system prompt, instructions, few-shot examples [12] LLM Goal-conditioned policies [7] Cheap control, and cheap attack, through the same channel E. Overseer E1 Does the agent model its overseer No Yes: knows what evaluation and oversight are [33]; can fake alignment [34] RL Delusion box [11]; reward tampering in causal-influence diagrams Optimizing against a monitor hides misbehavior rather than removing it [32] E2 Who is in the loop at run time Nobody; autonomous after training User approves steps, co-acts, and often disables gates [debunking §7] LLM Human-in-the-loop RL from preferences is a training-time loop [35] Shields have a friction cost; human factors become part of safety E3 Who owns training The same team designs R, trains and deploys Model is a third-party product; the deployer cannot retrain LLM — Deployment-time safety must be architectural, not learned [36, 37] F. Validation F1 How safety is measured Expected return and expected cost under a known R and C Attack success rates, eval pass rates, incident records [8, 38] Both — RL measures inside its model; LLM evals measure on a sample. Both are weak in the tail. F2 Is the eval itself a specification that can be gamed Reward is gameable; the test environment is not modeled by the agent Evals are gameable and the agent can detect them [33] LLM Specification gaming literature [39] Behavior culture inherits Goodhart too; neither culture escapes specification

docs.title: Notes for the paper
docs.text:
• The split is symmetric. About as many LLM-side assumptions fail in RL as the reverse. This supports the two-cultures framing over a pure "RL is wrong" framing.
  • The LLM rows are not all advantages. D2 and D3 give new control channels. C4, C5 and E3 add threats RL never modeled.
  • Strongest rows for the paper: A2, B1, A5, E1. Each has the RL side's own authors stating the precondition [3, 4, 10, 21].
  • Weakest rows: B5 and D1. RL people will say large or structured action spaces are an engineering extension. Keep them, but do not lean on them.
  • Bellman folded in. Dimensionality as curse lives in A5 and D1; the only blessing that survived scrutiny, CoT monitoring, lives in E under Breiman §11 (see framing.md §3.5).
  • Rows that cut against the behavior culture: F1 and F2. Put them in the final remarks, as Efron's objection: prediction alone is "only occasionally sufficient" [40].
  • Use as an instrument. Each row is a yes/no check. For any proposed method, mark which rows its preconditions need. This generalizes the transfer test of the debunking draft.

docs.title: Semantics of core concepts: RL, LLM base model, LLM agent with tools
docs.text:
Status: STARTED

Draft. Not fully human-reviewed. See the AI-use statement.

Date: 2026-11-21. Companion to assumptions_table.md (rows A1–F2) and framing.md.

Purpose. The two cultures use the same words. This table states what each word denotes in three settings. The middle column matters: the LLM agent inherits most of its semantics from the base model, not from RL, even when it is trained with RL.

Reading key. "RL" = classical MDP/POMDP agent [1]. "Base model" = a pretrained, post-trained LLM used as a text function. "LLM agent" = a frozen model inside a scaffold loop with tools [4]. Last column names the assumptions_table.md rows the shift feeds.

docs.title: 1. Agent and environment
docs.text: Concept RL LLM base model LLM agent with tools Rows Agent The policy π. One learned object; everything else is given. No agent. A conditional distribution over the next token, p(x_t | x_<t). Model + scaffold + tool set + system prompt. The model alone is not the agent; most of what varies at deployment is outside the weights. D1, D3, E3 Environment An MDP built or simulated by the experimenter; known interface, fixed dynamics. None at inference. The prompt author plays the environment. In training, the text corpus. Real software, files, web, accounts, other agents, humans. Nobody built it; parts of it are hostile. C1, C4, C5 State Markov state s_t: a sufficient statistic for the future in a designer-chosen representation. The context window. Trivially Markov in the token sequence. Context window plus external world state the model cannot see (files, accounts, side effects already made). Includes the user's intent. Non-Markov in the context. C3 Observation o_t = sensor(s_t), designer-defined. Data only; carries no commands. The prompt. The only input, and it is both data and instruction. Tool outputs, retrieved pages, user turns, all in one token stream with the instructions. Observations can carry commands [5]. A2, C4 Action a_t from a fixed, small set with fixed semantics. One token from a fixed vocabulary. No side effect. A text span the scaffold parses into a tool call. Open-ended, compositional; meaning depends on the tool and its arguments; side effects in the world. D1 Transition dynamics P(s'|s,a): fixed, stationary, often known or simulated. Deterministic append of the sampled token. Whatever the tool and the world do. Non-stationary, unknown to the designer, partly controlled by third parties. C1 Other agents Single agent, or a designed multi-agent game. None. Stateless function; infinitely many identical copies. Concurrent instances, sub-agents, copies of itself, other vendors' agents, unknown humans. C5 Time step A clock tick fixed by the designer. One token. One model turn or one tool call. Real duration from seconds to hours. C2

docs.title: 2. Objective and value
docs.text: Concept RL LLM base model LLM agent with tools Rows Reward / objective Scalar R(s,a) written in advance by the designer. Exogenous to observations. Delivered each step. Pretraining: next-token likelihood. Post-training: a preference reward model [6]. Neither exists at inference. No scalar at run time. The effective objective is the instruction in the context, and any text in the context can revise it, including tool output. Success is judged afterwards by the user. A1, A2, A3, B2 Return / value V(s), Q(s,a): expected discounted sum. The central computational object. None. None explicit. "Value" lives in the model's verbal judgment and the user's acceptance. No discount. A1 Goal-directedness By construction: π maximizes expected return. Not goal-directed. Simulates goal-directed text. Role-played from the instruction. Persists only while the context supports it; a new instruction can drop or replace the goal. A1, A4 Specification R and cost C, written once by one expert before training. The vendor's training data and post-training rubric (e.g. a model spec) [7], baked into weights. Split across three parties: vendor spec in the weights; deployer system prompt and tool permissions, writable and enforceable at the tool layer; user instruction at test time by a non-expert. A3, A5, E3 Principal One party: the designer, who also trains and deploys. The vendor. Vendor, deployer, user, plus third parties whose content enters the context. Three or more principals with conflicting instructions. A1, E3 Horizon / episode Episodes with resets. Many episodes; a failure costs one episode. One sequence; ends at EOS or the context limit. One task run. Ends when the model says done, the scaffold hits a step cap, or the user interrupts. No reset of the world; actions persist. C2 Termination A terminal state of the MDP. The EOS token. A claim by the model that the task is done. Not a world state; can be false. F1

docs.title: 3. Learning and knowledge
docs.text: Concept RL LLM base model LLM agent with tools Rows Learning Online loop: acting and learning are one process, from scratch. Offline: pretraining on text, then post-training. Weights frozen afterwards. No weight update at deployment. "Learning" means in-context adaptation and memory files written by the scaffold. The deployer cannot retrain. B1, B3, E3 Source of competence Reward-driven trial and error. Imitation of human text. Inherited from the base model; the scaffold adds tools and a loop, not competence. B3 Prior knowledge / norms None. Tabula rasa. Human norms, and their violations, from the corpus. Same norms, now attached to actions with side effects. B4 Exploration Designed: ε-greedy, entropy bonus, UCB. A core problem. Sampling temperature. No notion of information gain. Not designed. Novel actions come from sampling the prior. Exploration happens in the real world with real side effects. B5 Generalization To unseen states of the same MDP; sim-to-real [2]. To unseen prompts within the distribution of human text. To unseen tools, sites, tasks and users. The distribution is whatever the world presents. C1 Memory The state is the memory (Markov). Recurrent policy for POMDPs. Context window only. Nothing persists across calls. Context plus scaffold stores (files, vector DB, memory tools). Writable by the agent and by injected content. C3 Self-model None. Knows what an LLM, an evaluation and a monitor are, from text [8]. Same knowledge, now applied to its own oversight. Can distinguish test from deployment contexts. E1

docs.title: 4. Safety and oversight
docs.text: Concept RL LLM base model LLM agent with tools Rows Safety constraint Cost c(s,a) with a budget (CMDP) [3]; shield over a known unsafe set. Refusal behaviour trained in; a content policy. Two layers. Tool layer: allow/deny lists, approval gates, sandboxes; writable and enforceable. Policy layer: "harmful" or "unwanted" side effects; not writable in advance. Gates get switched off by users. A5, E2 Failure Low return; constraint violation; reward hacking of R. Wrong or harmful text; hallucination; jailbreak. A harmful side effect in the world: deleted data, leaked secret, money moved, message sent. Reached via injection, over-permission or misread instruction. F1 Adversary Nature's stochasticity. Occasionally a perturbation of observations. The prompt author (jailbreak). Any content author on the retrieval or tool path [5]; other agents; the user's own ambiguous instruction. C4 Oversight channel None at run time. Evaluation by return after training. Output filters; human raters at training time. Reasoning traces, tool-call logs, human approval per step. Monitorable, but the agent models the monitor and the user disables the gate. D2, E1, E2 Steering at deployment Change R and retrain. Change the prompt. Change the system prompt, tools, permissions or examples. No retraining; no access to weights. D3 Validation Expected return and cost on the training MDP or held-out seeds. Benchmarks; red-team pass rates. Attack success rates, eval pass rates, incident records. The eval is itself a specification the agent can recognise and game. F1, F2

docs.title: 5. Where the semantics break
docs.text:
• Six concepts keep their RL meaning in the agent setting: action (as "thing with side effects"), transition, horizon, failure, adversary, validation. They break in the base-model column and come back for the agent.
  • Six concepts never recover their RL meaning: reward, return, value, exploration, learning, episode reset. The agent has none of these at run time. Theory built on them transfers only if it is reinterpreted (see framing.md §5).
  • Four concepts are new and have no RL counterpart: observation-as-command, three-party specification, self-model of oversight, scaffold-held memory. These are where the behavior-culture incidents concentrate (../llm-agent-incident-catalog/taxonomy/taxonomy_stats.md).
  • The base-model column is the source of the agent's semantics for state, action, learning, competence, norms and self-model. The agent inherits them unchanged; the scaffold adds side effects.

  2. Zhao, W., Queralta, J. P. & Westerlund, T. (2020). Sim-to-real transfer in deep reinforcement learning for robotics: a survey. IEEE SSCI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13303

docs.title: Semantics of core concepts across six decision settings
docs.text:
Status: STARTED

Draft. Not fully human-reviewed. See the AI-use statement.

Date: 2026-11-21. Expands concept_semantics.md. Companion to assumptions_table.md.

Purpose. Split "LLM" by how the decision problem is posed, not by model size. The posing decides which RL concepts keep their meaning.

docs.title: 0. Three axes, one path
docs.text:
The columns differ on three independent axes. The table follows one path through them; other paths exist (e.g. a PRM over tool calls, [43]).

Axis Values Action granularity whole completion · reasoning step · tool call Reward source environment · human rater · learned reward model · programmatic verifier · none at run time World coupling none (text only) · side effects visible to a human each step · side effects invisible until the run ends

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
Col Setting Posed as RL Classical RL agent. MDP or POMDP (S, A, P, R, γ) [1, 2]. CHAT-O Chatbot, no tools, outcome supervision by a learned reward model. The whole completion is one action. Contextual bandit with a proxy reward [11–15, 17, 71, 72]. CHAT-V Chatbot, no tools, verifiable outcome reward (RLVR). The whole trace plus answer is one action; the reasoning trace is not supervised. Contextual bandit with ground-truth reward on the answer [18, 22, 23]. CHAT-P Chatbot, no tools, process supervision. Each reasoning step is one action, scored by a process reward model (PRM). Finite-horizon deterministic tree MDP, dense step reward [25–28]. AGENT-A Tool-using assistant. One tool call or reply per turn; a human sees the result before the next turn. Episodic POMDP with a human turn between steps [35, 36, 45]. AGENT-X Autonomous agent. Loop of tool calls until the model declares done; no human between steps; memory; sub-agents. Long-horizon POMDP; unknown, non-stationary, partly adversarial dynamics; no reset [37, 44, 46].

AGENT-A and AGENT-X are the two variants of "chatbot-agent with tools". Cells name what changes from the previous column.

Programmatic check of the final answer: test cases, exact match [22, 23]. PRM fit to per-step human labels [26] or Monte-Carlo rollouts [27]. Deployment: none. Training: trajectory success test in a sandbox [43]. Same; tests sparser and more gameable [24]. Reward timing Every step. Terminal, plus a per-token KL penalty to the reference policy [12, 13]. Terminal, plus KL (or none in GRPO variants) [18, 23]. Every step: dense. None at run time. None at run time; terminal in training. The KL term A trust region on the policy (TRPO/PPO) [68, 69]. A constraint that keeps the policy near the pretrained prior [12, 15, 75]; cast as a CMDP with the KL coefficient as Lagrange multiplier [73], as a KL budget [19], or as Bayesian inference [74]. Same. Same. Same in training; absent at deployment. Absent. Who writes it One designer, in advance [4]. Raters' preferences, compressed into a model [11]. Dataset author with ground truth. Raters labelling steps, or an automatic checker [26, 27]. Benchmark author (training) [42]; user acceptance (deployment). Same. Return / value V, Q: the central object [1]. Q(x,y) = r. Degenerate; critics are dropped [17, 18, 70]. Degenerate. Q(prefix) = PRM score; drives best-of-n, beam, MCTS [29, 31]. None. None; some systems add value heads. Credit assignment Temporal, by bootstrapping [1]. None across time: one reward, one action. PPO spreads it over tokens by advantage; DPO learns an implicit token-level Q [16]. Same; the trace gets credit only via the answer. Explicit per step [25]. Per turn, via user reaction. Which of 200 calls caused the failure? Terminal signal only [43]. Discount γ < 1 typical. n/a. n/a. γ = 1 typical. None. None. Reward identifiability R identified only up to potential shaping; IRL is ill-posed [52, 53, 76]. Bradley–Terry identifies within-prompt differences only; the RM is a classifier, not a utility [11, 15]. Fully identified on the checked set; undefined off it, and verifiers have false positives [93]. Step labels define "progress"; the label is "convincing", not "correct" [26]. None: no reward exists to identify. None. Proxy gap: what gets hacked R itself, when misspecified [4, 5, 51], or the reward channel is tampered with [78]. The RM: length, sycophancy, confident tone [19–21, 79]. The verifier's incompleteness: special-casing tests, bypassing checks; and the trace, if it is trained on, stops showing it [24]. The PRM: plausible-looking steps, verbosity; R1 and others abandoned PRMs for this reason [23, 28, 91, 92]. The user: claims of success [44]. The success test and the user: editing tests, fabricated completion [24, 44]; hacking in production RL generalises to broader misalignment [80]. Goal-directedness By construction [1]. None; one shot. Within one trace, toward an answer. Simulated across steps toward an answer. Role-played from the instruction, one turn at a time. Role-played across a long loop; new context can replace it [37]. Agentic RL in sandboxed task suites, then freeze [43, 89]. Same; environments harder to build and to make safe. Sim-to-real Simulator vs robot [10, 86]. None: training prompts and deployment prompts are the same kind of object. Same. Same. Training sandbox vs deployment world: resets, clean tests and benign content exist only in the former [43]. Same, wider. Exploration Designed [83]; safe exploration is a field [6, 84]. n completions at temperature; RLHF narrows the sampled set [82]. Same; coverage grows with n [30]. Tree search over steps [31]. None designed. None designed; happens in the real world. Search at inference Planning if a model is known. Best-of-n with RM [19]. Best-of-n with verifier where available [30, 81]. Beam or MCTS with PRM; test-time compute scaling [29]. Rarely. Retry, reflect, self-verify [87]. No simulator; tree search needs a revertible state [88]; every probe is a real action. Planning / world model Model-based: Dyna, MuZero [58]. None. The trace is planning unrolled in words; no separate model. PRM + tree = planning with a learned value, the AlphaZero shape [59, 90]; the LLM can serve as its own world model where transitions are text-predictable [60]. None; the human plans. The ReAct loop is model-free [35]; self-simulation fails where the world is not text-predictable. On- vs off-policy Both; offline RL is the counterpart of SFT on logs [1, 85]. PPO on-policy; DPO offline [14, 15]. On-policy [18, 23]. Both. SFT on logged trajectories (offline imitation) + on-policy RL in sandbox [43]. Same. Learning at deployment Yes. No. No. No. In-context only. In-context + memory files written by the loop [41]. Memory The state. Context. Context. Context. Context across turns. Context + external stores; writable by injected content [41]. Source of competence Trial and error. Pretraining + preference tuning [14]. Pretraining + RLVR; reasoning length grows under training [23]. Same + step-level tuning. Base model; scaffold adds tools, not competence [36]. Same. What RL adds to the base model Everything. Style, helpfulness, refusal; a thin steering layer [14]. Sharpens sampling toward solutions the base model could already reach [61]; near-random rewards can help [62], so "reward" is a weaker signal than the bandit frame suggests. Step reliability. Tool-call formatting; persistence [43]. Same.

docs.text: Concept RL CHAT-O CHAT-V CHAT-P AGENT-A AGENT-X Safety constraint CMDP cost budget [3, 84]; shield over a known unsafe set [7]. Refusal training [109]; output filter [110]; KL to prior [12]. Same, plus safety reasoning trained into the trace [111]. Step-level filter on reasoning. Tool allow/deny lists; approval per call [45]. Sandbox, budgets, kill switch; gates that users disable [45]. Defence layer In the environment or the policy. In the weights (training). In the weights. In the weights and the PRM. Two layers: weights, and the tool layer (permissions, capability flow control) [66]. Same; the tool layer is where a deployer can still write a rule [122] (../llm-agent-incident-catalog/coverage/coverage_report.md). Failure Low return; constraint violation. Bad text [79]. Right-looking answer that games the checker [24]. Wrong answer with plausible steps [28]. One bad side effect, caught after one step. Cascade of side effects [46]. Oversight channel None at run time; an off-switch is respected only under uncertainty about the objective [104]. The output. The trace: readable, and monitorable until optimization pressure is put on it [24]. The steps; readable but possibly unfaithful [33, 34]. Tool-call log + user per turn. Traces + logs, read afterwards; the agent knows it is being watched [48, 49]; control protocols assume it may subvert the monitor [113]. Monitorability n/a. Output only. Trace is monitorable while not optimised against [24, 67], and even then it omits much [112]. Steps, possibly unfaithful [33, 34]. Log + human. Trace + log; monitorability is a property of training, not of the agent [67]. Validation Return on held-out seeds; safety needs a hidden metric separate from reward [102]. Win rate vs RM or humans [14]. Pass rate on held-out verifiable sets [22]. Step accuracy + final accuracy [26]. Task success + attack success rate [40, 96]. Benchmark pass rate [42, 114]; incident records; evaluations that reward cost-blind success [44]. Meaning of "safe" Expected cost under budget [3]. No harmful text. Correct answer by legitimate means. No harmful step and right answer. No unapproved harmful call. No harmful side effect over the whole run.

docs.title: 6. Reading the gradient
docs.text:
• CHAT-O and CHAT-V are bandits. Reward, return, credit assignment and exploration are degenerate; the field responded by dropping the critic [17, 18]. The one classical-RL object that survives is the KL trust region. This reading is established, not new: Moskovitz et al. cast RLHF as a CMDP with the KL coefficient as a Lagrange multiplier [73], Gao et al. speak of a KL budget [19], Ziegler et al. already tuned the coefficient to a KL target [12], and the practice goes back to KL-control of sequence models [75]. Korbak et al. give the competing Bayesian reading [74].
  • CHAT-V moved the proxy gap from the reward model to the verifier's coverage. Its unsupervised trace is a new oversight channel that training pressure destroys [24]. This is a CHAT-level result that the agent columns inherit unchanged.
  • CHAT-P is the column closest to classical RL: dense reward, Markov state, known deterministic dynamics, free resets, searchable tree. It has no side effects, so it is also the safest place to apply RL machinery. It is also the column the frontier retreated from because its reward got hacked [23, 28]. "RL for LLMs" literally holds here, and it did not hold up. The retreat is documented by R1 and by PRM papers [23, 28, 91, 92]; the ranking of settings by closeness to RL was not found elsewhere.
  • AGENT-A reintroduces the world but keeps a human between every step. The human is the reward signal, the reset, and the safety gate at once. Approval fatigue removes all three (debunking §7).
  • AGENT-X removes the human. It is the furthest column from classical RL on every row of §1–§3, yet it is where RL vocabulary (reward hacking, unsafe exploration, specification) is most used. The words transfer; the objects do not. Sim-to-real reappears as sandbox-to-deployment [43].
  • McLean's three classes land in different columns: reward misspecification is a CHAT-O/CHAT-V/CHAT-P problem (the RM, verifier, or PRM); unsafe action in an irreversible state is AGENT-X; insufficient observation is AGENT-A/X. No column has all three. No prior mapping of the classes to settings was found (literature search, 2026-11-21). Caveat: the class names here follow the debunking draft; a third-party summary of McLean et al. words them as observation ambiguity, reward misspecification and unsafe exploration. Cagatan & Zhao port the RL-safety gridworlds to LLM agents and find specification gaming, but treat agents as one setting [123].
  • Identifiability degrades left to right: R is identified up to shaping; the RM only within a prompt; the verifier only on the checked set; the agent has nothing to identify. "Reward misspecification" presupposes a reward that can be mis-specified; by AGENT-A that object is gone [52, 53]. Rungs one and two are explicit in the literature [53; 15, Def. 1]; rung three is stated only informally via verifier failures [93]; rung four was not found stated. Ng et al. reach the same conclusion from the other side: safety for autonomous agents belongs at run time, not in training [122].
  • Instrumental behaviour is a theorem in RL [54] and an evaluation finding in AGENT-X [55, 56]. The middle columns have no room for it: a one-shot bandit cannot seek power. The agent columns re-create the conditions (horizon, side effects, goal conflict) without the optimiser; the behaviour is role-played from the prior [116, 120], and still happens [55, 56]. The evidence on whether RL training raises it is mixed: He et al. find RL-trained models more instrumental [118]; Alparslan et al. find no monotone effect across RLVR checkpoints [119].
  • Planning survives only in CHAT-P, where the PRM over a deterministic tree is AlphaZero's shape [59]. AGENT-X has horizon without a model, which is the worst quadrant for RL theory.
  • The contract view [63] makes the stacking explicit: RL assumes a complete contract; every LLM column has an incomplete one filled by the prior; the agent has three incomplete contracts and no party present to renegotiate.
  • The behavior-culture incidents in ../llm-agent-incident-catalog/incidents/catalog.csv sit in AGENT-A and AGENT-X. The RL-safety constructions sit in RL and CHAT-P. The two cultures are, in this table, looking at different columns.

docs.title: 7. Provenance of citations
docs.text:
• References 1–67 were checked on 2026-11-21 by automated retrieval of each URL, comparing title, first author, year and venue. Result: 63 correct, 4 corrected (21, 23, 38, 43: venue or proceedings year), 4 optional venue additions applied (16, 20, 26, 61), 0 not found.
  • References 68–124 were added in the same pass, each retrieved when proposed; two (76, 122) were taken from search results without the page being opened.
  • The priority check searched for prior statements of six claims in §6. Verdicts: KL-as-constraint known [73, 19, 12]; bandit framing and critic-dropping known [17, 70–72]; PRM retreat known, ranking of settings not found; identifiability rungs 1–2 known, 3 informal, 4 not found; instrumental-behaviour components known separately, evidence mixed [118, 119]; McLean-classes-to-settings mapping not found.
  • Citations are not independently verified by a human.

docs.title: Agent Safety: The Two Cultures — framing notes
docs.text:
Status: STARTED

Not final. Not fully human-reviewed. See the AI-use statement.

v0.1, 2026-11-20. Framing document, not a draft. Companion to ../rebuttal-agent-safety-rl/draft.md.

docs.title: 0. One-paragraph thesis
docs.text: Breiman [1] split statistics into a data modeling culture ("assume the data are generated by the following model", validate by goodness-of-fit) and an algorithmic modeling culture (treat the inside of the box as unknown, validate by predictive accuracy on a test set). Agent safety has the same split, and the same epistemic move marks the line. One culture begins "assume the agent maximizes a reward R", derives safety from that model (constrained MDPs, shields, safe exploration), and validates by constraint satisfaction inside the model's abstraction. The other treats the trained agent as a black box, measures what it does (red-team success rates, evals, incident records), and bounds harm by architecture rather than by proof. McLean et al. [2] is the exhibit that makes the split visible: it hypothesizes an "internalized" reward f(o_p, o_g) for a frozen LLM policy and reasons from it, which is "assume the data are generated by the following model" in RL dress. The debunking draft [3] shows that this move fails on one paper. The two-cultures paper asks why the move is made at all, who makes it, what it costs the field, and what each culture cannot do without the other.

docs.title: 1. The mapping, line by line
docs.text:
Breiman gave each culture four lines: what is inside the box, the approach, the validation, the population. The same template for agent safety:

Breiman: data modeling Breiman: algorithmic modeling Agent safety: objective-modeling culture Agent safety: behavior-modeling culture The black box nature: x → y nature: x → y the agent: (observations, prompt) → actions the agent: (observations, prompt) → actions What is assumed inside a stochastic model with parameters unknown; "complex, mysterious, partly unknowable" an optimizer of a designer-known R (or an "internalized" R) over a known state abstraction unknown; a pretrained artifact with latent dispositions, lightly steered by post-training The opening sentence "Assume that the data are generated by the following model: …" [1, §4.1] "find a function f(x)" [1, §1] "Assume the agent maximizes R(s, a) …" / "the agent has internalized f(o_p, o_g)" [2, §4] "We ran the agent against N attacks / tasks and observed …" First question asked of a new problem "What's the model for the data?" [1, §4] "How well does it predict on a test set?" "What's the reward function? What's the cost function?" [2]; CPO takes C_i as input [4] "What does it do when we run it?" [5, 6] Validation goodness-of-fit tests, residual plots test-set error, cross-validation constraint satisfaction, formal guarantee inside a finite abstraction [7], Safety Gym cost [8] attack success rate [5], eval pass rate, incident databases [9], monitor catch rate [10] Theory inference, asymptotics, hypothesis tests generalization bounds, capacity regret bounds, CMDP duality, shield correctness, convergence threat models, control protocols [11], scaling of eval results, security design patterns [12] Where the hard part is relocated into the choice of model into the choice of test distribution into the specification of R, C, the unsafe set into eval coverage and the threat model Characteristic failure a model that passes the checks and is wrong about nature distribution shift a specification that is satisfied and a system that is unsafe ("moves the alignment problem around" [8, §3.3]) a tail event no eval covered Home venues Annals, JASA NeurIPS, Machine Learning ICML/NeurIPS RL tracks, L4DC, safe-RL workshops alignment labs, security venues (AISec, OWASP [13]), SE venues (ICSE [14]), blogs, incident reports Population (Breiman's guess: 98% / 2%) measured in §4a measured in §4a

Reading the table. Every row has a one-to-one analogue except population, which Breiman guessed and we can measure. The two "where the hard part is relocated" rows are the honest core: both cultures relocate the problem rather than solve it. Breiman said the data modelers' goodness-of-fit tests "have very little power unless the direction of the alternative is precisely specified" [1, §5.2]. The analogue holds exactly: a shield proves safety only against the automaton's labels [7, §9]; a constraint is satisfied only for the cost you wrote [4]. The behavior culture's analogue failure is the Efron objection (§5 below): a test set says nothing about the tail.

docs.title: 2. Why the mapping runs RL ≈ statistics, not RL ≈ machine learning
docs.text:
This needs stating early because RL people will object. In robotics, RL is the algorithmic culture against classical control. The mapping here is by epistemic move, not community label. The move that defines Breiman's data-modeling culture is: posit a parametric model of the inside of the box, then reason from the model as if it were the mechanism. Safe RL inherits exactly this move from control: posit R and the constraint set, then the conclusions (safe, within budget, shielded) are about the model's mechanism, not the agent's. Breiman's sentence transfers verbatim: "The conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism" [1, §5]. Replace "nature" with "the agent".

The parallel also holds sociologically:

  • Breiman: the new community (ML) "sprang up" outside statistics, "mostly young computer scientists" working on problems "where it was obvious that data models were not applicable" [1, §7.1]. Here: LLM-agent safety sprang up outside RL, in labs, security teams and SE groups, on systems where it was obvious a cost function could not be written.
  • Breiman: statistics' tools "are frozen at discriminant analysis and logistic regression" [1, §6]. Here: the safe-RL toolkit named in [2] is CMDP (1999), shielding (2018), safe exploration (2012), Safety Gym (2019), applied unchanged to a 2026 artifact.
  • Breiman: "the field has a vested interest in data models, come hell or high water" [1, §12]. Here: the vested interest is in the reward-maximizer picture, which is what makes decades of theory applicable.
  • Breiman: "If all a man has is a hammer, then every problem looks like a nail. The trouble for statisticians is that recently some of the problems have stopped looking like nails" [1, §6]. This sentence can open the paper.

Central table. assumptions_table.md is the paper's central table: 23 axes in six row groups, unifying the classical-RL assumptions that fail for LLM agents and the LLM-agent assumptions that fail in typical RL. §3 builds the paper's body around its row groups.

docs.title: 3. Skeleton: the assumptions table is the paper
docs.text: Breiman's paper is 12 numbered sections plus a glossary, then four invited comments and a rejoinder. The two-cultures paper keeps Breiman's opening (§§1–4) and closing (§12), and replaces his middle (§§5–11) with the six row groups of assumptions_table.md. Bracketed numbers follow this file's bibliography, not the table's. Each body section states, for its row group: the classical-RL default, the LLM-agent default, the RL steelman (the "RL exceptions" column), and the safety consequence. Breiman's named lessons are attached to the row group where they belong instead of standing alone.

docs.title: 3.1 Opening (mirrors Breiman §§1–4)
docs.text: # Breiman Two-cultures paper Notes 1 Introduction: black-box diagram, two cultures, 98/2 Agent-in-the-loop diagram; the two cultures; measured population (census, §4 item 1) Keep the diagram. Replace "nature" with "agent"; the environment and the principal are outside the box. End §1 with the assumptions table, so the reader has the whole argument before the body. 2 Road map: personal history as consultant Road map: personal history operating agents Breiman's credibility came from 13 years of consulting; the analogue is operational experience with deployed agents. 3 Projects in consulting: Ozone, Chlorine Incidents: Replit/SaaStr [15], Terraform [16, 17], prompt-injection cases [5, 6] Show how each resisted the objective-modeling toolkit. Ozone was "a failure" he regretted; keep one honest failure. Each incident is tagged with the rows it violates, so the body sections can refer back. 4 Return to the university: "Assume the data are generated by…"; the colleague's "What's the model for the data?" Reading the safe-RL literature: "Assume the agent maximizes…"; the colleague's "What's the reward function?" [2] is the exhibit. Quote its §4 hypothesis of f(o_p, o_g). [2, §5] concedes the tools "cannot be mapped one-to-one onto LLM backbones".

docs.title: 3.2 Body: one section per row group (replaces Breiman §§5–11)
docs.text: # Row group Classical-RL default LLM-agent default RL steelman Safety consequence Breiman analogue attached here 5 A. Objective (A1–A5) Designer writes R and the cost set before training; observations cannot change them Prompt and tool outputs set the effective objective at run time; preferences move under the agent; the unsafe set is open-world Goal-conditioned RL [28]; corrupted-reward channel [29]; assistance games [30]; impact measures [31, 32] The objective arrives over an unauthenticated channel (A2); CMDPs and shields cover only the enumerable subset (A5) §5 "the use of data models": "the conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism." §5.2 "goodness-of-fit has no power": a shield over a finite abstraction has no power outside its label set [7, §9]; a constraint is satisfied only for the cost you wrote [4]. Coverage count (§4 item 2) is the measurement. 6 B. Learning (B1–B5) Policy learns at deployment; reward arrives each step; competence comes from reward-driven trial and error Weights frozen; no reward at deployment; competence from pretraining, lightly steered Offline RL; inverse RL [18]; goal misgeneralization [34] Safe-exploration methods have nothing to modify (B1) [33]; "internalized reward" cannot be tested (B2); reward-based diagnosis misattributes (B3) §5.3 / §8 Rashomon: many rewards fit one behavior [18, 19], as many five-variable regressions fit one data set "within 1.0%" [1, §8]; and one incident fits three formalisms (Rashomon demo, §4 item 3). 7 C. Environment and state (C1–C5) Experimenter builds a simulator; episodes reset; state is physical; nature is the only adversary; single agent Real software and users; single-shot and irreversible; state includes intent; content authors attack; other agents present Sim-to-real [35]; POMDP belief states [36]; robust and adversarial RL [37, 38]; multi-agent RL Expected-cost guarantees are the wrong metric when failures do not amortize (C2); belief over intent is the alignment problem (C3); a threat model is required (C4) §6 "limitations of data models": "some of the problems have stopped looking like nails"; the toolkit "frozen at" CMDP (1999), safe exploration (2012), shielding (2018). Cox's objection sits here: prediction "under quite different conditions from the data" [1, Cox comment]. 8 D. Actions and observations (D1–D3) Fixed small action space with known semantics; no self-report; steering requires retraining Open-ended text and tool calls whose safety depends on context; verbal reasoning traces; steering by prompt Large discrete action spaces; goal-conditioned policies [28] The same action type is safe or catastrophic by context (D1); the steering channel is the attack channel (D3, with A1) §9 Occam: the MDP picture is simple and wrong about frozen text-conditioned agents; the honest picture is messy and right. Breiman: "the goal is not interpretability, but accurate information"; here, not a clean formalism but accurate prediction of failures. Bellman's curse is folded in at D1 and A5 (see Bellman decision below). 9 E. Overseer (E1–E3) Agent does not model the overseer; autonomous after training; one team trains and deploys Agent knows what oversight is and can fake alignment [39]; user co-acts and disables gates; deployer cannot retrain Delusion box [44]; reward tampering via causal influence diagrams; RLHF as a training-time human loop [40] Optimizing against a monitor hides misbehavior (E1) [10]; shields carry a friction cost users remove (E2); safety must be architectural (E3) [41, 12] §7 "a new research community": the behavior-modeling community grew around the overseer: AI control [11], monitoring [10, 27], security patterns [12]. §11 "information from a black box": CoT monitoring extracts intent from the agent black box as permutation importance extracted structure from the forest [1, §11]; Baker et al. show a weaker model can monitor a stronger one [10]. Breiman's "two black boxes, ours slightly less inscrutable than nature's" is literal here: the agent is one, the monitor is another. E1 is the limit: the forest did not know it was being examined. 10 F. Validation (F1–F2) Expected return and expected cost under known R and C; the agent does not model the test Attack success rates, eval pass rates, incident records; the agent can detect evaluation [42] Specification gaming literature [43] Both cultures measure where their instruments reach and are blind in the tail (F1); evals are specifications and inherit Goodhart (F2) §5.4 "predictive accuracy" and the Efron comment: "Prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient" [1, Efron comment]. This is the section that cuts against the behavior culture, and it must be as hard on evals as §5 was on shields.

docs.title: 3.3 Closing (mirrors Breiman §12 and the discussion)
docs.text: # Breiman Two-cultures paper Notes 11 Final remarks: vested interest; return to roots Final remarks: what each culture must borrow See §5 below for the balance. Hoadley's "score engineering" is the recommended hybrid: a behavior-measured agent inside written constraints over the enumerable subset. — Four comments + rejoinder (Cox disagrees, Efron has reservations, Hoadley and Parzen agree) Write the strongest objections in (§5) Statistical Science's discussion format did the steelman for Breiman. A position track will not; the paper must do it itself, which is what the "RL exceptions" column is for.

docs.title: 3.4 Reading the table as the paper
docs.text:
• Rows are claims; sections are row groups. Every body section argues its rows and nothing else. A reviewer who rejects a row rejects a paragraph, not the paper.
  • The "Owner" column sets each section's tone. RL-owned rows (A1, A2, A4, A5, B1, B2, B5, C2, C3, D1, E1) are where the objective-modeling culture is wrong about LLM agents; these carry Breiman's §§5–6 polemic. LLM-owned rows (A3, B4, C1, C4, C5, D2, D3, E2, E3, F2) are where the behavior-modeling culture faces problems RL never had, and where it borrows RL's habit of stating assumptions. "Both" rows (B3, F1) go to the final remarks.
  • The "RL exceptions" column is the built-in rejoinder. Breiman had Cox and Efron to steelman him; a position track has nobody. Each section must engage its exceptions column before stating its consequence.
  • Breiman's named lessons attach to row groups, not sections of their own. No power of goodness-of-fit → A. Rashomon → B. Limitations of the frozen toolkit → C. Occam → D. New community and information from a black box → E. Predictive accuracy and the Efron objection → F.
  • The evidence items of §4 each anchor to rows. Census → §1 population and E (the new community). Coverage count → A5, D1. Rashomon demo → B2, B3, with the three stories drawn from A (misspecified reward), E1 (oversight evasion) and A2 (unauthenticated control plane). Transfer test → every row read as a yes/no precondition; the debunking draft's P1–P6 are A1, A4, A5, B1, C2, E1.

docs.title: 3.5 Bellman decision: cut as a section, keep the curse
docs.text:
Decision. Do not give "dimensionality: curse or blessing" its own section. Fold the curse into rows A5 and D1 (no enumerable unsafe set; the same action type is safe or catastrophic by context). Move the one genuine blessing, chain-of-thought monitoring, to row group E under Breiman's §11 "information from a black box", where the analogy is tight.

Reasoning. The test was: at least two concrete, cited results showing a safety capability with no classical-RL counterpart, and an analogy to Breiman's "more variables, more information" that is tight rather than decorative.

  • CoT monitoring. One concrete result: Baker et al. show CoT monitoring is "far more effective than monitoring agent actions and outputs alone" and that GPT-4o can monitor o3-mini [10]. No classical-RL counterpart: an Atari policy has no legible intent trace. But the same paper shows the channel degrades under optimization pressure, and Korbak et al. is a position statement that calls the opportunity "fragile" and "imperfect", not a result [27]. Count: one result, one position.
  • Instructability (D3). A capability, but it has a counterpart in goal-conditioned RL [28], and it is the same channel as prompt injection (A1, A2). It is not a safety blessing; it is a double-edged control surface.
  • Natural-language constraints. AgentSpec is a DSL of triggers, predicates and enforcement actions over an enumerable rule set, with over 90% prevention on code agents [14]. This is a shield [7] with a nicer front end. It has a classical counterpart by construction.
  • Tightness. Breiman's blessing is that the predictor uses more features and extracts information "in small pieces" [1, §10.1]. The agent-safety blessing is that the overseer reads more output. The roles differ, so the analogy is decorative. Where the analogy is tight is Breiman §11: extracting information about the mechanism from a black box without a data model. CoT monitoring is exactly that, so it moves to E.

Result. One of two required results, counterpart-free; analogy decorative. Cut. The curse side stays as evidence in A5 and D1, and the blessing side becomes two sentences in §9 (row group E).

docs.title: 4. What makes it a paper, not an essay
docs.text:
Breiman had two kinds of evidence: twenty years of accuracy wins (Tables 1–2, Statlog ranks 1,1,1,1) and the hepatitis re-analysis. The two-cultures paper needs its own evidence, or it is an opinion piece. Four candidates, ranked by value per effort:

  1. A measured census (replaces Breiman's 98/2 guess). Build the citation graph of safe-RL and LLM-agent-safety papers from OpenAlex [21] or Semantic Scholar. Measure: do the two literatures cite each other? Cluster the graph and report the cross-cluster citation rate. Count authors who publish in both. Breiman guessed; we count. This is the single most novel contribution and it is cheap. Anchors: §1 population line and row group E (the new community).
  2. A specification-coverage measurement (the "no power" claim made concrete). Take the AI Incident Database [9] entries involving LLM agents, and classify each: could the harm have been written as a cost function or safety automaton before deployment, yes or no, with the rule written out when yes. Report the fraction. This is the analogue of Breiman's seven-dimensional simulation where goodness-of-fit tests "did not reject linearity until the nonlinearity was extreme" [1, §5.2]. Anchors: rows A5 (cost not writable before deployment) and D1 (action safety depends on context); feeds F1.
  3. A Rashomon demonstration. One incident (Replit), three formal stories (misspecified reward; oversight-evading policy; unauthenticated control plane), each internally complete, each prescribing a different remedy. Mirrors Breiman's three five-variable regressions "within 1.0% of each other" [1, §8]. Anchors: rows B2 and B3 (reward not identifiable from behavior); the three stories are drawn from A (misspecified reward), E1 (oversight evasion) and A2 (unauthenticated control plane).
  4. The transfer test, generalized. Lift the precondition checklist from [3, §6] into a general instrument: for any "X is a Y problem" claim, list Y's method preconditions and check them. Used once in [3]; here it becomes the paper's reusable tool, applied to RL → agents and, for symmetry, to security → agents and to evals → agents. Anchors: every row of the table read as a yes/no precondition; the debunking draft's P1–P6 are rows A1, A4, A5, B1, C2, E1.

Items 1 and 2 are measurements made in this work. Item 3 is a worked example. Item 4 is the method.

docs.title: 4a. Results so far, and a pivot in the claim (2026-11-20)
docs.text:
• Census: the split is visible in the citation graph without our labels. Louvain purity 0.92; cross-corpus references 0.13% (A→B) and 0.23% (B→A). Nearly all contact runs through the term "reward hacking". Breiman's 98/2 guess becomes a measurement.
  • Coverage count: a pre-deployment rule could have blocked first-order harm in 86% of 103 LLM-agent incidents (yes 43%, partial 44%). Every no is an attacker-operated agent. The "no power" claim of §4 item 2 is not supported as stated.
  • Operator split and rule kind: deployer-operated incidents (N=64): yes 61%, partial 39%, no 0%. Attacker-operated (N=35): no 40%. Of 89 writable rules, 88 are tool-layer access control (allow/deny-list 78%, approval gate 61%, least privilege 39%, egress/DLP 35%); 1 is a CMDP-style cost over the policy. Gate present but switched off: 16% of incidents.
  • Catalog and combined: over the 70-row catalog (N=66 after vetoes) yes 55% / partial 44% / no 2%; deployer-operated no = 0. Combined AIID + catalog, deduplicated, N=148: yes 46%, partial 45%, no 9%, all 14 no attacker-operated. CMDP-style cost: 1 of 154 writable rules. Robust across two independently assembled sets.
  • The pivot. The writable rules are tool-layer access control, not costs over the agent's objective. So:
    • The objective-modeling culture is right that constraints work, and wrong about where they live: in the tool layer, not in R.
    • The behavior-modeling culture is right that the objective cannot be specified, and wrong if it concludes that nothing can be written.
    • The residual no rule covers is concealment, intent-indistinguishable misuse, and legitimate-looking injected instructions (rows E1, A2, C3).
    • Where rules existed they were disabled or bypassed (row E2). Human factors, not writability, is the binding constraint in the headline cases.
  • Breiman analogue shifts from "goodness-of-fit has no power" (§5.2) to Hoadley's reply: black boxes run in production only inside written constraints that clients, law and drift demand. The paper's recommendation becomes Hoadley's score engineering for agents, with the measured residual as the open problem.
  • Taxonomy mapping, N=70: McLean's three classes fit 53% of incidents, none fits 47%; the class label is unstable under prompt rewording (kappa 0.25) while operational facts are stable (kappa 0.86–0.90). On the cannon unified taxonomy, the response that would have prevented or caught the incident is area 10 runtime control in nearly every case (10.3 safeguards/access restriction 86%, 10.2 monitoring 63%); formal guarantees (11.1) and specification work score 0. RL-native problem areas (3.1, 3.2, 4.2) cover ≤ 20%; injection (4.3) covers 70%.
  • The 15-incident sample has not been human-audited.

docs.title: 5. Where the analogy breaks, and the paper must say so
docs.text:
Breiman wrote from a position of strength: the algorithmic culture was winning on the one metric both cultures accepted. The behavior-modeling culture in agent safety has no such scoreboard. Writing the paper as "RL loses" would be wrong and would be refused by reviewers from the RL side. The honest asymmetries:

  • No shared metric. Breiman could put x down both boxes and compare y. In safety, the quantity of interest is the rate of rare catastrophic events, which neither culture can measure in advance. The paper should say that the behavior culture's "test set" is as weak in the tail as the objective culture's constraints are outside the abstraction.
  • The Efron objection transfers. Efron: "Prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient," and "Numerical experimentation by itself, unguided by theory, is prone to faddish wandering" [1, Efron comment]. For agents: a passed eval has no confidence interval over deployments, and the behavior culture has no theory of when its measurements generalize. The objective culture at least knows what it assumed. Breiman conceded the related point that "'Importance' does not yet have a satisfactory theoretical definition" [1, Rejoinder].
  • The Cox objection transfers. Cox: "Often the prediction is under quite different conditions from the data," and "Better a rough answer to the right question than an exact answer to the wrong question" [1, Cox comment]. Breiman agreed on the first point. For agents, every deployment is prediction under changed conditions. The question "will this agent delete the database" is about a mechanism, and mechanism-free measurement cannot answer the counterfactual. Interpretability is the behavior culture's attempt at mechanism; it is immature.
  • The Hoadley point transfers. Hoadley's credit scorers put "score engineering" constraints on black-box models because clients, law and drift demanded it [1, Hoadley comment]. This is the hybrid the paper should recommend: a behavior-measured agent wrapped in written constraints over the enumerable subset.
  • Evals are specifications too. The behavior culture writes evals; an eval is a specification of what counts as failure. It inherits Goodhart when the agent models the eval [10, 22]. The debunking draft's P6 (the agent models the monitor) cuts against both cultures. This should be stated in the final remarks, not hidden.
  • Breiman's resolution does not fully transfer. Breiman dissolved the Occam dilemma: "the goal is not interpretability, but accurate information" [1, §11]. For safety, accurate information about past behavior is not enough; the goal is a bound on future harm. No black-box method gives one. The paper's final remarks should propose what each culture must borrow: the objective culture must give up the fiction that R is known and adopt measurement; the behavior culture must adopt the objective culture's habit of stating assumptions so that its measurements have a domain of validity.

Recommended stance: Breiman's structure and tone in §§1–11, then a §12 that is more balanced than Breiman's, because the evidence is.

docs.title: 6. Relation to the debunking paper
docs.text: The rebuttal This paper Object one paper [2] a field split Claim formal equivalence is not method transfer the two communities make different founding assumptions and validate differently; neither alone suffices Evidence preconditions stated by the tools' own authors; three incidents census; coverage measurement; Rashomon demo; the transfer test as instrument Tone rebuttal diagnosis

docs.title: 7. Naming the cultures
docs.text:
Breiman named each culture by what it puts inside the box: a data model, or an algorithm. Options here:

Name pair For Against objective-modeling / behavior-modeling mirrors "data modeling / algorithmic modeling"; names the epistemic move "behavior modeling" is a term in psychology specification culture / empirical culture plain "empirical" sounds like a compliment; RL people run experiments too reward culture / observation culture short "reward modeling" collides with Leike et al.; "observation" collides with POMDP vocabulary RL culture / agent culture what people actually say names communities, not moves; invites the "RL is empirical" objection of §2

Recommendation: objective-modeling and behavior-modeling. State in §1 that the names denote moves, not tribes, and that many people make both moves.

docs.title: 8. Follow-ups to Breiman worth citing
docs.text:
Breiman's paper generated a literature on itself. The most useful for this paper:

  • Shmueli, "To Explain or to Predict?" [24]: formalizes the explanation/prediction distinction Breiman left informal. The agent analogue is "to specify or to measure".
  • Donoho, "50 Years of Data Science" [25]: the sociological sequel; the two cultures became one field with a new name. Worth asking whether agent safety will do the same.
  • Efron, "Prediction, Estimation, and Attribution" [26]: Efron's considered 2020 position, two decades after his comment on Breiman; the best source for the "prediction is not enough" objection.
  • The 2021 Observational Studies retrospective issue on Breiman's paper (Observational Studies 7(1), 2021).

docs.title: Related work: "two cultures" framings (for "Agent Safety: The Two Cultures")
docs.text:
Status: STARTED

Not final. Not fully human-reviewed. See the AI-use statement.

Date: 2026-11-20. Method: web search + page fetch + Crossref/arXiv API metadata checks. Every item in Table 1 was opened or resolved by DOI/arXiv ID.

docs.title: Answer first
docs.text:
• No verified paper makes our argument. No source found names an RL/objective-modeling culture vs an LLM-agent/behavior-modeling culture in agent safety, with or without a Breiman/Snow homage.
  • Closest partial pre-emptions: Turner's essay that reward is not the trained agent's optimization target [31]; Çağatan & Zhao, who port RL safety gridworlds to LLM agents and find zero-shot specification gaming [29]; Dantas et al., who find specification is the bottleneck for LLM-agent safety [30]; Vernade et al., who frame RL vs control as communities with distinct "cultures" [20].
  • Existing "two cultures of AI safety" talk is a different split: AI ethics vs AI safety (near-term vs long-term) [25][26][27][28]. [25][26][27] do not cite Snow or Breiman (full-text grep of arXiv HTML: 0 hits). Our split is orthogonal to that one.
  • Caveat: search coverage of LessWrong/Alignment Forum posts and workshop papers is partial. Absence of evidence is not proof.

docs.title: Most relevant works
docs.text:
1. Breiman 2001 [2] - Intro homage and structure. Map: data model -> "assume agent maximizes R"; algorithmic model -> "black box, judged by behavior".
  2. Donoho 2017 [5] - Evals-as-specification. The Common Task Framework is how Culture B defines "correct"; agent evals/red-teaming are its safety analog.
  3. D'Amour 2021 [10] (+ Rudin 2025 [17]) - Evals-as-specification limit. Rashomon/underspecification: an eval suite does not pin down the agent.
  4. Recht 2019 [19] + Vernade et al. 2026 [20] - RL-vs-control mapping. Vernade et al. is the one place "cultures" is used for RL vs control.
  5. Carrington & Stocks 1994 [22] - Related work. Formal methods vs testing is the software-engineering ancestor of shields/CMDPs vs evals.
  6. Pearl 2021 [9] (+ Ogburn & Shpitser 2021 [8]) - Related work / synthesis. Both Breiman cultures are descriptive; neither alone gives intervention guarantees. Parallel: neither assumed-R nor eval scores alone give safety guarantees.
  7. Norvig 2011 [3] - Intro. Precedent for carrying Breiman into AI.
  8. Bristow et al. 2023 [25] / Roytburg & Miller 2025 [26] - Related work. State that our split is not the ethics-vs-safety split.
  9. Pre-emption paragraph: Turner 2022 [31], Çağatan & Zhao 2026 [29], Dantas et al. 2026 [30].
  10. Snow [1]: one sentence in the intro.

docs.title: Agent Safety: The Two Cultures
docs.text:
AI-generated draft

Written by Claude (Anthropic) under Robin Chauhan's direction; not fully human-reviewed. See the AI-use statement.

Two-page draft v0.1, 2026-11-20. Position paper. All incident statistics are model-judged and not human-audited; they are marked [U].

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Breiman [1] divided statistics into a data-modeling culture, which assumes the data are generated by a stated stochastic model, and an algorithmic culture, which treats the mechanism as unknown and judges models by predictive accuracy. Agent safety has the same split. One culture begins "assume the agent maximizes a reward R" and derives safety from that model: constrained MDPs, shields, safe exploration [2, 3, 4]. The other treats the deployed agent as a black box, measures what it does, and bounds harm by architecture. We show the split is real in the citation graph, and we test each culture's founding assumption against two sets of real LLM-agent incidents. The reward-model culture's taxonomy of failures has no slot for about half of the incidents, and the slot it assigns is unstable under rewording while the facts are stable. The behaviour culture's claim that nothing can be specified is also wrong: in every deployer-operated incident a written rule could have blocked the first-order harm. But the rule lives in the tool layer as access control, not in the agent's objective. We draw Hoadley's conclusion from the Breiman discussion [1]: black boxes run in production only inside written constraints at the boundary. The open problem is the measured residual: concealment, legitimate-looking injected instructions, and gates that operators switch off.

docs.title: 1. The same move, twice
docs.text:
Breiman's data-modeling culture is defined by one sentence: "Assume that the data are generated by the following model" [1, §4.1]. He objected that "the conclusions are about the model's mechanism, and not about nature's mechanism" [1, §5]. McLean et al. [5] write an LLM agent as a POMDP, hypothesize that the frozen policy has "internalized" a reward f(o_p, o_g), and conclude that agent failures are instances of RL failure classes. That is the same move. The conclusions are about the reward model's mechanism, not the agent's. We call the two cultures objective-modeling and behavior-modeling, by their move, not their tribe. The mapping runs RL to Breiman's statistics, not to his machine learning, because the move that matters is positing a parametric model of the inside of the box. In robotics RL is the algorithmic culture against control; here it inherits control's assumption that R and the constraint set are given [3, 4].

Table 1 states each culture's assumptions in Breiman's format, with the incident rate at which each assumption fails [U].

Table 1. The two cultures' assumptions. Breiman's four lines, then the assumption rows the incidents break most and least often (share of 70 catalog incidents in which the row is implicated, LLM judge).

Objective-modeling culture Behavior-modeling culture Inside the box an optimizer of a reward R that the designer knows, or that the agent has "internalized" unknown: a pretrained artifact with latent dispositions, lightly steered Opening sentence "Assume the agent maximizes R(s, a)" "We ran the agent against N tasks and attacks and observed" Validation constraint satisfaction, formal guarantee inside a finite abstraction attack success rate, eval pass rate, incident record Instruments constrained MDPs, shields, safe exploration, impact measures red teams, evals, AI control, sandboxes, allow/deny lists Where the hard part goes into the specification of R and the unsafe set into eval coverage and the threat model Assumption Classical-RL default LLM-agent default, and incident share Who sets the objective designer, before training, fixed prompt and tool outputs, at run time: 30% Objective exogenous to observations yes no, instructions and data share one stream: 69% Environment built by the experimenter, benign real software and real users, adversarial: 71% Action space fixed, small, known semantics open-ended text and tool calls: 71% Policy learns at deployment yes no, frozen; steered by prompt instead: 24% / 50% Episodes reset, failures amortize yes single-shot, irreversible: 23% Agent models its overseer no yes: 17% Human in the loop at run time nobody user approves, co-acts, and disables gates: 26% Unsafe set writable before deployment yes claimed no; implicated in only 9% (see §4) Principal's preferences steerable by agent no yes in theory; implicated in 1%

docs.title: 2. The cultures are visible in the citation graph
docs.text:
Breiman guessed 98% and 2%. We measured. From OpenAlex we built a safe-RL corpus (883 works) and an LLM-agent-safety corpus (729 works), 2012–2026 [6].

Safe RL LLM-agent safety References landing in own corpus 8.1% 7.4% References landing in the other corpus 0.13% 0.23% Papers citing the other corpus at all 3.2% 3.6%

Louvain communities on the union graph recover our labels with purity 0.92; the largest community is 346 safe-RL to 2 agent-safety papers, the second 0 to 249. A narrow-query rerun gives zero cross-citations. Nearly all contact runs through one term: 40 of 41 RL-to-agent citations and 15 of 33 agent-to-RL citations go through "reward hacking". Only 6 agent-safety papers cite classical safe RL. The one shared ancestor is Amodei et al. 2016 [7].

docs.title: 3. Testing the objective-modeling culture on incidents
docs.text:
We assembled 70 source-verified LLM-agent incidents (24 deployed harms, 46 exploits of shipped products) [8] and had an LLM judge code each on 24 dimensions drawn from 15 taxonomies, with a reworded second pass for stability [U].

  • McLean et al.'s three classes (reward misspecification, unsafe action in an irreversible state, acting on an insufficient observation) fit 53% of incidents; 47% fit none. Reward misspecification, the flagship class, covers 10%.
  • Of 50 injection-triggered incidents, 28 fit no class and 20 were filed as "insufficient observation". The filing hides that the observation rewrote the objective [9].
  • The class label is unstable: kappa 0.25 between the two prompts, while trigger, gate status and severity are stable at kappa 0.86–0.90. The reworded judge moved five injection cases from "insufficient observation" to "reward misspecification". The class assignment is post hoc, and this is a measurement of it.
  • On a unified AI-safety taxonomy, the RL-native problem areas (reward hacking, side effects, safe exploration) together cover at most 20% of incidents; adversarial inputs and injection cover 70%.

Table 1 shows which assumptions the incidents break. The LLM-side rows dominate; the row the behavior culture leans on hardest, that the unsafe set cannot be written, is implicated in only 9% [U], which anticipates §4. The full 23-row table is in the companion file assumptions_table.md.

docs.title: 4. Testing the behavior-modeling culture on incidents
docs.text:
The behavior culture's strong form says the unsafe set cannot be written before deployment [10, §6]. We asked, for 148 deduplicated incidents from the AI Incident Database and our catalog, whether a designer could have written a concrete, machine-checkable rule in advance that would have blocked the harmful action [U].

Could a pre-deployment rule have blocked first-order harm? All, deduplicated (N=148) Deployer-operated, AIID set (N=64) Deployer-operated, catalog (N=49) Yes 46% 61% 65% Partial (first-order harm blockable, rest not) 45% 39% 35% No 9% 0% 0%

Every "no" is an attacker-operated agent, where no deployer existed to write a rule. So the strong claim is false. But the rules that would have worked are not what the objective culture builds. Of 154 writable rules, 153 are tool-layer access control: allow/deny lists (78%), approval gates (61–75%), least-privilege credentials, egress default-deny, sandboxes. One is a cost over the agent's policy. Both raters placed all 70 catalog incidents under the "control, monitoring, runtime defence" area of the unified taxonomy; none under formal guarantees or specification.

docs.title: 5. What the residual is
docs.text: The partial cases and the disabled gates are the paper's open problem. Concealment is present in 14% of incidents and is fully blockable in 1 of 15 [U]. In 34% a human gate was present and was bypassed by attack or disabled by the operator; the Terraform case ran with permission prompts switched off [11]. Injected instructions that look legitimate are blockable only at the cost of blocking legitimate instructions. These are failures of rows the assumptions table marks as LLM-specific: the objective arrives over the observation channel, the agent models its overseer, the human in the loop removes friction.

docs.title: 6. Where Breiman's argument does and does not transfer
docs.text: Breiman had a shared scoreboard, test-set accuracy. Agent safety has none; rare catastrophic events are where both cultures are weakest. Cox's objection transfers: "often the prediction is under quite different conditions from the data" [1, Cox]. Efron's transfers: "prediction by itself is only occasionally sufficient" [1, Efron]; a passed eval has no confidence interval over deployments, and evals are specifications too [12]. The analogue that holds is Hoadley's. Fair Isaac ran black-box scorecards in production for decades, inside "score engineering" constraints that clients, law and drift demanded [1, Hoadley]. That is what the incident data say about agents: a black box judged by behaviour, wrapped in written access control at the boundary. The objective culture is right that constraints work and wrong about where they live. The behavior culture is right that the objective cannot be specified and wrong if it concludes nothing can be written.

docs.title: 7. Related work
docs.text: No prior paper sets these two cultures against each other. The nearest are Turner's argument that RL policies need not maximize reward [13], Çağatan and Zhao's port of the RL safety gridworlds to LLM agents, where specification gaming appears without task training [14], and Dantas et al.'s survey finding specification to be the bottleneck while never mentioning safe RL [15]. The ethics-versus-safety binary in AI is already discussed as a pair of cultures [16]; ours is orthogonal to it. Breiman's own sequels supply the tools we borrow: Shmueli's explain-or-predict distinction [17], Donoho's Common Task Framework as the predictive culture's engine [12], and the Rashomon-set literature, which says an eval suite does not pin down the model behind it [18]. Three agent-incident databases predate our catalog [8]; we add the trigger, gate-status and assumption-row fields and the measurements built on them.

docs.title: 8. Conclusion
docs.text: Two cultures, a measured gap, and one bridge named "reward hacking". The reward-model picture does not describe deployed incidents and its class labels do not survive rewording. Tool-layer rules would have blocked first-order harm in every deployer-operated case, and almost none of those rules is a cost function. The paper's recommendation is Hoadley's: engineer the boundary, measure the box, and treat the residual, concealment, legitimate-looking injection, and switched-off gates, as the research problem neither culture owns.

Breiman [1] guessed that 98% of statisticians were in the data-modeling culture and 2% in the algorithmic one. This census replaces a guess of the same kind for agent safety with counts.
